stem: A 68-year-old male suffers an acute ischemic stroke involving the right Frontal Eye Field (FEF) in the precentral gyrus. On physical examination, toward which side will the patient's eyes preferentially deviate at rest?

options.A: Toward the side of the lesion and away from the hemiplegia
options.B: Away from the side of the lesion and toward the hemiplegia
options.C: Pure upward vertical deviation toward the superior orbital rim
options.D: Fixed bilateral inward convergence toward the nasal midline
options.E: Rapid downbeat vertical nystagmus with conjugate oscillopsia

explanation: The frontal eye field (FEF), located in the posterior portion of the middle frontal gyrus / precentral cortex (Brodmann area 8), generates voluntary horizontal conjugate saccades to the contralateral side by projecting across the midline to the contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF). An acute destructive stroke involving the right FEF abolishes the drive to look leftward. Unopposed input from the intact left FEF drives horizontal gaze toward the right side. Consequently, at rest, the patient's eyes preferentially deviate TOWARD the side of the hemispheric cortical lesion (to the right) and AWAY from the side of contralateral hemiplegia.
high_yield_pearl: Destructive cortical FEF lesions cause conjugate eye deviation TOWARD the lesion (away from the hemiplegia); pontine PPRF lesions cause deviation AWAY from the lesion.

stem: An investigator conducts an experiment evaluating descending motor control in non-human primates. A localized stereotactic lesion is made in the red nucleus of the midbrain. The physiological changes in muscle tone and posture are subsequently measured. Which descending pathway is directly disrupted by this lesion, and what is its primary physiological role in modulating motor function?

options.A: Reticulospinal tract; facilitation of axial extensor muscle tone
options.B: Rubrospinal tract; suppression of stretch reflexes and modulation of flexor tone
options.C: Lateral corticospinal tract; execution of fine motor movements of the distal digits
options.D: Anterior corticospinal tract; bilateral innervation of axial trunk musculature
options.E: Vestibulospinal tract; maintenance of posture against gravity

explanation: Upper motor neurons that modulate movement originate in the cortex and brainstem nuclei (e.g., red nucleus giving rise to the rubrospinal tract, reticular formation giving rise to reticulospinal tracts). These brainstem descending pathways act alongside corticospinal projections to suppress the monosynaptic stretch reflex circuit and reduce resting muscle tone. Interruption removes descending inhibition, contributing to hyperreflexia and spasticity. Option (A) misattributes reticulospinal origin to the red nucleus; Option (C) describes lateral corticospinal tract; Option (D) describes anterior corticospinal tract; Option (E) describes vestibulospinal tract from vestibular nuclei.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Rubrospinal tract; suppression of stretch reflexes and modulation of flexor tone

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with a Horner syndrome on the right side. The clinician considers potential lesion sites along the three-neuron sympathetic chain. Which of the following lesions can cause an ipsilateral Horner syndrome?

options.A: Lateral medullary stroke causing ipsilateral Horner and contralateral pain loss
options.B: Superior pulmonary sulcus tumor invading the brachial plexus and thoracic outlet
options.C: Internal carotid artery dissection causing ipsilateral periorbital neck pain
options.D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis causing multilesional extraocular ophthalmoplegia
options.E: Stylomastoid foramen peripheral facial nerve trauma causing facial paralysis

explanation: Lateral medullary infarction (Wallenberg syndrome) is classically caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). The infarct damages the uncrossed descending hypothalamospinal tract in the lateral medullary tegmentum, producing an ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Simultaneously, it interrupts the adjacent anterolateral spinothalamic tract, resulting in loss of pain and temperature sensation over the CONTRALATERAL body. This crossed sensory finding combined with ipsilateral Horner syndrome localizes the lesion unequivocally to the brainstem.
high_yield_pearl: Lateral medullary stroke (Wallenberg) causes ipsilateral Horner syndrome alongside contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and extremities.

stem: A 38-year-old female with a history of hypertension presents with an acute stroke involving the caudal pons on the left side, destroying the left abducens nucleus. How does a lesion of the left abducens nucleus differ clinically from an isolated lesion of the left abducens nerve root?

options.A: Abducens nucleus lesion causes horizontal gaze palsy; nerve root lesion causes isolated abduction failure
options.B: Abducens nucleus lesion causes upward vertical gaze palsy; nerve root lesion causes lateral gaze palsy
options.C: Abducens nucleus lesion spares extraocular movements; nerve root lesion causes complete ophthalmoplegia
options.D: Abducens nucleus lesion causes contralateral eyelid ptosis; nerve root lesion causes miosis and anhidrosis
options.E: Abducens nucleus lesion causes bilateral pupillary mydriasis; nerve root lesion spares all pupillary responses

explanation: The abducens nucleus in the caudal pons contains two distinct populations of neurons: 1) lower motor neurons that project directly via the exiting CN VI nerve root to the ipsilateral lateral rectus, and 2) internuclear interneurons whose axons decussate and ascend within the contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to innervate the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus of CN III. Therefore, a lesion of the abducens NUCLEUS causes a complete conjugate horizontal gaze palsy toward the side of the lesion (neither eye can look ipsilaterally). In contrast, a lesion of the exiting abducens NERVE ROOT affects only the peripheral motor axons to the lateral rectus, resulting in isolated failure of ipsilateral abduction with preserved contralateral adduction.
high_yield_pearl: An abducens nucleus lesion causes a conjugate horizontal gaze palsy; an abducens nerve root lesion causes isolated ipsilateral abduction failure.

stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with a visual field defect caused by an aneurysm compressing the uncrossed fibers on the lateral aspect of the optic chiasm on the right side. What visual field loss occurs from damaging these uncrossed temporal retinal fibers on the right?

options.A: Loss of the nasal visual field in the right eye
options.B: Loss of the temporal visual field in the right eye
options.C: Loss of the temporal visual field in both eyes
options.D: Total blindness in the left eye
options.E: Right upper quadrantanopia

explanation: Uncrossed fibers on the lateral aspect of the optic chiasm originate from the temporal hemiretina of the ipsilateral (right) eye. The temporal hemiretina receives light from the nasal visual field of that same eye. Damage to right lateral chiasm uncrossed fibers causes loss of the nasal visual field in the right eye. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) misidentify pathway laterality and fields.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Loss of the nasal visual field in the right eye

stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the clinic due to sudden onset of mild vertigo, nausea, and unsteady gait. Neurological exam reveals dysmetria on left arm movement, horizontal nystagmus that beats to the left and does NOT suppress with visual fixation, and no hearing loss. MRI confirms a small cerebellar stroke. Which of the following features best distinguishes central vertigo from peripheral vertigo?

options.A: Presence of visual suppression of nystagmus in central vertigo
options.B: Association with low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in central vertigo
options.C: Non-fatigable nystagmus and presence of additional central neurological signs
options.D: Complete resolution of vertigo within 30 seconds of head position change
options.E: Positive Dix-Hallpike test with a latency of 10 seconds

explanation: Central vertigo features non-fatigable, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, absence of visual suppression, and central brainstem/cerebellar signs (dysmetria, ataxia). Peripheral vertigo features fatigable nystagmus, latency, and visual suppression. Option (A) occurs in peripheral vertigo; Option (B) occurs in peripheral Ménière disease; Option (D) describes peripheral BPPV; Option (E) describes peripheral BPPV.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Non-fatigable nystagmus and presence of additional central neurological signs
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 29-year-old woman is evaluated for hearing loss in her left ear. A Rinne test is performed using a 512 Hz tuning fork: bone conduction is heard longer and louder than air conduction when placed on the left mastoid process (negative Rinne). When the tuning fork is placed on the midline forehead (Weber test), the sound is heard loudest in the left ear. What type of hearing loss is present in the left ear, and what is a classic middle ear cause?

options.A: Sensorineural hearing loss; presbycusis
options.B: Conductive hearing loss; otosclerosis
options.C: Sensorineural hearing loss; vestibular schwannoma
options.D: Conductive hearing loss; labyrinthitis
options.E: Central auditory processing loss; cortical stroke

explanation: Negative Rinne on the left (Bone Conduction > Air Conduction) indicates conductive hearing loss in the left ear because bone vibration bypasses middle ear mechanical obstruction. Weber lateralizes to the affected (left) ear. Otosclerosis (stapes footplate fixation) is a classic cause of conductive hearing loss in young adults. Option (A) causes positive Rinne; Option (C) causes sensorineural loss; Option (D) causes sensorineural loss; Option (E) is central.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Conductive hearing loss; otosclerosis
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 52-year-old accountant suffers an ischemic stroke involving the caudal pons on the left side. Examination reveals an inability to abduct the left eye. Additionally, the patient exhibits weakness of both the upper and lower facial muscles on the left side, including an inability to close the left eye or wrinkle the left forehead. Which combination of neural structures in the caudal pons is involved in this patient's lesion?

options.A: Left abducens nucleus and left facial nerve motor nucleus/fibers
options.B: Left oculomotor nucleus and right corticobulbar tract
options.C: Left trochlear nucleus and left facial motor nucleus
options.D: Right abducens nucleus and left corticospinal tract
options.E: Left Edinger-Westphal nucleus and left trigeminal motor nucleus

explanation: The caudal pons houses the motor nucleus of CN VI (abducens) and the motor nucleus of CN VII (facial). Exiting facial nerve fibers loop around the abducens nucleus forming the facial colliculus. A lesion in the left caudal pons damages the left abducens nucleus/nerve (inability to abduct the left eye) and left facial motor nucleus/nerve (total, lower motor neuron paralysis of ipsilateral upper and lower facial muscles). Option (B) involves midbrain CN III; Option (C) involves midbrain CN IV; Option (D) involves right side; Option (E) involves Edinger-Westphal in midbrain.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left abducens nucleus and left facial nerve motor nucleus/fibers

stem: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency clinic following a motor vehicle collision. Neurological examination reveals complete loss of voluntary movement, loss of pain and temperature sensation below the level of the T10 dermatome, and preserved fine touch, vibration, and proprioception bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities are initially absent but become hyperactive four weeks later with bilateral clonus. Which of the following arterial territories was most likely compromised in this patient?

options.A: Brown-Séquard syndrome involving unilateral spinal cord hemisection
options.B: Anterior spinal artery syndrome causing bilateral ventral cord ischemia
options.C: Central cord syndrome affecting crossing spinothalamic commissural fibers
options.D: Tabes dorsalis causing bilateral demyelination of posterior dorsal columns
options.E: Subacute combined degeneration affecting dorsal and lateral columns

explanation: The anterior spinal artery (ASA) supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the lateral corticospinal tracts, anterolateral system (spinothalamic tracts), and ventral horns bilaterally. ASA occlusion causes Anterior Cord Syndrome, resulting in bilateral motor paralysis and bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion level, with complete preservation of the dorsal columns (fine touch, vibration, proprioception) supplied by posterior spinal arteries. Option (A) causes Posterior Cord Syndrome; Option (C) produces internal capsule hemiplegia; Option (D) causes lateral medullary syndrome; Option (E) causes contralateral leg weakness without anterior cord syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterior spinal artery

stem: A 42-year-old male presents with difficulty walking down stairs. He reports that when looking down at the steps, he experiences vertical diplopia. To compensate and eliminate the double vision, he tilts his head away from the affected side (head tilt to the left). Physical examination demonstrates weakness of depression when the right eye is in an adducted position. Which cranial nerve is injured?

options.A: Right oculomotor nerve exiting the interpeduncular fossa
options.B: Right trochlear nerve exiting the dorsal midbrain tegmentum
options.C: Right abducens nerve exiting the pontomedullary junction
options.D: Left trochlear nerve exiting the dorsal midbrain tegmentum
options.E: Right trigeminal nerve exiting the mid-pontine tegmentum

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the superior oblique muscle, which depresses, intorts, and abducts the eye; its depressive action is greatest when the eye is in an adducted position. Patients with a trochlear nerve palsy experience vertical diplopia that is most pronounced when looking down and inward (e.g., reading a book or walking downstairs). To eliminate the diplopia, patients characteristically tilt their head AWAY from the affected side (contralateral head tilt, here tilting to the left for a right CN IV palsy), which minimizes the need for intorsion by the paralyzed superior oblique muscle.
high_yield_pearl: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy causes vertical diplopia when walking downstairs and a compensatory head tilt AWAY from the affected side.

stem: An investigator traces the reflex loop for the pupillary light reflex. Light shone into the retina stimulates retinal ganglion cell axons that travel via the optic nerve, optic chiasm, and optic tract. Where do these reflex fibers bypass the LGN to synapse in the rostral midbrain?

options.A: Superior colliculus brachium projecting to the pretectal nucleus
options.B: Inferior colliculus brachium projecting to the medial geniculate nucleus
options.C: Paramedian pontine reticular formation projecting to the abducens nucleus
options.D: Hypothalamic projection fibers entering the ciliospinal center
options.E: Red nucleus rubrospinal projections entering the rostral spinal cord

explanation: In the pupillary light reflex, visual sensory axons originating from retinal ganglion cells travel through the optic nerve, optic chiasm, and optic tract. Before reaching the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), the reflex fibers leave the optic tract via the brachium of the superior colliculus to synapse in the pretectal nucleus of the rostral midbrain. Interneurons from each pretectal nucleus then project bilaterally to both the ipsilateral and contralateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei (crossing fibers traverse the posterior commissure), establishing the anatomical basis for the consensual light reflex.
high_yield_pearl: Afferent pupillary light reflex fibers bypass the LGN and travel via the brachium of the superior colliculus to synapse in the pretectal nucleus.

stem: A 70-year-old male with a history of dream enactment behavior (REM sleep behavior disorder) presents with a rest tremor and bradykinesia. Which neurodegenerative disease entity is strongly associated with REM sleep behavior disorder?

options.A: Huntington disease with trinucleotide CAG repeat expansion
options.B: Lewy body disease with pathological alpha-synuclein aggregation
options.C: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with superoxide dismutase mutation
options.D: Multiple sclerosis with oligoclonal immunoglobulin bands in CSF
options.E: Alzheimer dementia with hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles

explanation: REM sleep behavior disorder (loss of REM muscle atonia with dream enactment) is strongly associated with neurodegenerative alpha-synucleinopathies, including Parkinson disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) are not alpha-synucleinopathies.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Lewy body disease / Parkinson disease
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 50-year-old female presents with a lesion interrupting the posterior commissure in the dorsal midbrain. Which ocular movement pathway is specifically disrupted by damaging crossing fibers in the posterior commissure?

options.A: Horizontal conjugate gaze pathway mediated by the PPRF and MLF
options.B: Vertical conjugate gaze pathway coordinated by the pretectal area
options.C: Oculosympathetic pupillary dilation pathway through the reticular formation
options.D: Primary auditory transmission pathway through the lateral lemniscus
options.E: Lateral vestibulospinal tract modulating lower extremity extensor tone

explanation: The posterior commissure is a vital cross-linking tract located in the dorsal midbrain tegmentum immediately rostral to the superior colliculus. It carries decussating fibers essential for vertical conjugate gaze (linking the bilateral rostral interstitial nuclei of the MLF and the interstitial nuclei of Cajal) as well as consensual pupillary light reflex fibers linking pretectal neurons to contralateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei. Interruption of the posterior commissure selectively disrupts vertical conjugate gaze (particularly upward vertical gaze, as seen in Parinaud syndrome) while leaving horizontal gaze completely intact.
high_yield_pearl: The posterior commissure coordinates vertical conjugate gaze; its disruption selectively paralyzes upward gaze while sparing horizontal gaze.

stem: A neuroanatomy student examines a cross-section of the thalamus. The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) is identified as the thalamic relay center for vision. LGN neurons receive third-order axons from retinal ganglion cells via the optic tract and project fourth-order axons to the primary visual cortex via which fiber bundle?

options.A: Lateral lemniscus auditory transmission pathway
options.B: Geniculocalcarine optic radiation projection pathway
options.C: Medial longitudinal fasciculus conjugate gaze tract
options.D: Internal capsule anterior limb frontopontine tract
options.E: Trapezoid body decussating auditory relay fibers

explanation: Fourth-order neurons in the LGN project axons via the optic radiations (geniculocalcarine tract)—divided into temporal Meyer's loop and parietal dorsal loop—through the subcortical white matter to the primary visual cortex (V1) surrounding the calcarine sulcus. Lateral lemniscus (A) is auditory; MLF (C) coordinates eye movements; Internal capsule anterior limb (D) carries frontopontine fibers; Trapezoid body (E) decussates auditory fibers.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Optic radiations (geniculocalcarine tract)

stem: A 24-year-old medical student participates in a sleep physiology study. Electroencephalogram (EEG) electrodes are placed on her scalp while she lies comfortably in a quiet, dark room with her eyes closed, remaining relaxed but awake. Which of the following EEG wave patterns will predominate during this relaxed, awake state with eyes closed?

options.A: High-frequency, low-voltage desynchronized beta waves
options.B: Synchronized regular sinusoidal alpha waves
options.C: Low-voltage, mixed-frequency irregular theta waves
options.D: Stage two sleep spindles and prominent K-complexes
options.E: High-voltage, slow synchronized delta waves

explanation: EEG frequency rhythms depend on arousal state. Awake, alert, active concentration displays beta waves (>13 Hz). Awake, relaxed state with eyes closed displays synchronized alpha waves (8–12 Hz), predominantly over occipital/parietal lobes. Option (A) occurs with eyes open/alert concentration; Option (C) occurs in N1 sleep; Option (D) occurs in N2 sleep; Option (E) occurs in N3 slow-wave sleep.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Synchronized alpha waves (8–12 Hz)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 52-year-old male with a history of recurrent middle ear infections presents with progressive, painless conductive hearing loss in his left ear. Otoscopic exam reveals a pearly-white mass behind the tympanic membrane with erosion of the incus. What is a serious intracranial complication of an untreated, expanding cholesteatoma?

options.A: Temporal lobe or epidural abscess secondary to tegmental bone erosion
options.B: Cavernous sinus thrombosis secondary to facial venous thrombophlebitis
options.C: Pituitary apoplexy secondary to intrasellar ischemic hemorrhage
options.D: Subclavian steal syndrome secondary to proximal subclavian stenosis
options.E: Carotid-cavernous fistula secondary to basal skull trauma

explanation: Expanding cholesteatomas release lytic enzymes that erode surrounding bone. Superior erosion through the roof of the middle ear cavity (tegmen tympani) allows infection to spread into the middle cranial fossa, causing temporal lobe abscess, epidural abscess, or meningitis. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) do not occur from temporal bone erosion.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Temporal lobe abscess or epidural abscess due to erosion of the tegmental bone
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 22-year-old patient presents to the emergency department following an acute overdose of an over-the-counter medication. The patient complains of high-pitched ringing in both ears (tinnitus) and nausea. Which of the following ototoxic substances was most likely ingested?

options.A: Salicylates such as high-dose aspirin
options.B: Macrolides such as erythromycin base
options.C: Penicillins such as oral amoxicillin
options.D: Cephalosporins such as cephalexin
options.E: Antifungals such as fluconazole

explanation: High-dose salicylates (aspirin) cause reversible high-pitched tinnitus and mild sensorineural hearing loss by inhibiting outer hair cell motor function (prestin) and altering cochlear blood flow. Salicylates also stimulate medullary respiratory centers. Option (B) causes hepatotoxicity; Option (C) causes anticholinergic signs; Option (D) causes nephrotoxicity/ulcers; Option (E) causes pseudotumor cerebri.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Salicylates (Aspirin)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 61-year-old female presents with balance impairment. Neurological examination reveals lower extremity hyperreflexia (3+ patellar, 3+ Achilles), velocity-dependent spasticity in both legs, and bilateral ankle clonus. Plantar response shows upgoing toes bilaterally. Upper extremity reflexes and strength are entirely normal. A lesion at which level of the neuraxis best accounts for these findings?

options.A: Thoracic spinal cord lateral corticospinal tracts bilaterally
options.B: Cervical spinal cord anterior horn cells
options.C: Caudal medulla pyramids bilaterally
options.D: Bilateral precentral gyrus arm motor representation
options.E: Peripheral nerves of the lumbosacral plexus

explanation: Bilateral lower extremity hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, spasticity, and extensor plantar responses represent upper motor neuron deficits isolated to both legs. Normal upper extremity strength and reflexes exclude lesions in the cervical cord, brainstem, or cerebral hemispheres. Thus, the lesion is in the thoracic spinal cord lateral corticospinal tracts bilaterally (below cervical enlargement, above lumbar enlargement). Option (B) causes LMN arm weakness; Option (C) causes spastic quadriplegia involving arms and legs; Option (D) affects arms; Option (E) causes LMN leg flaccidity.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Thoracic spinal cord lateral corticospinal tracts bilaterally

stem: An investigator studies the neurochemical control of circadian rhythms. Neurons in the master circadian pacemaker respond to light signals transmitted directly from melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells via the retinohypothalamic tract. What is the location of this primary circadian pacemaker in the brain?

options.A: Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus
options.B: Suprachiasmatic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus
options.C: Lateral hypothalamic area containing orexinergic neurons
options.D: Arcuate nucleus regulating adenohypophyseal secretion
options.E: Mammillary bodies projecting through the mammillothalamic tract

explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the anterior hypothalamus above the optic chiasm is the master circadian pacemaker. Melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) project via the retinohypothalamic tract to entrain the SCN to external light-dark cycles. Option (A) is the sleep-promoting GABA center; Option (C) contains orexin neurons; Option (D) produces dopamine; Option (E) secretes melatonin downstream of SCN signals.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 30-year-old male medical resident undergoes EEG testing during a call shift. While actively working on a complex patient chart, his EEG shows low-voltage, high-frequency beta waves (>13 Hz). What state of arousal is characterized by beta wave activity?

options.A: Deep slow-wave N3 sleep with delta rhythms
options.B: Awake, alert mental concentration with beta rhythms
options.C: Drowsy, relaxed eyes-closed rest with alpha rhythms
options.D: Light stage N1 sleep with vertex sharp waves
options.E: Stage N2 sleep with sleep spindles and K-complexes

explanation: Beta waves (>13 Hz, low-voltage) define an awake, alert state with active mental concentration or eyes open. Alpha waves (8–12 Hz) define relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed. Theta waves (4–7 Hz) define N1 sleep. Delta waves (<4 Hz) define N3 deep sleep. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misidentify EEG wave correlations.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Awake, alert, and active mental concentration
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 35-year-old female complains of daytime fatigue. A full-night sleep study is performed. The report describes sleep architecture metrics. Which sleep stage is characterized by slow delta waves on EEG, represents the deepest restorative sleep, and features the lowest levels of blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration?

options.A: Stage 3 NREM
options.B: Stage 1 NREM
options.C: Stage 2 NREM
options.D: REM sleep
options.E: Awake state

explanation: Stage 3 NREM (slow-wave sleep) is characterized by slow delta waves on EEG, represents the deepest restorative sleep, features peak growth hormone secretion, and exhibits lowest baseline blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) do not define slow-wave deep sleep.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Stage 3 NREM
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 68-year-old male is brought to the neurology clinic by his wife. She reports that for the past two years, her husband has been violently flailing his arms, punching, and kicking in his sleep, often shouting at imaginary intruders. Last week, he accidentally struck his wife while dreaming that he was defending himself. Polysomnography reveals loss of normal somatic muscle atonia during REM sleep. What neurological condition is strongly associated with the long-term development of this parasomnia (REM sleep behavior disorder)?

options.A: Huntington chorea with caudate nucleus atrophy
options.B: Lewy body disease with alpha-synuclein inclusions
options.C: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with motor neuron loss
options.D: Multiple sclerosis with periventricular demyelination
options.E: Alzheimer dementia with cortical amyloid plaques

explanation: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) involves loss of normal somatic muscle atonia during REM sleep, causing patients to physically act out dreams. RBD is a major prodromal biomarker for alpha-synucleinopathies, specifically Parkinson disease, Dementia with Lewy Bodies, and Multiple System Atrophy. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) are not primary alpha-synucleinopathies associated with RBD.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Lewy body disease / Parkinson disease
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: An investigator analyzes visual acuity across the retina. Why does the fovea centralis achieve the highest visual acuity in the retina?

options.A: High concentration of rods with massive convergence onto single ganglion cells
options.B: Exclusively cones with one-to-one wiring to bipolar cells and pushed aside layers
options.C: Dense network of overlying retinal capillaries providing intense aerobic perfusion
options.D: High concentration of melanopsin ganglion cells driving circadian photoentrainment
options.E: Thick overlying extracellular gelatinous matrix containing mineralized statoconia

explanation: Maximum visual acuity at the fovea centralis is achieved because it contains exclusively cone photoreceptors tightly packed with a 1:1 synaptic ratio to bipolar and ganglion cells (no spatial convergence) and overlying neural layers/capillaries are displaced laterally to minimize light scattering. Rods (A) convergence lowers acuity; Capillaries (C) scatter light; ipRGCs (D) mediate circadian lighting; Otoliths (E) are vestibular.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Exclusively cone photoreceptors with 1:1 wiring to bipolar and ganglion cells and minimal overlying cell layers

stem: A 70-year-old male presents with an acute stroke. Physical examination shows left-sided spastic body hemiplegia, left-sided lower face droop, and tongue deviation to the left on protrusion. Forehead wrinkling is intact bilaterally. No sensory loss is identified. Which specific vascular structure was most likely occluded?

options.A: Left middle cerebral artery cortical branches supplying the insular cortex
options.B: Right middle cerebral artery lenticulostriate arteries supplying internal capsule
options.C: Right anterior cerebral artery branches supplying medial paracentral lobule
options.D: Basilar artery paramedian penetrating branches supplying the pontine base
options.E: Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplying lateral medullary tegmentum

explanation: Penetrating lenticulostriate branches of the right MCA supply the posterior limb and genu of the right internal capsule. Ischemia interrupts uncrossed corticospinal fibers (causing left-sided body spastic hemiplegia) and corticobulbar fibers (causing left lower facial droop and left tongue deviation upon protrusion), with upper forehead sparing. Option (A) causes right-sided body/face weakness; Option (C) causes bilateral paraplegia; Option (D) causes lateral medullary syndrome; Option (E) causes contralateral leg weakness.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right middle cerebral artery (penetrating lenticulostriate branches)

stem: A 62-year-old male presents with sudden onset of vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, and left-sided Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Neurological exam shows loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of his face and right side of his body. Hearing is completely normal. An ischemic stroke involving the lateral medulla (Wallenberg syndrome) is diagnosed. Which artery was occluded?

options.A: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
options.B: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
options.C: Middle cerebral artery (MCA)
options.D: Internal carotid artery (ICA)
options.E: Anterior spinal artery (ASA)

explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) results from occlusion of PICA, supplying the dorsolateral medulla. Damaged structures include vestibular nuclei (vertigo, nystagmus), nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia, hoarseness, palatal droop), sympathetic fibers (ipsilateral Horner syndrome), spinal trigeminal nucleus (ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss), and anterolateral system (contralateral body pain/temp loss). Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) do not cause lateral medullary syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 22-year-old medical resident evaluates extraocular muscle innervation. Which extraocular muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (CN IV), and what is its primary physiological action when the eye is adducted?

options.A: Lateral rectus muscle causing horizontal abduction of the eye
options.B: Superior oblique muscle causing depression when adducted and intorsion
options.C: Inferior oblique muscle causing elevation when adducted and extorsion
options.D: Medial rectus muscle causing horizontal adduction of the eye
options.E: Superior rectus muscle causing elevation when abducted and intorsion

explanation: Extraocular motor innervation follows the classic mnemonic SO4 LR6 EE3 (Superior Oblique by CN IV, Lateral Rectus by CN VI, and Everyone Else by CN III). The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates exclusively the superior oblique muscle. Because the tendon of the superior oblique passes through the fibrous trochlea before inserting on the posterolateral sclera, its primary actions are intorsion (internal rotation) and depression of the eye when it is in an adducted (turned inward) position.
high_yield_pearl: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates exclusively the superior oblique muscle, which depresses the adducted eye and intorts the globe.

stem: An anatomical study traces the geniculocalcarine tract. Axons forming the dorsal loop of optic radiations pass through which cerebral lobe on their way to the cuneus gyrus?

options.A: Temporal lobe
options.B: Parietal lobe
options.C: Frontal lobe
options.D: Insular lobe
options.E: Limbic lobe

explanation: The geniculocalcarine tract (optic radiations) divides into two bundles: the superior optic radiations (dorsal loop) travel through the parietal lobe to the cuneus gyrus, while the inferior optic radiations (Meyer loop) travel through the temporal lobe to the lingual gyrus. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misidentify the lobe for dorsal loop fibers.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Parietal lobe

stem: A 52-year-old patient undergoes an ocular examination. The clinician evaluates aqueous humor flow. Aqueous humor passes from the posterior chamber into the anterior chamber through which opening?

options.A: Pupil opening between the iris margins
options.B: Canal of Schlemm at the iridocorneal angle
options.C: Optic disc where ganglion cell axons exit
options.D: Cornea transmitting anterior incident light
options.E: Fovea centralis containing cone receptors

explanation: Aqueous humor is secreted by the ciliary body into the posterior chamber, flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and drains via the trabecular meshwork into the Canal of Schlemm. Canal of Schlemm (B) drains fluid out of the anterior chamber; Optic disc (C), cornea (D), and fovea (E) do not form the flow aperture between posterior and anterior chambers.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Pupil

stem: A 35-year-old male with narcolepsy is prescribed modafinil to treat severe daytime sleepiness. What is the primary mechanism of action of modafinil in promoting wakefulness?

options.A: Direct agonist at GABAA receptor chloride channels
options.B: Non-amphetamine wake-promoting agent that enhances wakefulness centers
options.C: Antagonist at MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors
options.D: Irreversible inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase
options.E: Selective histamine H1 receptor antagonist

explanation: Modafinil is a first-line non-amphetamine wake-promoting agent used in narcolepsy to treat excessive daytime sleepiness by modulating wake-promoting brain centers and monoamine dynamics. Option (A) describes GABAA hypnotics; Option (C) describes ramelteon antagonists; Option (D) describes cholinesterase inhibitors; Option (E) describes antihistamines.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Non-amphetamine wake-promoting agent that enhances wakefulness centers
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with hyperopia (farsightedness). Refractive evaluation shows that light rays entering the eye are focused behind the retina when viewing near objects. What structural problem causes hyperopia?

options.A: Eye axial length too short
options.B: Eye axial length too long
options.C: Corneal curvature irregularity
options.D: Lens opacity from denatured proteins
options.E: Failure of the optic fissure to close

explanation: Hyperopia (farsightedness) occurs when the axial length of the eyeball is structurally too short relative to its refractive power, causing light rays from nearby objects to focus behind the retina. Eye too long (B) causes myopia; Corneal irregularity (C) causes astigmatism; Lens opacity (D) causes cataracts; Optic fissure defect (E) causes coloboma.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Eye axial length too short

stem: A 30-year-old female presents with anisocoria (unequal pupil sizes). In room light, her left pupil is larger than her right pupil. When the room lights are dimmed, the degree of anisocoria increases significantly (the right pupil fails to dilate in darkness). Which autonomic pathway is impaired, and in which eye?

options.A: Parasympathetic defect in the left eye where anisocoria increases in bright light
options.B: Sympathetic defect in the right eye where anisocoria increases in dim darkness
options.C: Parasympathetic defect in the right eye where anisocoria increases in darkness
options.D: Sympathetic defect in the left eye where anisocoria increases in bright light
options.E: Bilateral complete transection of ascending optic nerve sensory projections

explanation: Evaluation of anisocoria (asymmetric pupil size) requires comparing the pupil sizes in both bright light and dim darkness. When anisocoria is GREATER IN BRIGHT LIGHT, the abnormal pupil is the larger one because it fails to constrict appropriately, indicating an impaired parasympathetic pupillomotor pathway (e.g., CN III compression or Adie tonic pupil). Conversely, when anisocoria is GREATER IN DIM DARKNESS, the abnormal pupil is the smaller one because it fails to dilate in the dark, indicating an impaired sympathetic pathway (Horner syndrome). Here, the left pupil is larger in room light, and if anisocoria worsens in light, the lesion is a left parasympathetic defect.
high_yield_pearl: Anisocoria greater in bright light indicates a parasympathetic defect in the larger pupil; anisocoria greater in dim darkness indicates a sympathetic defect in the smaller pupil.

stem: An anatomical study evaluates the dorsal midbrain. The superior colliculi are identified on the tectal plate. What is the primary physiological function of the superior colliculi in response to visual stimuli?

options.A: Transduction of high-frequency acoustic pitch
options.B: Direct relay of visual signals to the medial geniculate nucleus
options.C: Coordination of head and eye turning reflexes toward visual stimuli
options.D: Secretion of aqueous humor into the posterior chamber
options.E: Processing of complex speech syntax

explanation: The superior colliculi in the rostral midbrain tectum receive visual projections and mediate visual reflexes, specifically coordinating reflex head and eye movement orienting toward visual stimuli in the environment. Inferior colliculi (A, E) mediate auditory reflexes. MGN (B) is thalamic. Ciliary body (D) secretes fluid.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Coordination of head and eye turning reflexes toward visual stimuli

stem: A clinician performs a pupillary examination on a patient with a left CN III palsy. When light is shone into the healthy right eye, what pattern of pupillary response will be observed?

options.A: Direct right pupil constriction and absent consensual left pupil constriction
options.B: Absent direct right pupil constriction and intact consensual left pupil constriction
options.C: Complete absence of pupillary constriction in both pupils upon illumination
options.D: Prompt direct and consensual pupillary constriction in both pupils bilaterally
options.E: Active pupillary dilation mediated by dilatator pupillae in the right eye

explanation: The patient has a left oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy, which damages the efferent parasympathetic fibers supplying the left sphincter pupillae muscle. When light is shone into the healthy right eye, the afferent signal travels normally through the right optic nerve (CN II) to both pretectal nuclei and bilaterally to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. The right oculomotor nerve (CN III) is intact, so the right pupil constricts promptly (intact direct response). However, the left oculomotor nerve is injured, so parasympathetic motor impulses cannot reach the left sphincter pupillae, resulting in absent left pupil constriction (absent consensual response).
high_yield_pearl: In a unilateral efferent CN III lesion, light in the contralateral healthy eye elicits an intact direct response but an absent consensual response in the paretic eye.

stem: A 50-year-old male cancer patient undergoing chemotherapy with high-dose cisplatin reports new-onset bilateral ringing in his ears (tinnitus) and difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds. Which of the following drug classes is also well-recognized for its ototoxic potential targeting cochlear hair cells?

options.A: Macrolide antibiotics such as azithromycin and clarithromycin
options.B: Aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin and tobramycin
options.C: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin
options.D: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as ceftriaxone and ampicillin
options.E: Tetracycline antibiotics such as doxycycline and minocycline

explanation: Ototoxic drugs damage cochlear hair cells and vestibular sensory epithelia, causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo. Major ototoxic classes include aminoglycoside antibiotics, platinum chemotherapeutics (cisplatin), loop diuretics (furosemide), and salicylates. Option (A) is non-ototoxic; Option (C) is non-ototoxic; Option (D) is non-ototoxic; Option (E) is non-ototoxic.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 56-year-old female presents with difficulty chewing. Examination reveals that when she opens her jaw, it deviates to the right. Left-sided jaw opening is normal. Facial sensation to light touch and pinprick is completely normal across all three trigeminal divisions on both sides of the face. Corneal reflexes are present bilaterally. What is the location of the lesion?

options.A: Left trigeminal motor nucleus
options.B: Right trigeminal motor nucleus or nerve root
options.C: Left precentral gyrus motor cortex
options.D: Right corticobulbar tract in the genu of the internal capsule
options.E: Nucleus ambiguus on the right side

explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle opens the jaw and protrudes it toward the opposite side. An LMN lesion of the right trigeminal motor nucleus or nerve root (CN V) in the mid-pons weakens the right lateral pterygoid, causing the jaw to deviate toward the weak/lesioned side (right) upon opening. Intact facial sensation confirms an isolated motor root/nucleus lesion. Option (A) causes jaw deviation to the left; Option (C) and (D) do not cause functional jaw deviation due to bilateral corticobulbar input; Option (E) affects soft palate.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right trigeminal motor nucleus or nerve root

stem: A 52-year-old obese male with a history of hypertension presents with excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, and loud, irregular snoring punctuated by gasping episodes during the night reported by his wife. Polysomnography demonstrates recurrent collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep, resulting in respiratory apneas and arterial desaturations. What is the primary first-line treatment for this patient's condition (Obstructive Sleep Apnea)?

options.A: Modafinil wakefulness-promoting therapy at morning awakening
options.B: Nocturnal continuous positive airway pressure via nasal mask
options.C: Oral zolpidem non-benzodiazepine hypnotic therapy at bedtime
options.D: Permanent tracheostomy bypass surgery below the cricoid ring
options.E: Bilateral transcutaneous phrenic nerve pacemaker stimulation

explanation: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) involves recurrent pharyngeal airway collapse during sleep, producing apneas, oxyhemoglobin desaturations, and daytime fatigue. First-line therapy is Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP), which acts as a pneumatic splint to hold the pharyngeal airway open. Option (A) does not fix mechanical airway collapse; Option (C) sedatives worsen OSA; Option (D) is reserved for life-threatening refractory cases; Option (E) is for central sleep apnea.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 60-year-old male with chronic insomnia is prescribed ramelteon. What is the primary mechanism of action of ramelteon?

options.A: Agonist at central melatonin receptors
options.B: Positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors
options.C: Antagonist at orexin receptors
options.D: Antagonist at histamine H1 receptors
options.E: Inhibitor of monoamine oxidase

explanation: Ramelteon is a selective agonist at MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, mimicking endogenous melatonin to facilitate sleep onset. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) misdescribe its mechanism.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Agonist at central melatonin receptors
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with progressive difficulty maintaining an upright head position. Examination reveals weakness in cervical neck muscles. Axons of the medial vestibulospinal tract (MVST), which project bilaterally down the cervical spinal cord to control head position, originate from which vestibular nucleus?

options.A: Lateral vestibular nucleus
options.B: Medial vestibular nucleus
options.C: Superior vestibular nucleus
options.D: Inferior vestibular nucleus
options.E: Edinger-Westphal nucleus

explanation: The medial vestibulospinal tract (MVST) originates in the medial vestibular nucleus and descends bilaterally through the MLF into the cervical spinal cord to innervate neck muscles, controlling head position. Option (A) gives rise to LVST; Option (C) projects to extraocular nuclei; Option (D) integrates cerebellar inputs; Option (E) provides parasympathetic pupillary control.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Medial vestibular nucleus
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 59-year-old male presents following a localized stroke in the brainstem. On physical examination, he demonstrates weakness of the left lateral rectus muscle, causing medial deviation of the left eye at rest. He also presents with total paralysis of the left facial muscles, involving both the upper forehead and lower mouth. Which brainstem level is damaged?

options.A: Rostral midbrain
options.B: Caudal midbrain
options.C: Mid-pons
options.D: Caudal pons
options.E: Rostral medulla

explanation: The caudal pons houses the abducens nucleus (CN VI) and facial motor nucleus (CN VII). A left caudal pontine lesion injures left CN VI (inability to abduct left eye, medial deviation at rest) and left CN VII (total LMN facial paralysis involving upper forehead and lower mouth). Option (A) houses CN III; Option (B) houses CN IV; Option (C) houses CN V motor nucleus; Option (E) houses CN XII and nucleus ambiguus.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Caudal pons

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents because he frequently walks around the house during the middle of the night without waking up. Polysomnography confirms that these sleepwalking episodes (somnambulism) occur during the deepest, restorative phase of slow-wave sleep. Which EEG wave pattern defines this specific sleep stage (N3)?

options.A: High-frequency, low-voltage beta rhythms
options.B: Synchronized regular posterior alpha rhythms
options.C: Variable low-amplitude irregular theta rhythms
options.D: High-amplitude, synchronized slow delta rhythms
options.E: Sawtooth waves with rapid conjugate eye movements

explanation: N3 (Stage 3 NREM), or slow-wave sleep (SWS), is defined on EEG by low-frequency, high-voltage delta waves (<4 Hz). N3 is the deepest restorative sleep stage, featuring lowest heart rate/blood pressure and peak growth hormone release. NREM parasomnias—somnambulism (sleepwalking), night terrors, and nocturnal enuresis—occur during N3 sleep. Option (A) defines beta waves; Option (B) defines alpha rhythm; Option (C) defines N2 sleep; Option (E) defines REM sleep.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Low-frequency, high-voltage delta waves (<4 Hz)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 22-year-old female experiences brief paralysis upon falling asleep accompanied by terrifying dream-like visions. She is fully conscious during the episode but unable to move her arms or legs. What term describes the loss of voluntary motor movement on waking or falling asleep?

options.A: Sleep paralysis
options.B: Cataplexy
options.C: Somnambulism
options.D: Night terror
options.E: Bruxism

explanation: Sleep paralysis is the transient inability to perform voluntary movements or speak while falling asleep (hypnagogic) or awakening (hypnopompic), caused by persistent REM sleep muscle atonia during conscious wakefulness. Option (B) is emotion-triggered tone loss; Option (C) is sleepwalking; Option (D) is N3 terror awakening; Option (E) is teeth grinding.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Sleep paralysis
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 62-year-old male presents with an ischemic stroke in the territory of the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) involving both the cuneus and lingual gyri of the left occipital lobe, but sparing the occipital pole due to collateral MCA blood flow. What visual field defect is present?

options.A: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
options.B: Complete right homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Right upper quadrantanopia without macular sparing
options.E: Monocular blindness in left eye

explanation: An ischemic stroke destroying both the cuneus and lingual gyri of the left primary visual cortex interrupts processing for the entire contralateral (right) visual hemifield, producing a right homonymous hemianopia. Because the occipital pole (macular cortex) receives dual blood supply and is spared by collateral MCA flow, macular vision is preserved (macular sparing). Option (B) lacks macular collateral flow; Option (C) involves chiasm; Option (D) involves lingual gyrus only; Option (E) involves optic nerve.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

stem: A 30-year-old man presents for a sleep evaluation. Polysomnography demonstrates normal sleep architecture. An investigator measures neurochemical factors that promote wakefulness. Which lateral hypothalamic neuropeptide promotes wakefulness by inhibiting neurons of the VLPO?

options.A: Orexin lateral hypothalamic neuropeptide
options.B: Melatonin pineal gland indolamine hormone
options.C: Gamma-aminobutyric acid neurotransmitter
options.D: Leptin adipose-derived satiety hormone
options.E: Oxytocin paraventricular nonapeptide hormone

explanation: Orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus promote wakefulness and stabilize arousal by inhibiting sleep-promoting neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO). Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) do not function as the hypothalamic wake-stabilizing neuropeptide.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Orexin (hypocretin)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 75-year-old male presents with a 2-day history of difficulty swallowing and a nasal voice. Examination shows absent movement of the soft palate on the right side when he says "Ah," causing the uvula to pull toward the left. The gag reflex is absent on the right. When he is asked to turn his head to the left, strength in the right sternocleidomastoid muscle is normal. Tongue extension is in the midline. Where is the lesion located?

options.A: Right nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla
options.B: Left hypoglossal nucleus in the rostral medulla
options.C: Right spinal accessory nucleus in the cervical cord
options.D: Left trigeminal motor nucleus in the mid-pons
options.E: Bilateral facial motor nuclei in the caudal pons

explanation: The nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla houses LMN cell bodies for CN IX and X, innervating soft palate and pharyngeal muscles. A right nucleus ambiguus lesion causes right soft palate weakness and drooping. Upon saying "Ah," the intact left levator veli palatini contracts, pulling the uvula toward the healthy (left) side, away from the lesion. Right gag reflex is lost. Intact SCM and tongue extension confirm isolated nucleus ambiguus damage. Option (B) causes tongue deviation; Option (C) causes shoulder/neck weakness; Option (D) causes jaw deviation; Option (E) causes facial diplegia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla

stem: An investigator traces the sympathetic pathway for pupillary dilation. Preganglionic sympathetic axons exit the spinal cord via ventral roots at C8–T2 and enter the sympathetic chain via which structures?

options.A: Gray rami communicantes distributed at all spinal cord levels
options.B: White rami communicantes restricted to spinal levels T1 through L2
options.C: Dorsal sensory roots entering the posterior horn of the spinal cord
options.D: Long ciliary nerves traversing the posterior sclera into the choroid
options.E: Chorda tympani nerve traveling through the infratemporal fossa

explanation: Second-order preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies are located in the intermediolateral (IML) cell column of the spinal cord from C8 to T2 (ciliospinal center of Budge). The myelinated preganglionic sympathetic axons exit the spinal cord via ventral motor roots and enter the sympathetic paravertebral chain exclusively through white rami communicantes, which are anatomically restricted to thoracic and upper lumbar spinal segments (T1–L2). They then ascend through the cervical sympathetic chain without synapsing until they reach the superior cervical ganglion.
high_yield_pearl: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers exit the spinal cord and enter the sympathetic chain exclusively via white rami communicantes (T1–L2).

stem: A clinician performs the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) test on a comatose patient by rapidly rotating the patient's head to the left side (doll's eye maneuver). In a patient with an intact brainstem, both eyes smoothly deviate toward the right to maintain visual fixation. Which brainstem fiber tract links the vestibular nuclei to the contralateral abducens nucleus and ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus to coordinate this reflex eye movement?

options.A: Lateral lemniscus auditory tract in the brainstem
options.B: Medial longitudinal fasciculus connecting gaze nuclei
options.C: Medial lemniscus ascending epicritic pathway in medulla
options.D: Corticospinal tract descending in the cerebral peduncles
options.E: Spinothalamic tract carrying pain and thermal signals

explanation: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) maintains visual fixation during head rotation. Head turn to the left stimulates the left vestibular nucleus, which sends decussating fibers ascending via the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the right abducens nucleus (CN VI) and contralateral oculomotor nucleus (CN III) to coordinate compensatory eye movements. Option (A) is auditory; Option (C) is decussating auditory bundle; Option (D) carries rubro-olivary fibers; Option (E) carries voluntary motor drive.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with visual field loss. Testing shows complete blindness in the left eye (left monocular anopia), while the right eye's visual field is completely normal. Where is the lesion located?

options.A: Left optic nerve
options.B: Optic chiasm
options.C: Right optic tract
options.D: Left temporal lobe
options.E: Right visual cortex

explanation: Complete loss of vision restricted to one eye (left monocular anopia) indicates a lesion anterior to the optic chiasm in the left eye or left optic nerve. Lesions at or posterior to the optic chiasm produce visual field defects affecting both eyes simultaneously. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) cause binocular visual field defects.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left optic nerve

stem: An investigator traces projections from the Frontal Eye Fields (FEF). The FEFs generate voluntary rapid eye movements to explore the visual environment. What type of conjugate eye movement is driven by the FEFs?

options.A: Conjugate horizontal saccadic eye movements exploring the visual field
options.B: Smooth pursuit conjugate eye movements tracking a slowly moving target
options.C: Vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilizing retinal images during head rotations
options.D: Accommodation vergence adjusting focal depth for nearby visual targets
options.E: Optokinetic nystagmus slow phase maintaining continuity of visual scenes

explanation: The frontal eye fields (FEF, Brodmann area 8) in the posterior middle frontal gyrus are the primary cortical control centers for voluntary SACCADIC eye movements—rapid, ballistic conjugate movements that quickly shift the fovea to new objects of interest in the visual field. In contrast, SMOOTH PURSUIT eye movements (slow tracking of moving objects) are controlled by the parietal-occipital-temporal association cortex, while the VOR is mediated by the vestibular nuclei and flocculonodular lobe.
high_yield_pearl: The frontal eye fields (FEF) drive voluntary rapid saccadic eye movements, whereas parieto-occipital cortex mediates smooth pursuit.

stem: A 52-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of progressive, left-sided hearing loss, subtle imbalance when walking, and constant high-pitched tinnitus in his left ear. Physical examination reveals a positive Rinne test bilaterally (AC > BC) and a Weber test that lateralizes to the right ear. Neurological exam shows mild sensory loss to light touch over the left cheek (CN V1/V2 distribution) and subtle left lower facial weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals a 2.5 cm enhancing mass located in the left cerebellopontine angle. What cell type gives rise to this tumor?

options.A: Oligodendrocytes
options.B: Schwann cells
options.C: Astrocytes
options.D: Ependymal cells
options.E: Microglial cells

explanation: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) arises from Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA). Expanding tumors compress CN VIII (sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance), CN VII (facial weakness), and CN V (facial numbness). Option (A) myelinates CNS; Option (C) forms astrocytomas; Option (D) lines ventricles; Option (E) represents CNS macrophages.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Schwann cells
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with unstable gait and frequent falls. Neurological examination reveals bilateral lower extremity spasticity, hyperreflexia at the knees and ankles, and bilateral upgoing plantar reflexes. The examiner suspects damage to descending upper motor neuron pathways. Which of the following statements accurately characterizes the anatomical trajectory of the lateral corticospinal tract?

options.A: Axons originate in precentral gyrus, decussate in anterior commissure, and descend in ventral funiculus
options.B: Axons originate in postcentral gyrus, decussate in ventral midbrain peduncles, and descend in dorsal funiculus
options.C: Axons originate in primary motor cortex, decussate in medullary pyramids, and descend in lateral funiculus
options.D: Axons originate in pontine reticular formation, decussate in rostral pons, and descend in dorsal funiculus
options.E: Axons originate in ventral spinal gray horn, decussate in caudal medulla, and ascend in lateral funiculus

explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract originates from pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus), descends through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, forms the crus cerebri in the midbrain, passes through the basilar pons, and forms the medullary pyramids. Approximately 90% of these fibers cross the midline in the medullary pyramids (pyramidal decussation) to descend in the contralateral lateral funiculus of the spinal cord. Option (A) describes anterior corticospinal fibers; Option (B) mislocates origin and decussation; Option (D) describes reticulospinal tracts; Option (E) describes primary sensory/peripheral neurons.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Axons originate in the motor cortex, descend through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, decussate in the medullary pyramids, and descend in the lateral funiculus

stem: A 28-year-old patient complaining of difficulty falling asleep is prescribed zaleplon. How does zaleplon differ pharmacokinetically from zolpidem and eszopiclone?

options.A: Ultra-short elimination half-life that avoids next-day sedation
options.B: Irreversible 24-hour blockade of hypothalamic orexin receptors
options.C: Marked respiratory depression via non-selective barbiturate action
options.D: Long-acting prodrug requiring sequential renal tubular conversion
options.E: Selective stimulation of tuberomammillary histamine neurotransmission

explanation: Zaleplon is a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic with an ultrashort elimination half-life (~1 hour), allowing rapid sleep initiation without morning hangover effects or next-day psychomotor impairment. Option (B) describes suvorexant; Option (C) is false for Z-drugs; Option (D) is false; Option (E) is false.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: It has an extremely short elimination half-life, making it useful for sleep-onset insomnia without next-day grogginess
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 29-year-old female presents with weakness in turning her head. Examination demonstrates that she cannot turn her head to the right against resistance, and her left shoulder droops with 3/5 strength in left shoulder elevation. Strength in the right shoulder and right head turning is normal. Tongue extension is in the midline. Where is the primary lesion?

options.A: Left spinal accessory nucleus and peripheral motor nerve fibers
options.B: Left hypoglossal motor nucleus in the floor of the fourth ventricle
options.C: Right corticobulbar tract in the posterior limb of internal capsule
options.D: Right primary motor cortex within the precentral motor homunculus
options.E: Left ambiguus nucleus in the lateral medullary reticular formation

explanation: Lower motor neurons of CN XI innervate the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and trapezius. The left SCM turns the head to the right, and the left trapezius elevates the left shoulder. Damage to the left spinal accessory motor nucleus/nerve causes LMN weakness of the left trapezius (impaired left shoulder shrug) and left SCM (inability to turn head to the right against resistance). Option (B) impairs right shoulder shrug and head turning to the left; Option (C) causes complex/bilateral mild UMN effects; Option (D) causes tongue deviation; Option (E) causes uvular deviation.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left spinal accessory motor nucleus / nerve (CN XI)

stem: A 32-year-old male presents with severe pain and discharge from his right ear after swimming in a lake. Otoscopic exam reveals an erythematous, edematous right external auditory canal with purulent exudate; the tympanic membrane is partially obscured but intact. A Weber tuning fork test at 512 Hz lateralizes to the right ear. A Rinne test on the right ear shows bone conduction is greater than air conduction (negative test). Which pathogen is the most common cause of this condition (otitis externa)?

options.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.B: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Haemophilus influenzae
options.D: Moraxella catarrhalis
options.E: Epstein-Barr virus

explanation: Acute otitis externa ("Swimmer's ear") presents with ear canal pain, edema, erythema, purulent discharge, and conductive hearing loss (Weber to affected ear, negative Rinne). Excess water breakdown of cerumen allows bacterial infection, most commonly caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (followed by S. aureus). Option (A) causes otitis media; Option (C) causes otitis media; Option (D) causes otitis media; Option (E) causes mononucleosis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 24-year-old patient presents with double vision when looking down and inward. Examination shows a trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy on the left side. Where do trochlear nerve axons exit the brainstem before decussating?

options.A: Ventral surface of the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles
options.B: Dorsal surface of the midbrain caudal to the inferior colliculi
options.C: Lateral pontomedullary junction adjacent to the flocculus
options.D: Ventral medullary surface between the pyramid and olive
options.E: Pretectal region of the thalamus adjacent to the pineal gland

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) possesses two unique neuroanatomical distinctions among all twelve cranial nerves: 1) it is the ONLY cranial nerve that exits from the DORSAL (posterior) surface of the brainstem (emerging just caudal to the inferior colliculi of the midbrain), and 2) its fibers completely decussate within the superior medullary velum before exiting, meaning the left trochlear nucleus gives rise to the right trochlear nerve. Because of its long intracranial course around the midbrain tegmentum to reach the cavernous sinus, it is particularly susceptible to traumatic shearing injury during head collisions.
high_yield_pearl: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve that exits from the dorsal brainstem and decussates completely before exiting.

stem: A 30-year-old musician presents with hyperacusis (extreme sensitivity to everyday sounds), reporting that ordinary noises sound painfully loud in his left ear. Physical examination reveals an inability to wrinkle his left forehead, close his left eye, or smile on the left side. Which middle ear muscle is paralyzed in this patient, and which cranial nerve provides its innervation?

options.A: Tensor tympani muscle; trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
options.B: Stapedius muscle; facial nerve (CN VII)
options.C: Tensor veli palatini muscle; glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
options.D: Stapedius muscle; oculomotor nerve (CN III)
options.E: Tensor tympani muscle; vagus nerve (CN X)

explanation: The stapedius muscle is innervated by the stapedial branch of CN VII. It dampens stapes movement at the oval window. Facial nerve palsy (Bell palsy) paralyzes the stapedius, causing hyperacusis (ordinary sounds feel painful). Tensor tympani is innervated by CN V3. Option (A) misidentifies the muscle in facial palsy; Option (C) opens Eustachian tube; Option (D) misidentifies nerve; Option (E) misidentifies nerve.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Stapedius muscle; facial nerve (CN VII)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 58-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on chronic hemodialysis complains of an uncomfortable, creeping sensation deep in both legs whenever he lies down to sleep in the evening. The uncomfortable sensation is temporarily relieved by getting out of bed and walking around, but returns as soon as he rests, causing severe sleep disruption. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates serum ferritin of 15 ng/mL (iron deficiency). What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Obstructive sleep apnea with pharyngeal airway collapse
options.B: Narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy and orexin deficiency
options.C: Restless legs syndrome with uncomfortable leg sensations at rest
options.D: REM sleep behavior disorder with loss of motor atonia
options.E: Sleep terror parasomnia arising from slow-wave sleep

explanation: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) presents with an irresistible urge to move the legs accompanied by deep crawling dysesthesias, worsening during rest/evening, and temporarily relieved by movement. It is strongly associated with iron deficiency (low serum ferritin) and renal disease. Option (A) involves acting out dreams during REM; Option (B) involves upper airway apneas; Option (D) involves daytime sleepiness without cataplexy; Option (E) involves involuntary leg jerks during sleep.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Restless legs syndrome (RLS)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 48-year-old male with a history of malnutrition presents with night blindness (nyctalopia) and dry eyes. Deficiency of which essential vitamin impairs the synthesis of rhodopsin and cone opsins in photoreceptors?

options.A: Vitamin A
options.B: Vitamin B12
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Vitamin D
options.E: Vitamin K

explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) is the precursor for 11-cis-retinal, the essential chromophore bound to opsins forming rhodopsin (in rods) and cone opsins (in cones). Vitamin A deficiency impairs rhodopsin synthesis, causing night blindness (nyctalopia) and xerophthalmia. Vitamin B12 (B) causes subacute combined degeneration; Vitamin C (C) causes scurvy; Vitamin D (D) causes rickets; Vitamin K (E) causes coagulopathy.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Vitamin A

stem: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated during a full-night polysomnogram. The sleep technologist notes that the patient experiences cyclical transitions between NREM and REM sleep throughout the night. Approximately how long is a normal, complete NREM-to-REM sleep cycle in a healthy adult?

options.A: 15 to 20 minutes
options.B: 30 to 45 minutes
options.C: 90 to 110 minutes
options.D: 180 to 200 minutes
options.E: 300 minutes

explanation: Normal human sleep architecture cycles between NREM stages and REM sleep in regular intervals lasting approximately 90 to 110 minutes throughout the night. Options (A), (B), (D), and (E) do not represent the standard adult sleep cycle duration.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: 90 to 110 minutes
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 62-year-old male presents with difficulty speaking and swallowing. Examination reveals tongue atrophy and prominent fasciculations across the tongue surface. When asked to extend his tongue, it deviates to the left. The patient also exhibits hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (3+) in all four extremities and an upgoing plantar reflex on the right foot. Sensory exam is completely normal. Which disease process involves simultaneous degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons?

options.A: Decussation of the pyramids in the caudal medulla
options.B: Anterior white commissure in the cervical spinal cord
options.C: Dorsal midbrain tegmentum at the interpeduncular fossa
options.D: Posterior limb of the internal capsule in the forebrain
options.E: Corona radiata within the subcortical cerebral white matter

explanation: ALS is characterized by simultaneous degeneration of UMNs (motor cortex Betz cells, lateral corticospinal tracts) and LMNs (cranial motor nuclei V, VII, IX, X, XII, and spinal anterior horns). Tongue atrophy and fasciculations with deviation (LMN) occurring alongside hyperreflexia, spasticity, and Babinski signs (UMN) without sensory loss is pathognomonic for ALS. Option (A) is a CNS demyelinating disease; Option (C) is posterior column syphilis; Option (D) is acute demyelinating polyneuropathy; Option (E) causes cape-like pain/temperature loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with an eyelid problem. Physical examination demonstrates mild drooping of the right upper eyelid (ptosis). The examiner determines that the ptosis is caused by loss of sympathetic tone to smooth muscle fibers within the upper eyelid. What is the name of this smooth muscle?

options.A: Levator palpebrae superioris muscle innervated by the oculomotor nerve
options.B: Superior tarsal muscle innervated by postganglionic sympathetic fibers
options.C: Orbicularis oculi muscle innervated by the peripheral facial nerve
options.D: Superior rectus muscle innervated by the somatic oculomotor nerve
options.E: Inferior oblique muscle innervated by the somatic oculomotor nerve

explanation: Eyelid elevation is mediated by two separate muscles: 1) the levator palpebrae superioris (a skeletal muscle innervated by CN III somatic motor fibers, providing primary lid elevation), and 2) the superior tarsal muscle (Müller's muscle, a smooth muscle innervated by postganglionic oculosympathetic fibers, providing resting lid tone). In Horner syndrome, loss of sympathetic innervation to the superior tarsal muscle results in mild to moderate upper eyelid drooping (partial ptosis). In contrast, CN III palsy causes complete, severe ptosis because the primary elevator (levator palpebrae superioris) is paralyzed.
high_yield_pearl: Partial ptosis in Horner syndrome is caused by loss of sympathetic tone to the superior tarsal (Müller) muscle, whereas complete ptosis in CN III palsy involves levator palpebrae superioris.

stem: An emergency physician evaluates a comatose trauma patient. Shining a penlight into the patient's right eye fails to elicit pupillary constriction in either the right eye (absent direct response) or left eye (absent consensual response). However, when the penlight is shone into the left eye, both the left pupil (intact direct response) and right pupil (intact consensual response) constrict promptly. Where is the anatomical lesion located?

options.A: Left optic nerve anterior to the optic chiasm
options.B: Right optic nerve anterior to the optic chiasm
options.C: Right oculomotor nerve exiting the midbrain
options.D: Left Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the rostral midbrain
options.E: Posterior commissure in the dorsal pretectal tegmentum

explanation: The pupillary light reflex consists of an afferent sensory limb carried by the optic nerve (CN II) to the pretectal nuclei, and bilateral efferent parasympathetic limbs carried by the oculomotor nerves (CN III) from the Edinger-Westphal nuclei to the sphincter pupillae muscles via the ciliary ganglion. Shining light into the right eye produces no pupillary constriction in either eye (absent direct and consensual responses), indicating an afferent sensory defect in the right eye. Shining light into the left eye produces prompt, bilateral pupillary constriction (intact direct and consensual responses), confirming that both efferent CN III limbs and the left afferent CN II limb are intact. Therefore, the lesion localizes to the right optic nerve.
high_yield_pearl: An isolated afferent pupillary defect produces bilateral absent pupillary responses when light is shone into the affected eye, but normal bilateral responses when light is shone into the intact eye.

stem: A 32-year-old construction worker suffers a traumatic spinal cord injury resulting in complete transection of the lateral spinal cord on the right side at the T8 vertebral level. Physical examination two weeks post-injury demonstrates motor deficits. Which of the following motor exam findings will be present below the level of the lesion on the right side?

options.A: Flaccid paralysis with rapid, severe muscle atrophy
options.B: Spastic hemiplegia with hyperreflexia and Babinski sign
options.C: Fasciculations with absent deep tendon reflexes
options.D: Complete absence of voluntary movement with intact, normal plantar flexor response
options.E: Loss of deep tendon reflexes with normal muscle tone

explanation: Hemisection of the spinal cord at T8 interrupts the descending lateral corticospinal tract on the ipsilateral side below the pyramidal decussation. Because fibers have already decussated in the medulla, interruption of the corticospinal tract in the thoracic cord produces ipsilateral upper motor neuron signs below the level of the lesion (spasticity, hyperactive reflexes, upgoing Babinski sign). Option (A) describes LMN damage at the exact segment level; Option (C) represents LMN degeneration; Option (D) incorrectly assumes a flexor plantar response; Option (E) describes LMN hyporeflexia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Spastic hemiplegia with hyperreflexia and Babinski sign

stem: A 75-year-old female is evaluated for memory decline and poor sleep quality. Polysomnography demonstrates a dramatic age-related reduction in the total duration of slow-wave sleep (N3 stage). Which physiological process is primarily impaired when N3 slow-wave sleep is significantly reduced?

options.A: Execution of rapid eye movement ocular saccades
options.B: Deep tissue restoration and peak growth hormone release
options.C: Consolidation of emotional nightmares
options.D: Generation of nocturnal penile/clitoral tumescence
options.E: Maintenance of skeletal muscle tone during dreaming

explanation: N3 slow-wave sleep is restorative: peak growth hormone release occurs during early N3 sleep to facilitate tissue repair and protein synthesis, and metabolic/sympathetic activity reaches its nadir. Aging decreases N3 duration. Option (A) is REM; Option (C) is REM; Option (D) is REM; Option (E) is REM.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Deep tissue restoration and peak growth hormone release
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 52-year-old male smoker presents with right-sided drooping of the upper eyelid (ptosis), a constricted right pupil (miosis), and complete absence of sweating over the right side of his face (anhidrosis). Chest radiography reveals a mass in the apex of the right lung (Pancoast tumor). Compression of which autonomic structure accounts for this patient's Horner syndrome?

options.A: Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.B: Sympathetic trunk and superior cervical ganglion at the lung apex
options.C: Ciliary ganglion located within the posterior orbital cavity
