options.D: Cavernous sinus parasympathetic plexus surrounding CN III
options.E: Paramedian pontine reticular formation in the caudal pons

explanation: A superior pulmonary sulcus tumor (Pancoast tumor) originates in the apex of the lung and frequently invades contiguous neurovascular structures at the thoracic outlet, including the cervical sympathetic chain and the stellate / inferior cervical ganglion. Disruption of preganglionic sympathetic fibers ascending from the T1 intermediolateral cell column produces Horner syndrome, characterized by the classic triad of partial ptosis (loss of superior tarsal muscle tone), miosis (unopposed parasympathetic sphincter pupillae activity), and facial anhidrosis (loss of sympathetic innervation to eccrine sweat glands).
high_yield_pearl: Pancoast tumors at the lung apex compress the sympathetic trunk and stellate ganglion, causing ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

stem: A 22-year-old patient presents with diplopia. Examination shows that when looking to the right, the right eye abducts normally, but the left eye fails to adduct. Convergence during accommodation is completely normal. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a demyelinating MLF lesion
options.B: Left oculomotor nerve palsy from compressive posterior vascular aneurysm
options.C: Left abducens nerve palsy from microvascular ischemic pontine stroke
options.D: Right frontal eye field stroke from middle cerebral artery infarction
options.E: Parinaud dorsal midbrain syndrome from pineal gland compression

explanation: On attempted rightward horizontal gaze, the left eye fails to adduct past the midline, while the right eye abducts normally with horizontal nystagmus. Normal convergence during accommodation proves that the left medial rectus muscle and left oculomotor nucleus are completely functional. This selective adduction deficit on conjugate horizontal gaze with preserved convergence localizes the lesion to the LEFT medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), defining a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). In a 22-year-old patient, multiple sclerosis is the most common etiology.
high_yield_pearl: Adduction failure on contralateral horizontal gaze with abducting nystagmus and preserved convergence defines internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) on the side of the adduction deficit.

stem: An anatomical study reviews the cavernous sinus. Which of the following groups of cranial nerves and associated vascular structures passes through or within the cavernous sinus?

options.A: CN III, CN IV, CN V1, CN V2, and CN VI along with the internal carotid artery
options.B: CN III, CN IV, CN V3, and CN VII along with the middle meningeal artery
options.C: CN II, CN III, CN IV, and CN VI along with the ophthalmic artery
options.D: CN IX, CN X, CN XI, and CN XII along with the internal jugular vein
options.E: CN V1, CN V2, CN V3, and CN VII along with the facial venous plexus

explanation: The cavernous sinus is a trabeculated dural venous sinus situated on either side of the sella turcica. Traversing its lateral dural wall from superior to inferior are the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), and maxillary nerve (CN V2). Running freely through the central venous lumen, surrounded by venous blood and situated immediately adjacent to the internal carotid artery, is the abducens nerve (CN VI). The mandibular nerve (CN V3) does NOT pass through the cavernous sinus; it exits the middle cranial fossa directly via the foramen ovale.
high_yield_pearl: Structures in the cavernous sinus: CN III, IV, V1, V2 in the lateral wall; CN VI and internal carotid artery in the central venous lumen. CN V3 does NOT pass through.

stem: An investigator measures action potential generation in retinal cells. Which retinal cell layer contains the first order neurons that fire action potentials along their central processes to form the optic nerve?

options.A: Photoreceptor cells
options.B: Bipolar cells
options.C: Retinal ganglion cells
options.D: Horizontal cells
options.E: Amacrine cells

explanation: Retinal ganglion cells are 3rd order sensory neurons in the visual pathway. Unlike photoreceptors (1st order) and bipolar cells (2nd order)—which communicate via graded electrotonic potentials—retinal ganglion cells generate true action potentials that travel along their central axons forming the optic nerve, chiasm, and tract to the LGN. Options (A), (B), (D), and (E) do not form the optic nerve.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Retinal ganglion cells

stem: A 36-year-old female presents with brief, recurrent episodes of vertigo when turning her head to the left while lying in bed. A Dix-Hallpike test is performed, producing transient horizontal-rotatory nystagmus. The patient is successfully treated with an Epley maneuver. What is the underlying physical mechanism of the Epley maneuver?

options.A: Dissolving calcium carbonate crystals using topical acid drops
options.B: Mechanically repositioning dislodged otoconia out of the semicircular canal into the utricle
options.C: Ablating the vestibular ganglion using focused gamma radiation
options.D: Depleting endolymphatic fluid pressure via a surgical shunt
options.E: Suppressing neurotransmitter release in the cochlear nucleus

explanation: The Epley maneuver uses gravity through sequential head rotations to roll free-floating otoconia out of the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle, relieving BPPV. Option (A) is incorrect; Option (C) is for tumors; Option (D) is for Ménière disease; Option (E) is pharmacological.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Mechanically repositioning dislodged otoconia out of the semicircular canal into the utricle
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 46-year-old male presents with progressive weakness in both hands over the past 8 months. Examination shows severe atrophy of the interosseous muscles bilaterally, with fasciculations visible in the arms and chest. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ in the biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses are extensor bilaterally. Sensory perception is intact throughout. What is the fundamental cellular pathology?

options.A: Autoimmune demyelination of central white matter pathways
options.B: Simultaneous degeneration of cortical upper motor neurons and spinal lower motor neurons
options.C: Selective destruction of dorsal root ganglion cell bodies
options.D: Ischemic infarction of the anterior spinal artery territory
options.E: Compression of the cauda equina nerve roots

explanation: Simultaneous presence of UMN signs (generalized hyperreflexia, ankle clonus, extensor plantar responses) and LMN signs (hand interosseous muscle atrophy, fasciculations, weakness) without sensory deficits is pathognomonic for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). The underlying cellular pathology is progressive degeneration of both cortical UMNs (Betz cells/corticospinal tracts) and spinal/bulbar LMNs (alpha motor neurons in anterior horns and brainstem motor nuclei). Option (A) describes multiple sclerosis; Option (C) causes sensory loss; Option (D) causes acute anterior cord infarction; Option (E) causes lumbosacral LMN root compression.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Simultaneous degeneration of cortical upper motor neurons and spinal lower motor neurons

stem: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the clinic after tripping over objects located on her right side. Perimetry confirms a right homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing. A complete lesion of which of the following structures in the left hemisphere will cause this presentation?

options.A: Left optic tract
options.B: Right optic nerve
options.C: Optic chiasm
options.D: Left Meyer loop exclusively
options.E: Right lingual gyrus

explanation: Complete right homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing results from a total lesion of the left optic tract, left LGN, or left optic radiations. Right optic nerve (B) causes right monocular blindness; Optic chiasm (C) causes bitemporal hemianopia; Left Meyer loop (D) causes right upper quadrantanopia; Right lingual gyrus (E) causes left upper quadrantanopia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left optic tract

stem: An animal experiment investigates the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). When the head is rotated to the left at a constant angular velocity, primary vestibular afferents from the left horizontal semicircular canal increase their firing rate. These signals project to the left vestibular nucleus, which sends decussating excitatory axons to the contralateral right abducens nucleus (CN VI). What eye movements are produced to maintain visual fixation?

options.A: Both eyes deviate to the LEFT
options.B: Both eyes deviate to the RIGHT
options.C: Both eyes elevate UPWARD
options.D: Both eyes depress DOWNWARD
options.E: Both eyes converge MEDIALLY

explanation: The VOR drives compensatory eye movements opposite to head rotation. Turning the head to the left stimulates the left vestibular nucleus, which projects across the midline to the right abducens nucleus (CN VI). The right abducens contracts the right lateral rectus and projects via the MLF to contract the left medial rectus, smoothly deviating both eyes to the RIGHT. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misidentify VOR trajectory.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Both eyes deviate to the RIGHT
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with severe right ear pain, itching, and discharge after spending the weekend on a swim team trip. Examination demonstrates severe pain when the clinician gently pulls the right pinna upward and backward. The tympanic membrane is intact and mobile. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Acute otitis media with purulent middle ear effusion
options.B: Acute otitis externa affecting the external acoustic canal
options.C: Otosclerosis with progressive stapes ankylosis
options.D: Cholesteatoma invading the mastoid antrum cavity
options.E: Tympanosclerosis involving the tympanic membrane

explanation: Otitis externa ("Swimmer's ear") is an acute external canal infection causing severe pain elicited by pulling the pinna or tragus, with canal edema and exudate, while the eardrum remains intact and mobile. Option (A) causes bulging eardrum and fever; Option (C) causes vertigo and hearing loss; Option (D) causes post-auricular tenderness over mastoid; Option (E) is a chronic middle ear mass.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Otitis externa (Swimmer's ear)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive leg weakness and spasticity. Neurological examination reveals lower extremity hyperreflexia, bilateral ankle clonus, and upgoing toes on plantar stimulation. Upper extremity motor exam is normal. A lesion affecting which of the following descending motor pathways is responsible for her elevated muscle tone and clonus?

options.A: Lateral corticospinal and cortico-bulbo-spinal pathways
options.B: Ventral primary rami of the lumbar plexus
options.C: Primary afferent fibers from muscle spindles
options.D: Alpha motor neurons in the anterior horn
options.E: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers

explanation: Descending upper motor neuron pathways (corticospinal and cortico-bulbo-spinal, including reticulospinal/rubrospinal tracts) continuously suppress alpha motor neuron excitability and damp down monosynaptic stretch reflexes. Interruption of these UMN pathways removes descending tonic inhibition, causing hyperreflexia, clonus, spasticity, and Babinski sign. Option (B) causes LMN flaccid paralysis; Option (C) abolishes stretch reflexes; Option (D) causes LMN flaccidity and atrophy; Option (E) regulates autonomic vascular/sweat functions.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Lateral corticospinal and cortico-bulbo-spinal pathways

stem: A 65-year-old male suffers an ischemic stroke in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA) deep penetrating branches, damaging the left optic radiations in the internal capsule. What visual field deficit will be produced?

options.A: Right homonymous hemianopia
options.B: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.C: Left homonymous hemianopia
options.D: Monocular blindness in right eye
options.E: Binasal hemianopia

explanation: Complete interruption of optic radiations in the left hemisphere (e.g., internal capsule stroke) disconnects all visual input from the right visual hemifield (right upper and lower fields from both eyes), producing a complete right homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing. Chiasm (B) causes bitemporal loss; Right radiations (C) cause left homonymous loss; Right optic nerve (D) causes right eye blindness; Binasal (E) requires bilateral lateral chiasm compression.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right homonymous hemianopia

stem: A 40-year-old female presents for a routine eye exam. The clinician performs fundoscopy to inspect the fovea. What unique structural and functional characteristic defines the fovea centralis?

options.A: It contains high density of rods and mediates dim light peripheral vision
options.B: It is the site where optic nerve axons exit the retina, creating a blind spot
options.C: It is the point of highest visual acuity, containing exclusively cones
options.D: It secretes aqueous humor into the posterior chamber
options.E: It is perfused directly by the posterior spinal artery

explanation: The fovea centralis (located in the center of the macula) is specialized for maximum visual acuity and color vision. It contains exclusively cone photoreceptors with 1:1 synaptic connections to bipolar and ganglion cells and displaced overlying neural layers. Rods (A) predominate in peripheral retina; Optic disc (B) lacks photoreceptors; Ciliary body (D) secretes fluid; Posterior spinal artery (E) supplies spinal cord.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: It is the point of highest visual acuity, containing exclusively cones

stem: A patient is evaluated following a traumatic brain injury. The examiner notes that visual signals originating from the lower retina travel via Meyer's loop through the temporal lobe. Which portion of the visual field is carried by fibers in Meyer's loop?

options.A: Lower visual field
options.B: Upper visual field
options.C: Nasal visual field exclusively
options.D: Central macula exclusively
options.E: Ipsilateral visual hemifield

explanation: Fibers in Meyer's loop loop anteriorly through the temporal lobe, carrying signals from the lower retina. Because optics invert images, the lower retina detects stimuli from the upper visual field. Therefore, Meyer's loop carries upper visual field information. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misattribute spatial orientation.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Upper visual field

stem: A 22-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a knife fight. He sustained a stab wound to the back at the level of the T4 spinal segment. Neurological exam demonstrates complete loss of voluntary motor control and loss of vibration/position sense in the right leg. Conversely, he has complete loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg starting at the T6 dermatome level. What is the clinical diagnosis for this hemisection of the spinal cord?

options.A: Anterior cord syndrome
options.B: Central cord syndrome
options.C: Brown-Séquard syndrome
options.D: Cauda equina syndrome
options.E: Tabes dorsalis

explanation: Functional hemisection of the spinal cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome) at T4 interrupts three major tracts: ipsilateral lateral corticospinal tract (ipsilateral UMN leg weakness below lesion), ipsilateral dorsal column (ipsilateral loss of fine touch/proprioception below lesion), and decussating anterolateral system (contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting 1–2 segments below lesion, i.e., T6). Option (A) causes bilateral paralysis and pain/temperature loss; Option (B) affects upper limbs more than lower; Option (D) causes lumbosacral root compression; Option (E) causes posterior column degeneration.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Brown-Séquard syndrome

stem: A patient diagnosed with Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) involving the posterior semicircular canal undergoes a therapeutic repositioning procedure in the clinic. The clinician rotates the patient's head through a precise sequence of supine positions to guide displaced otoconia back into the vestibule. What is the name of this classic clinical maneuver?

options.A: Dix-Hallpike maneuver
options.B: Epley maneuver
options.C: Romberg maneuver
options.D: Valsalva maneuver
options.E: Head-thrust maneuver

explanation: The Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning procedure) uses sequential head rotations to guide free-floating otoconia out of the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle. Dix-Hallpike is the diagnostic test. Option (A) is diagnostic; Option (C) tests proprioception/balance; Option (D) increases intrathoracic pressure; Option (E) evaluates VOR.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Epley maneuver
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 45-year-old factory worker presents with progressive, bilateral high-frequency hearing loss. He reports working in a high-noise industrial stamping facility for 20 years without wearing hearing protection. An audiogram confirms sensorineural hearing loss, with maximal threshold elevation at 4000 Hz. Which cellular structures within the organ of Corti are most vulnerable to irreversible damage from chronic, high-intensity noise exposure?

options.A: Primary auditory neurons in the medial geniculate nucleus
options.B: Outer hair cells at the basal turn of the cochlea
options.C: Inner hair cells at the apical turn of the cochlea
options.D: Gelatinous otolithic membrane of the utricle
options.E: Fibrous connective tissue of the tympanic membrane

explanation: Chronic high-intensity noise trauma selectively damages outer hair cells in the organ of Corti. High-frequency sound waves enter via the oval window and cause maximum basilar membrane displacement near the base of the cochlea, making basal hair cells most vulnerable and producing classic 4000 Hz notch sensorineural hearing loss. Option (A) is central; Option (C) apical hair cells transduce low frequencies; Option (D) is vestibular; Option (E) is eardrum tissue.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Outer hair cells at the basal turn of the cochlea
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 21-year-old female with narcolepsy experiences frequent disruptive episodes of cataplexy triggered by emotional events like laughing or being startled. In addition to scheduled daytime naps and modafinil for daytime wakefulness, which of the following therapeutic choices is effective for suppressing cataplexy?

options.A: Zolpidem
options.B: Sodium oxybate
options.C: Ramelteon
options.D: Diphenhydramine
options.E: Triazolam

explanation: Cataplexy in narcolepsy is managed with sodium oxybate (or REM-suppressing antidepressants like SSRIs/SNRIs), which improves nocturnal sleep architecture and suppresses daytime cataplexy. Modafinil treats daytime sleepiness. Option (A) is for insomnia; Option (C) is a melatonin agonist for insomnia; Option (D) is an antihistamine that increases sleepiness; Option (E) is a benzodiazepine.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Sodium oxybate
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 47-year-old male presents with severe left periorbital pain, fever, swelling around his left eye, and double vision following a dental abscess. Physical examination reveals total ophthalmoplegia of the left eye (inability to move left eye in any direction), drooping of the left upper eyelid, a dilated left pupil, and complete anesthesia over the left forehead and cheek (CN V1/V2 distributions). MRI demonstrates a severe infection spreading via ophthalmic veins. What structure is affected?

options.A: Jugular foramen in the posterior cranial fossa
options.B: Cavernous sinus located lateral to the sella turcica
options.C: Foramen rotundum in the greater wing of the sphenoid
options.D: Internal acoustic meatus in the petrous temporal bone
options.E: Foramen magnum at the base of the occipital bone

explanation: The clinical presentation of severe periorbital pain, chemosis, proptosis, fever, total ophthalmoplegia (inability to move the eye due to paresis of CN III, IV, and VI), and sensory loss over the forehead and cheek (CN V1 and V2) following a dental or facial infection is the classic presentation of cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST). The cavernous sinus is a trabeculated venous structure situated bilaterally on either side of the sella turcica. Because facial and ophthalmic veins are valveless, infections from the "danger triangle" of the face or dental abscesses can spread retrograde into the cavernous sinus, compressing the cranial nerves that traverse its lateral wall (CN III, IV, V1, V2) and central lumen (CN VI).
high_yield_pearl: Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI), V1/V2 sensory loss, and proptosis following facial or orbital infection via valveless veins.

stem: An investigator tests phototransduction mechanics. In total darkness, photoreceptors maintain a steady resting membrane potential and continuously release glutamate. What bioelectric change occurs in a photoreceptor when light absorbs into rhodopsin or cone opsins?

options.A: Massive influx of sodium leading to depolarization
options.B: Hyperpolarization of the cell membrane and decreased glutamate release
options.C: Sudden action potential firing along the photoreceptor axon
options.D: Release of acetylcholine into the vitreous humor
options.E: Efflux of calcium leading to rapid cellular destruction

explanation: Photoreceptors are unique sensory cells: in darkness, they are depolarized and continuously release glutamate. Light absorption isomerizes 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, activating cGMP phosphodiesterase (PDE), closing Na+ channels, hyperpolarizing the photoreceptor, and decreasing glutamate release onto bipolar cells. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misrepresent phototransduction bioelectricity.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Hyperpolarization of the cell membrane and decreased glutamate release

stem: An anatomical cross-section of the rostral midbrain demonstrates the oculomotor nucleus and Edinger-Westphal nucleus. Fibers crossing in which commissure connect the pretectal nucleus bilaterally to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei?

options.A: Anterior commissure crossing between the anterior temporal lobes
options.B: Posterior commissure crossing through the dorsal pretectal midbrain
options.C: Corpus callosum rostrum carrying interhemispheric frontal connections
options.D: Habenular commissure carrying interconnections between epithalamic nuclei
options.E: Optic chiasm decussating nasal retinal fibers from both ocular retinas

explanation: The anatomical cross-coupling that underlies the consensual pupillary light reflex relies on decussating fibers in the dorsal rostral midbrain. When retinal ganglion cells stimulate pretectal neurons on one side, each pretectal nucleus projects bilaterally: ipsilaterally to the uncrossed Edinger-Westphal nucleus, and contralaterally to the opposite Edinger-Westphal nucleus. The crossing interneuronal axons pass through the posterior commissure. Interruption of the posterior commissure eliminates the consensual light reflex across the eyes while preserving unilateral direct pathways.
high_yield_pearl: Consensual pupillary light reflex fibers crossing from the pretectal nucleus to the contralateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel through the posterior commissure.

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with visual distortion. She can perceive light and shapes normally, but cannot recognize familiar faces (prosopagnosia) despite normal visual sensation. Visual agnosia results from damage to which cortical region?

options.A: Primary visual cortex striate area V1
options.B: Visual association cortex areas V2 and V3
options.C: Precentral gyrus primary motor cortex
options.D: Postcentral gyrus primary somatosensory cortex
options.E: Superior temporal gyrus auditory cortex

explanation: Visual agnosia is a cognitive perceptual deficit where primary visual sensation (V1) is intact, but visual association cortex (neighboring occipitotemporal/parietal pathways) is damaged, preventing higher-order interpretation and identification of visual objects or faces (prosopagnosia). V1 (A) damage causes cortical blindness/hemianopia; Precentral (C) is motor; Postcentral (D) is somatosensory; Temporal (E) is auditory.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Visual association cortex

stem: A neuro-otologist performs caloric reflex testing on an awake patient with normal brainstem and cortical function. Cold water is infused into the patient's right external auditory canal. Which pattern of ocular nystagmus (named by the fast resetting phase) will be produced in this healthy individual?

options.A: Fast phase beating to the RIGHT toward the irrigated ear
options.B: Fast phase beating to the LEFT away from the irrigated ear
options.C: Pure vertical upward nystagmus without horizontal motion
options.D: Pure vertical downward nystagmus without horizontal motion
options.E: Total cessation of all spontaneous and evoked ocular motion

explanation: Caloric testing follows the COWS mnemonic (Cold = Opposite, Warm = Same) for the fast resetting phase of nystagmus. Cold water in the right ear chills horizontal canal endolymph, decreasing baseline right vestibular firing. Eyes slowly drift toward the right ear (slow phase), followed by a rapid cortical fast phase beating to the LEFT (Opposite side). Option (A) occurs with warm water; Option (C) indicates central pathology; Option (D) indicates brainstem death; Option (E) is incorrect.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Fast phase beating to the LEFT (away from the irrigated ear)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his family noticed sudden weakness on the right side of his face. On examination, he has weakness of his right upper facial muscles and lower facial muscles, with an inability to smile, raise his right eyebrow, or close his right eye tightly. Body strength is entirely normal bilaterally. Which of the following conditions best matches these clinical findings?

options.A: Right-sided supranuclear corticobulbar lesion sparing upper facial muscles
options.B: Right-sided peripheral facial nerve palsy affecting all ipsilateral muscles
options.C: Left-sided primary motor cortex infarction within the precentral gyrus
options.D: Left-sided internal capsule posterior limb lacunar microvascular infarction
options.E: Bilateral pontine tegmental demyelination of corticobulbar projection tracts

explanation: A lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII (Bell palsy) injures the nerve distal to the motor nucleus, producing paralysis of all ipsilateral facial expression muscles, affecting both the upper face (forehead, eye closure) and lower face (smile, nasolabial fold). Option (A) describes an MCA stroke which causes contralateral lower face droop with upper forehead sparing (UMN pattern); Option (C) causes lower facial droop with forehead sparing; Option (D) spares the face; Option (E) causes pharyngeal/laryngeal paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right-sided Bell palsy (infranuclear CN VII lesion)

stem: A 33-year-old male presents to the urgent care clinic complaining of sudden, continuous room-spinning vertigo, severe nausea, and instability that began 24 hours ago following a viral upper respiratory infection. He also reports new hearing loss and ringing in his left ear. Neurological examination reveals horizontal nystagmus beating toward the right. MRI of the brain is completely unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
options.B: Acute labyrinthitis
options.C: Vestibular schwannoma
options.D: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency
options.E: Ménière disease

explanation: Acute labyrinthitis involves inflammation of both vestibular and cochlear divisions of CN VIII (or inner ear labyrinth), often following a viral URI. It presents with continuous severe vertigo, nausea, and gait instability lasting days, combined with sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. Vestibular neuritis spares hearing. Option (A) causes brief positional vertigo (<1 min) without hearing loss; Option (C) causes slow progressive loss; Option (D) causes central TIAs; Option (E) causes episodic attacks lasting hours.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Acute labyrinthitis
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 59-year-old woman presents with persistent balance loss and difficulty walking straight. Physical examination shows a positive Romberg sign with eyes closed. When her head is rapidly turned to the right while focusing on the examiner's nose, her eyes slip off the target and make a compensatory catch-up saccade back to the nose (positive head-thrust test on the right). What structure is damaged?

options.A: Cerebellar hemisphere or vermal flocculonodular lesion
options.B: Peripheral vestibular labyrinth or vestibular nerve lesion
options.C: Medial longitudinal fasciculus brainstem tegmental lesion
options.D: Frontal eye field cortical precentral motor stroke
options.E: Paramedian pontine reticular formation pontine stroke

explanation: The head-thrust test evaluates VOR integrity. When the head is rapidly turned to the side of a peripheral vestibular lesion (right side), the impaired VOR fails to maintain fixation on the target. The eyes drift off target and make a compensatory catch-up saccade back to the target, confirming a right peripheral vestibular or CN VIII lesion. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) do not produce a positive head-thrust test to the right.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right peripheral vestibular apparatus or CN VIII vestibular division
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with difficulty swallowing and slurred speech that has gradually worsened over four months. Inspection of the oral cavity reveals a normal, non-atrophic tongue with no fasciculations. When asked to protrude his tongue, it remains strictly in the midline. Gag reflex is brisk. Muscle tone in his limbs is elevated with hyperactive deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following best explains the presence of pseudobulbar motor features in this patient?

options.A: Bilateral lower motor neuron lesion of the trigeminal motor nucleus
options.B: Bilateral upper motor neuron lesion of the corticobulbar tract above the brainstem motor nuclei
options.C: Unilateral peripheral lesion of the mandibular branch of CN V
options.D: Isolated LMN degeneration within the nucleus ambiguus
options.E: Compressive lesion of the hypoglossal nerve in the hypoglossal canal

explanation: Cranial nerve motor nuclei (except lower face and tongue) receive bilateral corticobulbar UMN projections. Bilateral corticobulbar tract lesions above the brainstem interrupt supranuclear inhibitory input, producing pseudobulbar motor features (hyperactive reflexes, dysarthria, spastic bulbar weakness) while sparing lower motor neurons, thereby preventing muscle atrophy and fasciculations. Option (A) causes LMN jaw muscle atrophy and absent reflexes; Option (C) causes ipsilateral jaw weakness; Option (D) causes LMN dysphagia; Option (E) causes LMN tongue atrophy.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Bilateral upper motor neuron lesion of the corticobulbar tract above the brainstem motor nuclei

stem: A 66-year-old male presents with an acute stroke involving the left crus cerebri of the midbrain. Which combination of clinical motor deficits will be observed on physical examination?

options.A: Right-sided spastic body hemiplegia and right lower face droop
options.B: Left-sided flaccid body hemiplegia and left total face paralysis
options.C: Right-sided body flaccidity with absent deep tendon reflexes
options.D: Ipsilateral loss of fine touch and pain sensation across the body
options.E: Bilateral complete body paralysis with preserved facial movements

explanation: The crus cerebri in the ventral midbrain contains uncrossed descending corticospinal and corticobulbar UMN fibers. A lesion of the left crus cerebri interrupts motor drive prior to decussation, producing contralateral (right-sided) spastic body hemiplegia (corticospinal tract) and contralateral (right-sided) lower facial droop (corticobulbar tract) with forehead sparing. Option (B) mislocates side and describes LMN flaccidity; Option (C) describes LMN deficits; Option (D) describes sensory loss; Option (E) describes bilateral quadriplegia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right-sided spastic body hemiplegia and right lower face droop

stem: A 60-year-old male presents with a stroke in the caudal pons on the right side. Examination shows paralysis of rightward horizontal gaze in both eyes, total right-sided lower motor neuron facial paralysis, and right eye abduction failure. Which nuclear complex in the caudal pons is damaged?

options.A: Right facial colliculus involving the abducens nucleus and internal genu of CN VII
options.B: Right oculomotor nucleus and adjacent Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic nucleus
options.C: Left frontal eye field within the posterior precentral cerebral cortex
options.D: Left paramedian pontine reticular formation in the caudal pontine tegmentum
options.E: Right trochlear nucleus located in the caudal midbrain periaqueductal gray

explanation: The facial colliculus is a visible elevation on the dorsal floor of the fourth ventricle in the caudal pons. It is formed by motor axons of the facial nerve (CN VII) as they loop around the abducens nucleus (CN VI) before exiting the ventrolateral brainstem. A lesion in this exact region simultaneously destroys the abducens nucleus (causing complete horizontal conjugate gaze palsy to the ipsilateral right side) and the surrounding internal genu of the facial nerve (causing ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis involving both the upper and lower face).
high_yield_pearl: A facial colliculus lesion in the dorsal caudal pons causes an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy (CN VI nucleus) and ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis (CN VII loop).

stem: A 67-year-old male presents with dysarthria. Examination demonstrates that when he protrudes his tongue, it deviates to the left side. Inspection of the tongue reveals pronounced atrophy and active fasciculations on the left side. Examination of the body shows 5/5 strength throughout, with 2+ deep tendon reflexes and downgoing toes bilaterally. What type of lesion is present?

options.A: Right UMN lesion of the corticobulbar tract
options.B: Left LMN lesion of the hypoglossal nerve/nucleus
options.C: Left UMN lesion of the corticobulbar tract
options.D: Right LMN lesion of the hypoglossal nerve/nucleus
options.E: Bilateral UMN lesion of the motor cortex

explanation: Lower motor neurons in the hypoglossal nucleus project via CN XII to the ipsilateral genioglossus muscle. An LMN lesion of the left hypoglossal nerve/nucleus produces left tongue atrophy, active fasciculations, and tongue deviation toward the weak/lesioned side (left) upon protrusion. Option (A) causes contralateral tongue deviation without atrophy/fasciculations; Option (C) causes right tongue deviation without atrophy; Option (D) causes right tongue atrophy and right deviation; Option (E) causes pseudobulbar speech without isolated tongue atrophy.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left LMN lesion of the hypoglossal nerve/nucleus

stem: A 62-year-old female presents with a gradual, painless decline in vision in her right eye over the past year. Examination demonstrates central visual field loss in her right eye, while vision in her left eye is completely normal. What is the location of the lesion causing this monocular visual deficit?

options.A: Optic chiasm compression by a pituitary tumor
options.B: Left optic tract carrying contralateral hemifields
options.C: Right optic nerve anterior to the optic chiasm
options.D: Left temporal lobe Meyer loop fibers in white matter
options.E: Right primary visual cortex in the occipital pole

explanation: Monocular visual field loss (loss of vision restricted to one eye) indicates a lesion located anterior to the optic chiasm, involving either the ipsilateral optic nerve or retina. Lesions at or posterior to the optic chiasm affect visual fields in both eyes. Options (A), (B), (D), and (E) cause binocular visual field defects.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterior to the optic chiasm (right optic nerve or right retina)

stem: A 25-year-old patient reports that when awakening in the morning, he occasionally experiences a terrifying sensation where he is fully conscious and aware of his surroundings, but completely unable to move his limbs, trunk, or speak for 1 to 2 minutes. What is the physiological mechanism underlying this phenomenon (sleep paralysis)?

options.A: Sudden onset of generalized epileptic seizure activity
options.B: Persistence of REM sleep muscle atonia into conscious wakefulness
options.C: Ischemic infarction of the bilateral pyramids in the medulla
options.D: Paroxysmal hyperpolarization of dorsal column sensory neurons
options.E: Acute autoantibody blockade of skeletal muscle nicotinic receptors

explanation: Sleep paralysis is a benign intrusion of REM muscle atonia into wakefulness. Brainstem projections hyperpolarize spinal motor neurons during REM sleep to prevent dream enactment. Sleep paralysis occurs when conscious awareness awakens while REM somatic muscle atonia persists for 1–2 minutes. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) do not explain transient post-dormital paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Persistence of REM sleep muscle atonia into conscious wakefulness
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with astigmatism. Refractive evaluation demonstrates that images are unfocused on the retina due to an uneven shape of the ocular media. What structural irregularity causes astigmatism?

options.A: Eye axial length being too short
options.B: Irregular curvature of the cornea
options.C: Stiffening of the lens with age
options.D: High intraocular pressure in the anterior chamber
options.E: Detachment of the retinal pigment epithelium

explanation: Astigmatism results from asymmetrical, irregular curvature of the refractive surface of the cornea (or lens), preventing light rays from focusing onto a single focal point on the retina, causing blurred images. Eye too short (A) causes hyperopia; Lens stiffening (C) causes presbyopia; High IOP (D) causes glaucoma; RPE detachment (E) causes retinal detachment.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Irregular curvature of the cornea

stem: An investigator maps the pathway of visual signals from the retina to the cortex. Retinal ganglion cell axons carrying information from the nasal hemiretina cross the midline at the optic chiasm. Which portion of the visual field is detected by the nasal hemiretina of each eye?

options.A: Temporal visual field
options.B: Nasal visual field
options.C: Upper central field exclusively
options.D: Lower central field exclusively
options.E: Ipsilateral visual field

explanation: Lenses invert light rays laterally and vertically. Stimuli from the temporal (lateral) visual field strike the nasal (medial) hemiretina of that eye. Nasal retinal fibers decussate at the optic chiasm. Nasal visual field (B) strikes the temporal hemiretina.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Temporal visual field

stem: An experimental animal model evaluates posture and muscle tone following localized brainstem lesions. A transection interrupting the lateral vestibulospinal tract (LVST) is performed. Which of the following physiological deficits will be observed in the experimental subject?

options.A: Loss of neck muscle coordination for maintaining upright head position
options.B: Impairment of horizontal conjugate eye movements during head rotation
options.C: Loss of uncrossed tone in antigravity extensor muscles, causing instability
options.D: Total loss of high-frequency hearing in the contralateral ear
options.E: Complete paralysis of facial expression muscles

explanation: The lateral vestibulospinal tract (LVST) originates in the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters nucleus) and descends uncrossed (ipsilaterally) down the spinal cord to excite alpha/gamma motor neurons innervating antigravity extensor muscles. Disruption causes loss of ipsilateral extensor tone and balance instability. Option (A) is MVST function; Option (B) is VOR/MLF function; Option (D) is lateral lemniscus; Option (E) is facial nerve function.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Loss of uncrossed tone in antigravity extensor muscles, causing instability
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 48-year-old male with persistent insomnia is prescribed suvorexant. What is the precise mechanism of action of suvorexant in treating insomnia?

options.A: Agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 G-protein coupled receptors
options.B: Selective allosteric modulator at the GABA-A receptor complex
options.C: Competitive antagonist at dual OX1 and OX2 orexin receptors
options.D: Antagonist at postsynaptic H1 histamine receptors in brain
options.E: Agonist at postsynaptic D2 and D3 dopamine receptors in striatum

explanation: Suvorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA) that blocks OX1R and OX2R receptors, inhibiting wake-promoting orexin neuropeptides and facilitating sleep transition. Option (A) describes benzodiazepines/Z-drugs; Option (B) describes ramelteon; Option (D) describes pramipexole; Option (E) describes antihistamines.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Antagonist at dual orexin receptors (OX1R and OX2R)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 28-year-old male with narcolepsy complains of sudden loss of voluntary muscle tone triggered by laughter. What is the clinical term for this symptom?

options.A: Cataplexy
options.B: Catalepsy
options.C: Chorea
options.D: Myoclonus
options.E: Athetosis

explanation: Cataplexy is a sudden, brief loss of voluntary muscle tone triggered by strong emotions (such as laughter or excitement) with preserved consciousness, pathognomonic for Narcolepsy Type 1. Option (B) is fixed posture; Option (C) is involuntary dancing movement; Option (D) is sudden muscle twitching; Option (E) is slow writhing movement.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Cataplexy
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 55-year-old male suffers an acute ischemic stroke in the left temporal lobe affecting the sublenticular portion of the internal capsule. Which central auditory fibers pass through the sublenticular internal capsule to reach the primary auditory cortex?

options.A: Projections from medial geniculate nucleus to transverse temporal gyrus
options.B: Projections from lateral geniculate nucleus to calcarine fissure cortex
options.C: Projections from ventral posteromedial nucleus to postcentral gyrus
options.D: Projections from ventral posterolateral nucleus to precentral gyrus
options.E: Projections from anterior nucleus to cingulate gyral cortex

explanation: The sublenticular part of the internal capsule carries auditory radiations connecting 5th order neurons in the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) of the thalamus to the primary auditory cortex in Transverse Temporal (Heschl's) Gyrus. Option (B) travels in CN VIII; Option (C) forms trapezoid body/lateral lemniscus; Option (D) forms vestibulocerebellar tract; Option (E) ascends in brainstem.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Projections from the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) to Transverse Temporal (Heschl's) Gyrus
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 23-year-old female presents with normal distant vision and normal near vision, but reports that vertical and horizontal lines appear unevenly clear. Diagnosis of astigmatism is made. What optical remedy corrects astigmatism?

options.A: Spherical concave lens shifting focus posteriorly
options.B: Cylindrical lens correcting corneal astigmatism
options.C: Spherical convex lens shifting focus anteriorly
options.D: Surgical phacoemulsification of the native lens
options.E: Topical parasympathomimetic eye drop therapy

explanation: Astigmatism is caused by an irregular, asymmetrical curvature of the cornea or lens along specific meridians. It is corrected using a cylindrical lens that focuses light unevenly across different axes to compensate for corneal asymmetry. Concave lenses (A) correct myopia; Convex lenses (C) correct hyperopia/presbyopia; Lens removal (D) treats cataracts; Mydriatics (E) dilate pupil.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Cylindrical lens correcting corneal curvature irregularity

stem: A neuro-ophthalmologist tests pupillary responses in a comatose patient. Shining light into the right eye produces no response in either pupil. Shining light into the left eye produces prompt pupillary constriction in both eyes. What is the location of the lesion?

options.A: Right optic nerve carrying afferent sensory impulses from the right eye
options.B: Right oculomotor nerve carrying efferent parasympathetic impulses to the right pupil
options.C: Left optic nerve carrying afferent sensory impulses from the left eye
options.D: Left oculomotor nerve carrying efferent parasympathetic impulses to the left pupil
options.E: Posterior commissure carrying decussating pretectal axons in the midbrain

explanation: When shining a penlight into the right eye produces no response in EITHER pupil (absent direct and consensual responses), the afferent sensory pathway from the right eye is non-functional. When shining light into the left eye produces prompt, normal pupillary constriction in BOTH pupils (intact direct and consensual responses), the left afferent pathway (left optic nerve) and BOTH efferent motor pathways (bilateral oculomotor nerves) are confirmed to be intact. Therefore, the lesion is located in the right optic nerve (CN II).
high_yield_pearl: Absent direct and consensual responses upon illumination of one eye with intact bilateral responses upon illumination of the other localizes to the optic nerve of the unresponsive eye.

stem: A 68-year-old male suffers an ischemic stroke of the right posterior cerebral artery (PCA) affecting the right occipital pole. Examination reveals a left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Why does macular vision remain intact in PCA territory visual cortex strokes?

options.A: Macular pathways project exclusively to the anterior temporal lobe cortex
options.B: Macular cortical area is expansive and receives collateral MCA blood supply
options.C: Macular sensory fibers bypass the primary visual cortex to synapse in V2
options.D: Macular representation is localized entirely within the inferior parietal lobule
options.E: Dual sensory innervation from the ophthalmic nerve preserves central vision

explanation: Macular sparing occurs in occipital PCA infarcts because the primary visual cortex area representing the macula (at the occipital pole) is anatomically large and has dual vascular supply from terminal branches of both PCA and MCA. MCA collateral flow maintains macular cortex perfusion during PCA occlusion. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) are anatomically incorrect.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: The macular cortical area is large and receives collateral blood supply from the middle cerebral artery (MCA)

stem: A 64-year-old male presents with a midbrain stroke. Examination demonstrates that his left pupil is fixed and dilated, and he has ptosis of the left upper eyelid. When asked to look straight ahead, his left eye rests in a "down and out" position. Which cranial nerve nucleus or nerve root is damaged?

options.A: Left oculomotor nerve fascicles within the ventral midbrain tegmentum
options.B: Left trochlear nerve fascicles within the dorsal midbrain tegmentum
options.C: Left abducens nerve fascicles within the caudal pontine tegmentum
options.D: Right oculomotor nerve fascicles within the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.E: Left facial nerve fascicles looping around the abducens nucleus in the pons

explanation: The combination of upper eyelid ptosis (paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris), a fixed dilated pupil (paralysis of parasympathetic sphincter pupillae), and an eye resting in a "down and out" position (unopposed action of the intact lateral rectus innervated by CN VI and superior oblique innervated by CN IV) is the classic presentation of a complete oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. A midbrain stroke involving the ventral tegmentum and exiting CN III fascicles (as seen in Weber syndrome when accompanied by contralateral hemiplegia) explains this presentation.
high_yield_pearl: A complete CN III palsy causes severe ptosis, a fixed and dilated pupil, and a "down and out" resting eye position from unopposed CN IV and CN VI tone.

stem: A 45-year-old male chronic alcoholic presents with severe numbness and tingling in his feet, as well as weakness in both legs. Examination reveals loss of vibration and position sense in a stocking distribution, along with lower extremity spasticity, hyperreflexia, and bilateral upgoing toes. Laboratory evaluation confirms marked vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration). Which combination of spinal cord tracts is classically involved in this metabolic myelopathy?

options.A: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
options.B: Anterior spinothalamic tracts and ventral horns
options.C: Lateral spinothalamic tracts and dorsal root ganglia
options.D: Anterior horn lower motor neurons and spinocerebellar tracts
options.E: Ventral white commissure and fasciculus cuneatus

explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of the spinal cord, selectively involving the dorsal columns (loss of vibration and position sense, sensory ataxia) and lateral corticospinal tracts (UMN spasticity, hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski signs). Option (B) causes anterior cord syndrome; Option (C) causes spinothalamic deficits; Option (D) causes motor neuron disease; Option (E) causes central syrinx deficits.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts

stem: A 33-year-old female presents with a lesion affecting the optic chiasm (e.g., pituitary macroadenoma). Which nerve fibers are interrupted at the optic chiasm?

options.A: Uncrossed temporal retinal fibers from both eyes
options.B: Decussating nasal retinal fibers from both eyes
options.C: All fibers originating from the right eye exclusively
options.D: Auditory radiations from the thalamus
options.E: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion

explanation: The optic chiasm is the decussation site where axons originating from the nasal hemiretinae of both eyes cross the midline. These crossing fibers carry information from the temporal (lateral) visual fields of both eyes, so compression at the chiasm produces bitemporal hemianopia. Uncrossed temporal fibers (A) pass laterally without crossing; Option (C) affects only one eye; Options (D) and (E) are non-visual pathways.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Decussating nasal retinal fibers from both eyes

stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents with mild vertigo, gait instability, dysmetria on left finger-to-nose testing, and skew deviation of the eyes. On gaze examination, he exhibits vertical and bi-directional horizontal nystagmus that does NOT fatigue and does NOT suppress with visual fixation. Audiometric evaluation reveals completely normal hearing bilaterally. Which localized central lesion best accounts for this patient's vertigo?

options.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the posterior canal
options.B: Acute peripheral vestibular neuritis of the superior branch
options.C: Central ischemic stroke of the cerebellum or brainstem nuclei
options.D: Ménière disease with fluctuating endolymphatic hydrops
options.E: Labyrinthitis with acute inflammatory cochlear involvement

explanation: Central vertigo features mild/variable vertigo, central neurological signs (ataxia, dysmetria, skew deviation), and non-suppressible, non-fatigable, vertical or bi-directional nystagmus without hearing loss. This presentation indicates a central cerebellar or brainstem stroke. Options (A), (B), and (D) represent peripheral vestibulopathies characterized by visual suppression and fatigability. Option (E) causes conductive hearing loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ischemic stroke of the left cerebellum or brainstem vestibular nuclei
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 33-year-old female presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the left side of her face. MRI shows an acute dissection of the left internal carotid artery. Postganglionic sympathetic fibers for facial sweating along the forehead and cheek travel along which arterial pathway?

options.A: External carotid artery plexus for the face and internal carotid plexus for the forehead
options.B: Internal carotid artery plexus exclusively supplying the entire face and scalp
options.C: Vertebral artery plexus traversing the cervical transverse foramina to the brain
options.D: Subclavian arterial plexus within the posterior triangle of the cervical neck
options.E: Basilar arterial plexus supplying circumferential pontine and cerebellar branches

explanation: Third-order sympathetic fibers emerge from the superior cervical ganglion and divide into two arterial pathways. Sudomotor (sweat) fibers supplying the majority of the face, cheek, and jaw travel with the external carotid artery (ECA) plexus along facial arterial branches. In contrast, sympathetic sudomotor fibers destined for the medial forehead, along with oculosympathetic fibers for the pupillary dilator and superior tarsal muscle, travel with the internal carotid artery (ICA) plexus through the carotid canal. Therefore, lesions of the internal carotid artery typically cause Horner syndrome with anhidrosis restricted strictly to the forehead or with completely spared facial sweating.
high_yield_pearl: Facial sudomotor sympathetic fibers divide at the superior cervical ganglion: the ECA plexus supplies the lower face, while the ICA plexus supplies the forehead and orbit.

stem: A 35-year-old worker at a chemical manufacturing plant presents with acute vertigo and ataxia following an occupational exposure. Anatomical mapping of his central vestibular projections is performed. Second-order vestibular neurons sending uncrossed descending fibers via the lateral vestibulospinal tract (LVST) originate primarily from which specific brainstem nucleus?

options.A: Superior vestibular nucleus projecting to the ocular motor nuclei
options.B: Medial vestibular nucleus projecting to cervical spinal segments
options.C: Lateral vestibular nucleus projecting to ipsilateral spinal cord
options.D: Inferior vestibular nucleus projecting to the cerebellar vermis
options.E: Abducens motor nucleus projecting to the ipsilateral lateral rectus

explanation: The lateral vestibulospinal tract (LVST) originates from second-order cell bodies in the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters nucleus) at the pontomedullary junction. LVST axons descend uncrossed through the spinal cord to excite motor neurons of antigravity extensor muscles. Option (A) projects via MLF to extraocular nuclei; Option (B) projects to cerebellum; Option (D) gives rise to MVST; Option (E) processes auditory signals.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters nucleus)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with a 2-day history of severe, continuous vertigo, nausea, and staggering gait. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus. Neurological exam reveals horizontal nystagmus beating to the left, which suppresses with visual fixation. Brain MRI is normal. The patient is diagnosed with acute vestibular neuritis. What is the primary management strategy for this self-limiting condition?

options.A: Immediate surgical endolymphatic shunt decompression
options.B: Short-term symptomatic vestibular suppressants and antiemetics
options.C: High-dose long-term daily aminoglycoside chemotherapy
options.D: Emergent suboccipital decompressive posterior fossa craniectomy
options.E: Long-term permanent dietary potassium restriction therapy

explanation: Acute vestibular neuritis is a self-limiting post-viral inflammation of the vestibular division of CN VIII. Hearing is completely preserved. Management focuses on short-term symptomatic relief using vestibular suppressants (meclizine, benzodiazepines) and antiemetics for 3–5 days, followed by vestibular rehabilitation. Option (A) is inappropriate; Option (C) is ototoxic; Option (D) is for central stroke; Option (E) is for tumors.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Symptomatic relief with short-term vestibular suppressants (e.g., meclizine) and antiemetics
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 45-year-old male is evaluated for weakness in his right hand. Examination demonstrates weakness of thumb abduction and finger spread. There is pronounced atrophy of the right thenar eminence. Reflexes in the right bicep and tricep are 1+. No Babinski sign is present. Sensory testing shows loss of pinprick and touch sensation along the medial hand and forearm (C8–T1 dermatomes). Which structure is damaged?

options.A: Left precentral gyrus lateral surface
options.B: Right ventral horn exclusively at C8–T1
options.C: Right spinal nerve / ventral and dorsal roots at C8–T1
options.D: Left corticospinal tract in the midbrain
options.E: Posterior limb of the internal capsule

explanation: LMN weakness and atrophy in the right hand combined with dermatomal sensory loss along the medial hand and forearm (C8–T1) indicate combined involvement of motor (ventral) and sensory (dorsal) root pathways at the C8–T1 segment (spinal nerve / nerve roots). Option (A) causes motor UMN deficits without dermatomal sensory loss; Option (B) causes pure motor LMN deficits; Option (D) causes contralateral UMN hemiplegia; Option (E) causes pure motor internal capsule hemiplegia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right spinal nerve / ventral and dorsal roots at C8–T1

stem: An investigator studies EEG wave characteristics across sleep stages. Match the following wave patterns with their corresponding sleep/awake states: (1) Alpha waves, (2) Sleep spindles and K-complexes, (3) Delta waves, (4) Sawtooth waves.

options.A: 1: Awake relaxed eyes closed, 2: Stage 2 NREM, 3: Stage 3 NREM, 4: REM sleep
options.B: 1: REM sleep, 2: Stage 3 NREM, 3: Stage 2 NREM, 4: Awake relaxed eyes closed
options.C: 1: Stage 2 NREM, 2: Stage 3 NREM, 3: REM sleep, 4: Awake relaxed eyes closed
options.D: 1: Stage 3 NREM, 2: REM sleep, 3: Awake relaxed eyes closed, 4: Stage 2 NREM
options.E: 1: Awake relaxed eyes closed, 2: REM sleep, 3: Stage 2 NREM, 4: Stage 3 NREM

explanation: Match: (1) Alpha waves = Awake relaxed with eyes closed; (2) Sleep spindles and K-complexes = Stage 2 NREM; (3) Delta waves = Stage 3 NREM slow-wave sleep; (4) Sawtooth waves = REM sleep. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) mispair wave patterns and sleep stages.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: 1: Awake relaxed eyes closed, 2: Stage 2 NREM, 3: Stage 3 NREM, 4: REM sleep
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with ptosis and miosis of the left eye following a neck dissection surgery. Anhidrosis is present on the left side of his face. Which ganglion houses the third-order cell bodies for postganglionic sympathetic fibers supplying the face and orbit?

options.A: Ciliary ganglion located in the posterior orbit adjacent to CN II
options.B: Superior cervical ganglion situated at the level of the C2 to C3 vertebrae
options.C: Pterygopalatine ganglion located within the pterygopalatine fossa
options.D: Otic ganglion located in the infratemporal fossa medial to CN V3
options.E: Dorsal root ganglion located within the intervertebral foramen of C2

explanation: In the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway, second-order preganglionic neurons ascend through the cervical sympathetic trunk to synapse onto third-order postganglionic cell bodies located in the superior cervical ganglion. The superior cervical ganglion is the largest sympathetic ganglion, situated in the upper neck at the level of the C2 and C3 vertebrae adjacent to the internal carotid artery. Axons of these third-order neurons then form postganglionic plexuses along the internal and external carotid arteries to reach the dilator pupillae, superior tarsal muscle, and facial sweat glands.
high_yield_pearl: Postganglionic sympathetic cell bodies supplying the head, orbit, and pupil reside in the superior cervical ganglion at the C2–C3 vertebral level.

stem: An investigator records electrical activity in the pretectal nucleus during pupillary testing. Axons from each pretectal nucleus project to both the ipsilateral and contralateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei. Crossing fibers traveling to the contralateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus pass through which midbrain commissure?

options.A: Anterior commissure carrying interhemispheric temporal connections
options.B: Posterior commissure carrying decussating pretectal projection fibers
options.C: Habenular commissure connecting bilateral epithalamic habenular nuclei
options.D: Corpus callosum splenium carrying interhemispheric occipital fibers
options.E: Optic chiasm decussating nasal retinal fibers from both eye retinas

explanation: In the pupillary light reflex arc, light stimulating retinal ganglion cells activates pretectal neurons in the rostral midbrain. To ensure that light in one eye produces equal pupillary constriction in both eyes (consensual reflex), axons from each pretectal nucleus project bilaterally: one uncrossed pathway directly to the ipsilateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus, and one crossed pathway through the posterior commissure to the contralateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus. Interruption of the posterior commissure impairs consensual responses while sparing direct ipsilateral constriction.
high_yield_pearl: Consensual pupillary light reflex fibers decussate across the midbrain midline via the posterior commissure.

stem: An anatomical study traces retinal projections. Fibers originating from the temporal hemiretina of the left eye project to which anatomical structure?

options.A: Crosses at optic chiasm to right optic tract
options.B: Remains uncrossed and projects via left optic tract to left LGN
options.C: Crosses at optic chiasm to left superior colliculus
options.D: Projects directly to right visual cortex V1
options.E: Synapses in Edinger-Westphal nucleus bilaterally

explanation: Axons originating from the temporal hemiretina of the left eye carry signals from the nasal visual field of the left eye. These temporal retinal fibers remain UNCROSSED at the optic chiasm and ascend in the ipsilateral (left) optic tract to synapse in the left lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) violate uncrossed temporal fiber anatomy.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Remains uncrossed and projects via left optic tract to left LGN

stem: A 68-year-old male presents with severe lower back pain radiating down both legs, accompanied by urinary incontinence and bowel dysfunction that developed over the past 12 hours. Examination reveals sensory loss confined to the perianal and saddle region (S3–S5 dermatomes), loss of the anal wink reflex, and symmetrical lower extremity weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs. Which anatomical region of the spinal cord is acutely compressed in this patient?

options.A: Conus medullaris
options.B: Cauda equina
options.C: Cervical enlargement
options.D: Mid-thoracic spinal cord
options.E: Precentral gyrus motor homunculus

explanation: The conus medullaris is the terminal end of the spinal cord housing sacral segments (S1–S5) at L1–L2 vertebral level. Acute compression produces bilateral saddle anesthesia (S3–S5), early severe bowel/bladder dysfunction, loss of the anal wink reflex (S3–S4), and symmetrical lower extremity weakness with mixed UMN/LMN signs. Option (B) presents with asymmetric radicular pain and pure LMN signs; Option (C) causes quadriparesis; Option (D) causes thoracic sensory level and spastic paraplegia; Option (E) causes contralateral hemiparesis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Conus medullaris

stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with excessive daytime sleepiness. On several occasions while standing in line at the cafeteria, he has experienced sudden episodes of falling asleep without warning. He also reports seeing terrifying monster-like figures in his room just as he is waking up in the morning. What term describes hallucinations that occur specifically upon awakening from sleep?

options.A: Hypnagogic hallucinations
options.B: Hypnopompic hallucinations
options.C: Delirium tremens
options.D: Synesthesias
options.E: Illusionary palinopsia

explanation: Hypnopompic hallucinations occur upon awakening from sleep (transition from sleep to wakefulness). Hypnagogic hallucinations occur while falling asleep (transition from wakefulness to sleep). Option (A) occurs when falling asleep; Option (C) is alcohol withdrawal; Option (D) is sensory cross-wiring; Option (E) is visual persistence.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Hypnopompic hallucinations
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with severe insomnia. She takes a prescription medication that acts as a selective agonist at MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Which physiological process is directly regulated by MT1 and MT2 receptor activation?

options.A: Direct inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels in alpha motor neurons
options.B: Entrainment of circadian sleep-wake rhythmicity and promotion of sleep onset
options.C: Stimulation of growth hormone secretion from the anterior pituitary
options.D: Blockade of dopamine reuptake in the nucleus accumbens
options.E: Facilitation of chloride channel opening at GABA-A receptors

explanation: MT1 and MT2 receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) regulate circadian rhythmicity: MT1 promotes sleepiness and sleep onset, while MT2 shifts circadian timing. Ramelteon acts on these receptors to treat insomnia without GABA-mediated sedation. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) do not represent SCN melatonin receptor function.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Entrainment of circadian sleep-wake rhythmicity and promotion of sleep onset
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 48-year-old female presents with severe right-sided facial pain shooting into her cheek and jaw. During physical examination, the physician tests the motor function of the trigeminal nerve. Which maneuver specifically tests the integrity of the lower motor neuron axons traveling within the mandibular branch of CN V?

options.A: Asking the patient to wrinkle her forehead against resistance
options.B: Asking the patient to puff out her cheeks against pressure
options.C: Asking the patient to open her mouth against resistance while observing for jaw deviation
options.D: Asking the patient to show her upper and lower teeth
options.E: Asking the patient to puff her tongue into her cheek against resistance

explanation: Motor innervation to the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids) is supplied by V3 (mandibular division of CN V) from the trigeminal motor nucleus in the mid-pons. Asking the patient to open her mouth against resistance tests lateral pterygoid function; if weak, the jaw deviates toward the weak/lesioned side upon opening. Option (A) tests CN VII upper face; Option (B) tests CN VII cheek muscles; Option (D) tests CN VII lower face; Option (E) tests CN XII tongue.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Asking the patient to open her mouth against resistance while observing for jaw deviation

stem: A 42-year-old male executive presents with difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep for the past 4 months, leading to severe daytime fatigue and irritability. He has tried improving sleep hygiene without success. He is prescribed a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic agent that selectively binds to the GABA-A receptor alpha-1 subunit to facilitate GABA-mediated inhibition. Which drug was prescribed?

options.A: Suvorexant
options.B: Ramelteon
options.C: Zolpidem
options.D: Modafinil
options.E: Pramipexole

explanation: Zolpidem is a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic ("Z-drug") that selectively binds the alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, facilitating GABA-mediated inhibition to promote sleep onset. Option (A) is an orexin antagonist; Option (B) is a melatonin agonist; Option (D) promotes wakefulness; Option (E) is a dopamine agonist for RLS.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Zolpidem
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: An anatomical study reviews the cavernous sinus contents. Which cranial nerve lies freely within the central venous lumen of the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery, making it most susceptible to injury in cavernous sinus thrombosis?

options.A: Oculomotor nerve embedded in the lateral cavernous sinus wall
options.B: Trochlear nerve embedded in the lateral cavernous sinus wall
options.C: Abducens nerve running freely within the central venous lumen
options.D: Ophthalmic nerve embedded in the lateral cavernous sinus wall
options.E: Maxillary nerve embedded in the lateral cavernous sinus wall

explanation: The cavernous sinus contains cranial nerves organized into two distinct compartments. Embedded within the fibrous lateral dural wall from superior to inferior are: CN III (oculomotor), CN IV (trochlear), CN V1 (ophthalmic), and CN V2 (maxillary). In contrast, the abducens nerve (CN VI) runs freely within the central trabeculated venous lumen of the cavernous sinus, situated immediately adjacent to the internal carotid artery (ICA). Because of this central, non-adherent position, CN VI is the cranial nerve most susceptible to damage from an internal carotid artery aneurysm or septic thrombosis expanding within the sinus lumen.
high_yield_pearl: The abducens nerve (CN VI) runs freely within the central cavernous sinus lumen adjacent to the internal carotid artery, making it most vulnerable to cavernous sinus pathology.

stem: A 25-year-old patient with narcolepsy experiences hypnagogic hallucinations upon falling asleep. Which of the following describes hypnagogic hallucinations?

options.A: Vivid sensory hallucinations occurring while falling asleep
options.B: Auditory hallucinations occurring during intense physical exercise
options.C: Visual illusions occurring during acute alcohol withdrawal
options.D: Olfactory hallucinations occurring during a temporal lobe seizure
options.E: Tactile sensations occurring after peripheral nerve transection

explanation: Hypnagogic hallucinations are vivid sensory experiences occurring during the transition from wakefulness to sleep (as you go to sleep). Hypnopompic hallucinations occur upon awakening. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) describe other non-sleep sensory phenomena.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Vivid sensory hallucinations occurring while falling asleep
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 50-year-old female complaining of chronic sleep-onset insomnia is started on a medication that acts as a selective agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus. It has no affinity for GABA receptors and carries no risk of dependence or abuse. Which medication is this?

options.A: Zaleplon
options.B: Ramelteon
options.C: Suvorexant
options.D: Alprazolam
options.E: Pitolisant

explanation: Ramelteon is a hypnotic that acts as a selective agonist at MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). It promotes sleep onset without interacting with GABA receptors, carrying no abuse potential. Option (A) is a GABA-A non-benzodiazepine; Option (C) is an orexin antagonist; Option (D) is a benzodiazepine; Option (E) is an H3 antagonist.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ramelteon
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 64-year-old man with a long-standing history of untreated hypertension presents to the emergency department after experiencing a sudden onset of right-sided weakness. Neurological examination reveals marked weakness of the right upper extremity and lower right face. On passive extension of the right elbow, a velocity-dependent resistance is felt, followed by a sudden release of tone. Tendon reflexes are 3+ in the right bicep and tricep, and a stroke to the left cerebral hemisphere is suspected. Which of the following structures contains the descending axons responsible for transmitting the primary voluntary motor signals disrupted in this patient prior to their decussation?

options.A: Posterior column of the spinal cord
options.B: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
options.C: Anterior funiculus of the spinal cord
options.D: Ventral primary ramus of the cervical plexus
options.E: Postcentral gyrus sensory cortex

explanation: The patient presents with upper motor neuron (UMN) signs, including right upper extremity and lower facial weakness, hyperreflexia (3+ reflexes), and spasticity featuring velocity-dependent resistance. Voluntary motor commands originating from pyramidal cells in the precentral gyrus descend through the corona radiata and converge within the posterior limb of the internal capsule before reaching the crus cerebri of the midbrain and medullary pyramids. An ischemic stroke in the left internal capsule interrupts these descending upper motor neurons prior to their decussation at the medullary-spinal junction, leading to contralateral (right-sided) spastic hemiplegia. Option (A) carries ascending sensory info; Option (C) carries uncrossed anterior corticospinal fibers for axial muscles; Option (D) contains peripheral lower motor neurons; Option (E) is the primary somatosensory cortex.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Posterior limb of the internal capsule

stem: A 50-year-old male is forced to seek medical evaluation by his family because he has gotten into three minor motor vehicle collisions over the past four months. He repeatedly fails to see cars approaching from his far right or far left sides. Ocular examination demonstrates a bitemporal hemianopia. An enlarging mass arising from which structure located directly beneath the optic chiasm is the most common cause of this visual field loss?

options.A: Epithalamus
options.B: Pituitary gland
options.C: Pineal gland
options.D: Cerebellar vermis
options.E: Superior colliculus

explanation: The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica directly beneath the optic chiasm. An expanding pituitary adenoma compresses decussating nasal retinal fibers in the optic chiasm (which carry temporal visual fields from both eyes), producing a classic bitemporal hemianopia ("tunnel vision"). Epithalamus (A), pineal gland (C), cerebellar vermis (D), and superior colliculus (E) do not compress the optic chiasm.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Pituitary gland

stem: A 58-year-old male with long-standing hypertension suffers a brainstem stroke causing an isolated lesion of the right MLF. What extraocular movement deficit will be elicited when the patient attempts horizontal gaze to the left?

options.A: Right eye fails to adduct on leftward gaze, while left eye abducts with nystagmus
options.B: Left eye fails to adduct on rightward gaze, while right eye abducts with nystagmus
options.C: Both eyes fail to elevate vertically on attempted upward vertical gaze
options.D: Both eyes remain fixed in persistent lateral horizontal deviation to the right
options.E: Both pupils dilate widely and fail to constrict to direct or consensual light

explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) carries internuclear axons from the contralateral abducens nucleus (pons) to the ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus (midbrain) to drive the ipsilateral medial rectus during conjugate horizontal gaze. The affected MLF is named for the eye that fails to adduct. An isolated stroke involving the RIGHT MLF interrupts signals to the right medial rectus during leftward horizontal gaze. Therefore, on attempted leftward gaze, the right eye fails to adduct past the midline, whereas the left eye abducts normally but develops fine horizontal nystagmus; convergence remains intact.
high_yield_pearl: A right MLF lesion causes a right internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO): failure of right eye adduction on leftward horizontal gaze with left abducting nystagmus.

stem: An anatomical study traces parasympathetic fibers originating in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the rostral midbrain. Preganglionic parasympathetic axons travel within CN III to reach which peripheral ganglion in the orbit?

options.A: Superior cervical ganglion in the upper cervical neck
options.B: Ciliary ganglion located in the posterior orbital apex
options.C: Pterygopalatine ganglion within the pterygopalatine fossa
options.D: Otic ganglion located medial to the mandibular nerve
options.E: Submandibular ganglion suspended from the lingual nerve

explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers originating in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the rostral midbrain travel within the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Upon reaching the orbit, these fibers exit the inferior division of CN III to synapse in the ciliary ganglion, situated in the posterior orbit between the optic nerve and the lateral rectus. Postganglionic parasympathetic axons then travel via the short ciliary nerves to pierce the sclera and innervate the sphincter pupillae muscle (pupillary constriction) and the ciliary muscle (accommodation for near vision).
high_yield_pearl: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus synapse in the ciliary ganglion, projecting via short ciliary nerves to constrict the pupil and accommodate the lens.

stem: A 48-year-old male with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes presents with acute double vision. Physical examination reveals that his right eye is fixed in a "down and out" position at rest, with severe ptosis of the right upper eyelid. However, pupillary light reflexes are completely normal bilaterally, with prompt, equal pupillary constriction in response to direct and consensual light. What is the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy?

options.A: Extrinsic aneurysmal compression of superficial pupillomotor fibers
options.B: Microvascular ischemic infarction affecting central somatic motor fibers
options.C: Autoimmune demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus
options.D: Inflammatory neuropathy of the superior cervical ganglion in the neck
options.E: Infiltration of the cavernous sinus by an invasive pituitary adenoma
