explanation: Diabetic oculomotor neuropathy typically presents with acute-onset diplopia, ptosis, and a "down-and-out" resting eye position, but with characteristically preserved pupillary light reflexes (pupil-sparing). Somatomotor fibers supplying extraocular muscles are located in the central core of CN III and depend on microvascular perfusion by the vasa nervorum. In diabetes mellitus, microvascular ischemic hyalinosis damages these central somatic fibers while sparing the peripherally located parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers, which receive collateral perfusion from the pial capillary plexus. Compressive lesions (e.g., PComm aneurysms) compress the superficial perimeter first, causing early pupillary dilation.
high_yield_pearl: Diabetic CN III neuropathy causes microvascular ischemia to central somatic motor fibers, resulting in ptosis and extraocular paralysis with pupil sparing.

stem: A 65-year-old female presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe headache described as "the worst headache of my life." Physical examination reveals that her left pupil is broadly dilated (mydriasis) and unresponsive to light shone in either eye. Left eyelid ptosis is present, and the left eye is deviated laterally and downward. What underlying vascular lesion must be immediately ruled out in this patient?

options.A: Thrombotic occlusion of the anterior spinal artery in the medulla
options.B: Aneurysmal compression of CN III by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
options.C: Ischemic lacunar stroke involving descending fibers in the medullary pyramid
options.D: Embolic occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery in the brainstem
options.E: Microvascular hyalinosis of the abducens nerve within the cavernous sinus

explanation: The patient presents with an acute, severe "thunderclap" headache ("worst headache of my life"), characteristic of a ruptured or expanding intracranial aneurysm causing subarachnoid hemorrhage. The accompanying ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy with a fixed, widely dilated pupil (mydriasis), severe ptosis, and a "down-and-out" eye deviation is the classic clinical sign of an expanding posterior communicating artery (PComm) aneurysm compressing the superficial outer parasympathetic fibers of CN III at the junction of the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate neurovascular imaging.
high_yield_pearl: Acute CN III palsy with a fixed, dilated pupil and severe headache mandates immediate evaluation for an expanding posterior communicating artery (PComm) aneurysm.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with Multiple Sclerosis presents with bilateral Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO). What physical examination finding is pathognomonic for bilateral INO during attempted horizontal gaze to either side?

options.A: Inability to adduct the eye ipsilateral to each MLF lesion during conjugate gaze, with abducting nystagmus
options.B: Complete bilateral loss of vertical upward gaze elevation, with fixed pupillary dilation and light rigidity
options.C: Bilateral fixed mydriasis with complete absence of pupillary constriction to light and near targets
options.D: Unilateral severe eyelid ptosis with a resting "down and out" deviation of the affected globe
options.E: Bilateral dense sensory analgesia and thermal anesthesia across all three trigeminal facial divisions

explanation: Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is virtually pathognomonic of demyelinating disease, specifically multiple sclerosis, in young adults. Demyelination of both medial longitudinal fasciculi (MLFs) disconnects bilateral abducens gaze centers from the contralateral oculomotor medial rectus subnuclei. During attempted rightward horizontal gaze, the left eye fails to adduct while the right eye abducts with monocular horizontal nystagmus; during attempted leftward horizontal gaze, the right eye fails to adduct while the left eye abducts with monocular horizontal nystagmus. Crucially, convergence during accommodation remains completely intact because near-response fibers bypass the MLF.
high_yield_pearl: Bilateral INO features bilateral adduction deficits on horizontal gaze with abducting nystagmus and preserved convergence, classically caused by multiple sclerosis.

stem: A 22-year-old male undergoes a detailed ophthalmological examination. Fundoscopy reveals a distinct, pale, circular area on the nasal side of the posterior retina where retinal ganglion cell axons converge to exit the eye. No photoreceptors are present in this specific region, creating the physiological "blind spot." What is the name of this anatomical structure?

options.A: Fovea centralis
options.B: Optic disc
options.C: Macula lutea
options.D: Ciliary body
options.E: Canal of Schlemm

explanation: The optic disc is the anatomical region on the nasal side of the retina where 3rd order retinal ganglion cell axons converge and exit the eye as the optic nerve. Because no photoreceptors (rods or cones) reside over the optic disc, it creates the physiological blind spot. Fovea centralis (A) and macula lutea (C) mediate high-acuity central vision.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Optic disc

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with sudden difficulty speaking and right-sided face and hand weakness. On cranial nerve testing, when asked to stick out his tongue, it deviates to the right. When asked to smile, the right corner of his mouth droops, but he can wrinkle his forehead bilaterally. Strength in his right hand is 3/5. Speech is non-fluent and laboured. Which vascular territory is affected by an ischemic stroke in this patient?

options.A: Left anterior cerebral artery supplying the medial frontal paracentral lobule
options.B: Left middle cerebral artery superior division supplying lateral precentral cortex
options.C: Left posterior cerebral artery supplying medial occipital visual cortex
options.D: Right lenticulostriate penetrating arteries supplying the posterior internal capsule
options.E: Basilar artery paramedian branches supplying ventral pontine corticospinal tracts

explanation: The superior division of the left MCA supplies the lateral primary motor cortex (arm/face area) and Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus. Ischemia causes contralateral (right-sided) face/arm weakness, right lower facial droop, right tongue deviation (corticobulbar fibers), and non-fluent Broca's aphasia. Option (A) supplies medial cortex (leg); Option (C) affects right hemisphere; Option (D) affects visual occipital cortex; Option (E) affects spinal cord.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left middle cerebral artery (superior division)

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with sudden-onset weakness in his right leg following an ischemic stroke. On physical examination, his strength in the right lower extremity is 2/5, while strength in the right upper extremity and face is 5/5. Sensory loss is restricted to the right foot and leg. Plantar response on the right is extensor (upgoing toes). A lesion in which of the following cortical regions best accounts for this pattern of deficits?

options.A: Lateral aspect of the precentral gyrus
options.B: Anterior portion of the paracentral lobule
options.C: Posterior portion of the paracentral lobule
options.D: Premotor cortex on the lateral hemispheric surface
options.E: Genu of the internal capsule

explanation: Motor representation across the precentral gyrus is somatotopically organized. The trunk, upper extremity, and face are represented on the lateral convexity of the hemisphere (middle cerebral artery territory). The lower extremity motor representation resides on the medial surface of the hemisphere within the anterior portion of the paracentral lobule (anterior cerebral artery territory). A lesion restricted to this medial motor cortex causes UMN weakness and an extensor plantar response isolated to the contralateral lower extremity. Option (A) represents the face and arm; Option (C) is the sensory paracentral lobule; Option (D) plans complex tasks; Option (E) carries corticobulbar fibers.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterior portion of the paracentral lobule

stem: A 72-year-old male reports gradual difficulty understanding speech, particularly in crowded social environments with ambient background noise. He states that female and children's voices are especially hard to comprehend. Otoscopic examination is entirely normal bilaterally. Weber test is midline, and Rinne test shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. Which age-related physiological process accounts for this presentation (presbycusis)?

options.A: Sclerosis of the malleus and incus ossicular joints
options.B: Progressive loss of hair cells at the base of the cochlea
options.C: Fluid accumulation within the middle ear cavity
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of the endolymphatic sac
options.E: Ischemic necrosis of the transverse temporal gyrus

explanation: Presbycusis is age-related, symmetric sensorineural hearing loss caused primarily by progressive degeneration of hair cells at the basal turn of the cochlea (high-frequency loss). Speech comprehension (especially consonants and higher-pitched voices) relies on high frequencies, leading to difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments. Option (A) causes conductive loss; Option (C) causes otitis media; Option (D) causes Ménière disease; Option (E) is a stroke.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Progressive loss of hair cells at the base of the cochlea
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 29-year-old female medical student reviews the accommodation reflex. During accommodation, parasympathetic postganglionic fibers from the ciliary ganglion stimulate contraction of the ciliary muscle. What structural change occurs in the crystalline lens when the ciliary muscle contracts?

options.A: Zonular fibers tighten, pulling the lens into a flattened shape for distant vision
options.B: Zonular fibers relax, allowing the lens to round up into a convex shape for near vision
options.C: The crystalline lens displaces posteriorly into the vitreous body chamber
options.D: The crystalline lens develops immediate protein denaturation and total opacification
options.E: The anterior lens capsule ruptures spontaneously due to excessive ciliary tension

explanation: The crystalline lens is suspended by suspensory ligaments (zonular fibers) attached circumferentially to the ciliary body. At rest (during distant vision), the ciliary muscle is relaxed, which keeps the ring open and stretches the zonular fibers taut, flattening the lens and lowering its optical power. During accommodation for near vision, parasympathetic stimulation causes the ciliary muscle to contract (acting like a sphincter), which constricts the ring and REDUCES tension on the zonular fibers. Relieved of tension, the elastic crystalline lens naturally rounds up, becoming more spherical/convex, thereby increasing its refractive power to focus near images onto the retina.
high_yield_pearl: Contraction of the ciliary muscle RELAXES tension on zonular fibers, allowing the crystalline lens to round up and increase optical refractive power for near vision.

stem: A 70-year-old male suffers an ischemic stroke caused by occlusion of the calcarine branch of the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA). Perimetry reveals a right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Which cortical region surrounding the calcarine sulcus forms the primary visual cortex (V1)?

options.A: Precentral gyrus motor cortex homunculus
options.B: Postcentral gyrus primary somatosensory cortex
options.C: Cuneus and lingual gyri on the medial occipital lobe
options.D: Superior temporal gyrus primary auditory cortex
options.E: Inferior frontal gyrus motor speech association area

explanation: The primary visual cortex (V1, Brodmann area 17) surrounds the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe, composed of the cuneus gyrus (above calcarine sulcus) and lingual gyrus (below calcarine sulcus). Precentral gyrus (A) is primary motor cortex; Postcentral gyrus (B) is somatosensory; Superior temporal (D) is primary auditory; Inferior frontal (E) is Broca's area.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Cuneus and lingual gyri on the medial surface of the occipital lobe

stem: A neurophysiologist maps the primary auditory cortex in a primate model. Single-unit electrode recordings reveal that neurons in one portion of Heschl's gyrus respond preferentially to low-frequency sounds, whereas neurons in another portion respond to high-frequency sounds. What organizational principle describes this spatial mapping of sound frequencies from the cochlea to the cortex?

options.A: Somatotopical organization
options.B: Tonotopical organization
options.C: Retinotopical organization
options.D: Dermatomal organization
options.E: Columnar ocular dominance organization

explanation: Tonotopical organization describes the systematic spatial mapping of sound frequencies maintained from the cochlea (high frequencies at base, low at apex) through the ascending auditory pathway to the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus). Option (A) maps body parts; Option (C) maps visual space; Option (D) maps spinal dermatomes; Option (E) maps eye input in V1.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Tonotopical organization
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A researcher conducts a cellular neurophysiology study on retinal photoreceptors. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrate that when light strikes a photoreceptor cell, the cell hyperpolarizes and decreases its release of glutamate onto bipolar cells. Which visual pigment in rod photoreceptors absorbs light energy to initiate this phototransduction cascade?

options.A: Cone opsin
options.B: Rhodopsin
options.C: Melanopsin
options.D: Dopamine
options.E: Melatonin

explanation: Rod photoreceptors contain the visual pigment rhodopsin (opsin protein bound to 11-cis-retinal, synthesized from Vitamin A). Light absorption converts 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, activating transducin and PDE, which lowers cGMP, closes Na+ channels, hyperpolarizes the photoreceptor, and decreases glutamate release. Cone opsins (A) mediate color vision in cones. Melanopsin (C) is in ipRGCs for circadian entrainment.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Rhodopsin

stem: An investigator evaluates the accommodation reflex pathway. Cortical inputs from the visual association areas project to the midbrain reflex center. Which midbrain nucleus supplies the efferent somatic motor fibers to the medial rectus muscles to execute eye convergence during accommodation?

options.A: Edinger-Westphal nucleus and somatic oculomotor nucleus
options.B: Trochlear motor nucleus in the caudal midbrain tegmentum
options.C: Abducens motor nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum
options.D: Superior cervical ganglion in the upper cervical sympathetic trunk
options.E: Trigeminal motor nucleus located in the mid-pontine tegmentum

explanation: The accommodation reflex is a complex cortical reflex loop. Visual signals pass from the retina through the optic nerve, chiasm, tract, LGN, and optic radiations to the primary visual cortex (V1) and visual association areas (Brodmann areas 18 and 19). From the association cortex, corticofugal fibers descend through the internal capsule to the pretectal area and synapse directly onto the Edinger-Westphal nuclei (driving parasympathetic pupillary constriction and ciliary muscle contraction) and the somatic oculomotor motor nuclei (driving bilateral medial rectus contraction for convergence).
high_yield_pearl: Cortical accommodation pathways project directly to the Edinger-Westphal and oculomotor nuclei, bypassing the dorsal midbrain pretectal light-reflex arc and MLF.

stem: A 28-year-old male suffers a traumatic injury to the right orbit damaging the short ciliary nerves. What autonomic deficit will be present in the right eye?

options.A: Loss of sympathetic pupillary dilation resulting in persistent miosis
options.B: Loss of parasympathetic pupillary constriction resulting in persistent mydriasis
options.C: Loss of sympathetic sudomotor innervation over the ipsilateral cheek
options.D: Total flaccid paralysis of the ipsilateral lateral rectus muscle
options.E: Complete sensory anesthesia across the ophthalmic nerve distribution

explanation: The short ciliary nerves carry postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the ciliary ganglion to the sphincter pupillae muscle (responsible for pupillary constriction) and the ciliary muscle (responsible for lens accommodation). Traumatic or surgical injury to the short ciliary nerves interrupts parasympathetic outflow to the anterior segment of the eye, abolishing pupillary constriction (resulting in persistent mydriasis / pupillary dilation from unopposed sympathetic dilatator pupillae tone) and paralyzing the ciliary muscle (causing cycloplegia / inability to accommodate for near vision).
high_yield_pearl: Injury to short ciliary nerves destroys postganglionic parasympathetic innervation, producing a fixed, dilated pupil (mydriasis) and loss of accommodation (cycloplegia).

stem: A 60-year-old male presents with ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the right side of his face. Pharmacological testing confirms a postganglionic sympathetic lesion. Postganglionic sympathetic fibers destined for the pupillary dilator muscle travel along the surface of which vascular structure to enter the cranial cavity?

options.A: Vertebral artery plexus traversing the cervical transverse foramina
options.B: Internal carotid artery plexus along the petrous and cavernous segments
options.C: External jugular venous plexus draining the superficial face
options.D: Middle meningeal artery plexus passing through the foramen spinosum
options.E: Subclavian arterial plexus within the posterior triangle of the neck

explanation: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers originate from cell bodies in the superior cervical ganglion and diverge along two distinct arterial networks. Fibers destined for the forehead and medial orbital structures accompany the internal carotid artery (ICA) plexus through the carotid canal and cavernous sinus before branching into the orbit via the ophthalmic artery. In contrast, sympathetic sudomotor and vasomotor fibers supplying the remainder of the face, cheek, and jaw travel along the external carotid artery (ECA) plexus. Thus, an isolated ICA dissection produces Horner syndrome with anhidrosis restricted to the forehead or with completely spared facial sweating.
high_yield_pearl: Horner syndrome from internal carotid artery dissection spares sweating over the lower face because sudomotor fibers to the face travel via the external carotid artery.

stem: A 63-year-old male presents with right hand weakness. Examination shows atrophy of the first dorsal interosseous and hypothenar muscles of the right hand, with frequent visible fasciculations. Deep tendon reflexes in the right arm are 0. Sensory testing reveals intact pinprick, temperature, and touch perception throughout both upper extremities. What is the location of the primary pathology in this patient?

options.A: Precentral gyrus motor cortex
options.B: Internal capsule posterior limb
options.C: Anterior horn lower motor neurons at C8–T1
options.D: Dorsal root ganglion at C8–T1
options.E: Lateral corticospinal tract in the cervical spinal cord

explanation: Localized LMN signs restricted to the right hand (marked muscle atrophy, visible fasciculations, weakness, absent reflexes) with completely intact sensory perception indicate isolated destruction of lower motor neuron cell bodies in the right anterior horn of the C8–T1 spinal segments. Option (A) causes UMN signs; Option (B) causes contralateral spastic hemiplegia; Option (D) causes sensory loss; Option (E) causes UMN spasticity below the lesion.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterior horn lower motor neurons at C8–T1

stem: A 28-year-old patient presents with vertical diplopia when reading a book. She compensates by tilting her head to the right side. Physical examination confirms a left trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy. Which muscle is paralyzed in the left eye?

options.A: Superior oblique muscle causing depression when adducted and intorsion
options.B: Inferior oblique muscle causing elevation when adducted and extorsion
options.C: Superior rectus muscle causing elevation when abducted and intorsion
options.D: Inferior rectus muscle causing depression when abducted and extorsion
options.E: Lateral rectus muscle causing horizontal abduction in the transverse plane

explanation: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates exclusively the superior oblique muscle. The superior oblique depresses the eye when adducted, intorts the globe, and causes slight abduction. In a left trochlear nerve palsy, the left superior oblique is paralyzed. When the patient attempts to read a book or walk down stairs (tasks requiring depression of the adducted eye), vertical and torsional diplopia occurs. To compensate, patients tilt their head to the contralateral (right) side, which aligns the visual axes by utilizing intorsion in the normal right eye and reducing demand on the paralyzed left eye.
high_yield_pearl: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy paralyzes the superior oblique muscle, causing vertical diplopia on downgaze and compensatory contralateral head tilt.

stem: A 55-year-old male with a lateral brainstem lesion presents with a left-sided Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). A lesion in the lateral brainstem damages first-order sympathetic fibers as they descend adjacent to which sensory pathway?

options.A: Dorsal column pathway carrying ascending fine touch and proprioception
options.B: Anterolateral spinothalamic tract carrying contralateral pain sensation
options.C: Descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic tract in the lateral tegmentum
options.D: Medial lemniscus carrying ascending epicritic sensation to the VPL
options.E: Corticospinal tract carrying descending voluntary motor signals in the pyramid

explanation: In lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), typically caused by infarction of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), ischemia affects the dorsolateral tegmentum of the medulla. Within this region travel the uncrossed first-order descending sympathetic fibers of the hypothalamospinal tract. Interruption of these descending sympathetic axons abolishes sympathetic outflow to the ipsilateral ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T2), resulting in an ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
high_yield_pearl: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) causes ipsilateral Horner syndrome due to interruption of the descending hypothalamospinal sympathetic tract.

stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents because he frequently awakens during the first third of the night screaming, sweating, tachypneic, and inconsolable. During these episodes, he does not recognize his parents. After 5 minutes, he falls back asleep. In the morning, he has complete amnesia for the event. Which parasomnia is this, and during which sleep stage does it occur?

options.A: Nightmare disorder occurring during phasic REM sleep
options.B: Sleep terror disorder occurring during N3 slow-wave sleep
options.C: REM sleep behavior disorder occurring during desynchronized REM
options.D: Confusional arousal occurring during light N1 sleep
options.E: Sleep-related bruxism occurring during stage N2 sleep

explanation: Night terrors occur during N3 slow-wave sleep in early night. Symptoms include abrupt awakening with a scream, severe autonomic arousal (tachycardia, diaphoresis), inconsolable fear, failure to recognize parents, and complete amnesia for the event in the morning. Option (A) occurs during REM in late night with dream recall; Option (C) involves dream enactment in REM; Option (D) is motor atonia on waking; Option (E) occurs during wakefulness.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Night terrors (sleep terrors); N3 slow-wave sleep
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: An investigator measures brain stem neurotransmitter activity across the sleep-wake cycle in healthy human subjects. Acetylcholine levels in the pontine tegmentum reach their peak firing rates during which specific stage of sleep?

options.A: Stage N1 NREM sleep
options.B: Stage N2 NREM sleep
options.C: Stage N3 NREM sleep
options.D: Paradoxical REM sleep
options.E: Awake state with eyes open

explanation: Cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine and lateral dorsal tegmental nuclei (PPT/LDT) fire at peak rates during REM sleep. Acetylcholine release drives cortical desynchronization (sawtooth waves) and rapid eye movements. Monoamines (norepinephrine, serotonin) are silent during REM sleep. Options (A), (B), (C), and (E) feature lower relative cholinergic dominance over monoamines.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: REM sleep
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 45-year-old male with narcolepsy is started on a medication regime that includes scheduled naps and sleep hygiene optimization. Which medication class is used to promote daytime wakefulness in patients with narcolepsy?

options.A: Stimulants (e.g., modafinil)
options.B: Benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam)
options.C: Antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine)
options.D: Antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol)
options.E: Anticonvulsants (e.g., valproate)

explanation: First-line pharmacotherapy to promote daytime wakefulness and reduce excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy includes wake-promoting agents such as modafinil, armodafinil, or solriamfetol. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) cause sedation and exacerbate daytime sleepiness.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Stimulants (e.g., modafinil)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 65-year-old male presents with a PComm aneurysm compressing the outer surface of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Why are parasympathetic pupillary constrictor fibers affected earliest in compressive CN III lesions?

options.A: Parasympathetic fibers travel deep within the central core of the nerve
options.B: Parasympathetic fibers are situated superficially on the outer perimeter of the nerve
options.C: Parasympathetic fibers are unmyelinated and completely lack microvascular blood supply
options.D: Parasympathetic fibers synapse directly within the sensory trigeminal ganglion
options.E: Parasympathetic fibers exit through the internal acoustic meatus into the temporal bone

explanation: Within the oculomotor nerve (CN III), preganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers originating from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel superficially along the outer, peripheral circumference of the nerve sheath. This superficial anatomical orientation renders them exceptionally vulnerable to extrinsic compressive lesions, particularly aneurysms of the posterior communicating artery (PComm) or uncal herniation. Consequently, compressive CN III lesions present with early, pronounced pupillary dilation (mydriasis) and loss of pupillary light reflexes before somatic extraocular muscle weakness develops.
high_yield_pearl: Superficial peripheral localization of parasympathetic fibers on CN III explains early pupillary dilation in compressive lesions like PComm aneurysms.

stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with double vision. Examination reveals that when the patient is asked to look straight ahead, his left eye is fixed in a medially deviated position (esotropia) and cannot be abducted laterally past the midline. All other extraocular movements, palpebral fissure width, and pupillary reflexes are normal in both eyes. Which cranial nerve is damaged?

options.A: Left oculomotor nerve exiting the interpeduncular fossa
options.B: Left trochlear nerve exiting the dorsal midbrain tegmentum
options.C: Left abducens nerve exiting the pontomedullary junction
options.D: Right frontal eye field within the precentral motor cortex
options.E: Left trigeminal nerve exiting the mid-pontine tegmentum

explanation: The abducens nerve (CN VI) purely innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye. An isolated left abducens nerve palsy prevents the left eye from abducting past the midline. At rest, unopposed action of the ipsilateral medial rectus causes medial deviation (esotropia), leading to horizontal binocular diplopia that worsens when looking toward the affected left side. Normal palpebral fissure width and normal pupillary reflexes confirm that the oculomotor and sympathetic pathways are completely unaffected.
high_yield_pearl: Abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy causes isolated abduction failure and horizontal diplopia that worsens on attempted gaze toward the affected side.

stem: A 18-year-old male presents for a routine vision test. He can see distant objects clearly, but near objects appear blurry unless corrected with convex lenses. Refractive testing confirms hyperopia. How does a convex lens correct hyperopia?

options.A: Moves the focal point forward onto the retina
options.B: Moves the focal point backward behind the retina
options.C: Flattens the corneal curvature
options.D: Increases intraocular fluid drainage
options.E: Constricts the pupil

explanation: Hyperopia (farsightedness) occurs when the eye is structurally too short, focusing light rays behind the retina. A convex (converging) spherical lens increases refractive power, bending light rays inward sooner to move the focal point forward directly onto the retina. Concave lenses (B) correct myopia by moving focal point backward; Flattening cornea (C) is refractive surgery; Fluid drainage (D) treats glaucoma; Miosis (E) alters light entry.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Moves the focal point forward onto the retina

stem: A 40-year-old male complains of severe difficulty initiating sleep. He is diagnosed with primary insomnia. He is instructed on proper sleep hygiene principles. Which of the following is a key component of sleep hygiene?

options.A: Maintaining a regular sleep schedule and sleeping in a dark, quiet, cool room
options.B: Exercising vigorously 30 minutes before bedtime
options.C: Drinking a warm alcoholic beverage immediately before going to sleep
options.D: Lying in bed awake for 2 hours while watching television to relax
options.E: Taking long 2-hour naps in the late afternoon

explanation: Core components of sleep hygiene in cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) include maintaining a regular sleep-wake schedule, creating an optimal sleep environment (dark, quiet, cool), avoiding stimulants/alcohol near bedtime, and using the bed only for sleep and sex. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) violate sleep hygiene rules.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Maintaining a regular sleep schedule and sleeping in a dark, quiet, cool room
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 75-year-old male presents with symmetric, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss that has developed gradually over 10 years (presbycusis). When performing a Weber tuning fork test at 512 Hz on this patient, what is the expected finding?

options.A: Sound lateralizes distinctly to the right ear
options.B: Sound lateralizes distinctly to the left ear
options.C: Sound is heard equally in the midline / both ears
options.D: Sound is heard only through bone conduction on the mastoid
options.E: Sound is completely absent bilaterally

explanation: Presbycusis produces symmetric, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Performing a Weber test (512 Hz tuning fork) on a patient with symmetric hearing thresholds stimulates both cochleae equally via bone conduction, so sound is perceived equally in the midline / both ears. Options (A) and (B) require asymmetric loss; Option (D) indicates conductive loss; Option (E) is incorrect as low/intermediate frequencies remain detectable.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Sound is heard equally in the midline / both ears
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 50-year-old male with severe obstructive sleep apnea refuses to wear a CPAP mask. He asks about alternative management strategies. Which non-pharmacological management strategy is recommended for obstructive sleep apnea?

options.A: Weight reduction, positional therapy, and mandibular advancement appliances
options.B: High-dose oral zolpidem hypnotic pharmacotherapy administered at bedtime
options.C: Bilateral cervical sympathetic ganglionectomy and vagal neurotomy
options.D: Surgical stapedectomy with insertion of a Teflon middle ear prosthesis
options.E: Bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation electrode placement

explanation: In patients with OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP, effective non-pharmacological interventions include weight loss, positional therapy, custom mandibular advancement oral appliances, or hypoglossal nerve stimulation. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) are non-indicated or inappropriate.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Weight loss and positional therapy / mandibular advancement devices
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 66-year-old female presents with sudden onset of visual loss described as a "curtain drawn down" over her right eye, preceded by flashes of light (photopsia) and floaters. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Retinal detachment
options.B: Open-angle glaucoma
options.C: Cataracts
options.D: Dry macular degeneration
options.E: Presbycusis

explanation: Retinal detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), depriving photoreceptors of choroidal blood supply. Classic symptoms include sudden painless visual field loss described as a "curtain drawn down," preceded by flashes of light (photopsia) and floaters. Glaucoma (B) is insidious peripheral loss; Cataracts (C) cause gradual glare/clouding; Dry ARMD (D) causes central visual distortion; Presbycusis (E) is hearing loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Retinal detachment

stem: An investigator maps the pathway for pupillary dilation (sympathetic pathway). First-order neurons originate in the hypothalamus and descend through the lateral brainstem adjacent to the anterolateral system (ALS). Where do these first-order axons terminate onto second-order preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies?

options.A: Superior cervical ganglion in the upper cervical neck
options.B: Intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord from C8 to T2
options.C: Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.D: Ciliary ganglion located in the posterior orbital apex
options.E: Trigeminal motor nucleus located in the mid-pontine tegmentum

explanation: The oculosympathetic pathway is a three-neuron chain. First-order central neurons originate in the posterolateral hypothalamus and descend uncrossed through the brainstem (lateral medulla) to terminate onto second-order preganglionic sympathetic cell bodies in the intermediolateral (IML) cell column of the spinal cord from C8 to T2 (the ciliospinal center of Budge). Second-order axons exit via T1 ventral roots and white rami communicantes, traverse the lung apex, and ascend through the cervical sympathetic trunk to synapse in the superior cervical ganglion. Third-order postganglionic axons then ascend along the internal and external carotid arteries to reach the orbit and face.
high_yield_pearl: First-order central sympathetic neurons synapse onto second-order preganglionic neurons in the ciliospinal center of Budge (IML column at C8–T2).

stem: A 45-year-old female complains of restless legs syndrome (RLS) that impairs her ability to fall asleep. Laboratory evaluation shows a low serum ferritin level (12 ng/mL). What underlying medical etiology is evaluated and addressed in patients presenting with restless legs syndrome?

options.A: Iron deficiency
options.B: Hypercalcemia
options.C: Vitamin C deficiency
options.D: Elevated serum potassium
options.E: Hypothyroidism

explanation: Restless legs syndrome is strongly associated with central nervous system iron deficiency (low serum ferritin). Iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase in central dopamine synthesis; replacing iron improves RLS symptoms. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) are not the primary metabolic deficiency in RLS.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Iron deficiency
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 38-year-old female presents with progressive left-sided hearing loss and occasional foul-smelling ear discharge. Otoscopy reveals a white, keratinaceous cystic mass behind an intact left tympanic membrane, with erosion of the ossicles. Audiometry confirms a left conductive hearing loss. Which of the following is the primary diagnosis?

options.A: Glomus tympanicum tumor
options.B: Cholesteatoma
options.C: Vestibular schwannoma
options.D: Otitis externa
options.E: Presbycusis

explanation: A cholesteatoma is a benign epidermal cyst of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid, often resulting from chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction or eardrum perforation. It appears as a white mass behind the eardrum and produces lytic enzymes that erode middle ear ossicles, causing conductive hearing loss. Option (A) is a vascular glomus tumor; Option (C) is a CPA sensorineural tumor; Option (D) affects external canal; Option (E) is age-related sensorineural loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Cholesteatoma
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 71-year-old male with chronic hypertension suffers an ischemic stroke involving the right pyramid in the rostral medulla. Which of the following motor deficits will be observed on physical examination?

options.A: Left-sided spastic hemiplegia of the body with sparing of the face
options.B: Right-sided flaccid hemiplegia of the body
options.C: Left-sided lower facial droop with intact body motor function
options.D: Right-sided complete facial paralysis and body ataxia
options.E: Bilateral complete motor paralysis below the neck

explanation: The medullary pyramids contain uncrossed corticospinal fibers above the pyramidal decussation. Corticobulbar fibers for facial motor nuclei have already terminated in the pons. Therefore, a right medullary pyramid lesion selectively damages corticospinal axons, causing contralateral (left-sided) spastic hemiplegia of the body, completely sparing facial motor function. Option (B) describes LMN flaccidity; Option (C) misattributes facial fibers to medulla; Option (D) describes pontine/PICA lesion; Option (E) describes complete bilateral cord transection.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left-sided spastic hemiplegia of the body with sparing of the face

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a pineal gland tumor (pinealoma) compressing the dorsal midbrain tegmentum and posterior commissure. On examination, he exhibits total paralysis of upward vertical gaze, pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupils, and eyelid retraction. What is the name of this dorsal midbrain clinical syndrome?

options.A: Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome
options.B: Parinaud dorsal midbrain syndrome
options.C: Weber ventromedial midbrain syndrome
options.D: Horner oculosympathetic syndrome
options.E: Brown-Séquard spinal cord syndrome

explanation: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome) is caused by compression or damage to the dorsal midbrain tegmentum, pretectal area, and posterior commissure, classically due to a pineal gland tumor (pinealoma) in children or young adults, or dorsal midbrain strokes in older adults. The clinical tetrad consists of: 1) paralysis of vertical conjugate upward gaze (due to compression of the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF and posterior commissure), 2) pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupils (light-near dissociation from pretectal damage), 3) bilateral eyelid retraction (Collier sign), and 4) convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upward gaze.
high_yield_pearl: Parinaud syndrome is caused by pinealomas compressing the dorsal midbrain, presenting with upward gaze palsy, light-near dissociation, and eyelid retraction.

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with acute weakness in her lower limbs following a viral illness. Neurological exam reveals 1/5 strength in both legs, flaccid muscle tone, absent patellar and Achilles reflexes bilaterally, and muscle fasciculations in the calves. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing). Sensory perception is completely intact across all dermatomes. What is the anatomical location of the disrupted neural structures?

options.A: Precentral gyrus motor cortex bilaterally
options.B: Anterior horn motor neurons of the lumbosacral spinal cord
options.C: Lateral corticospinal tracts at the thoracic spinal cord
options.D: Dorsal column pathways at the L1 level
options.E: Bilateral genu of the internal capsule

explanation: Acute, symmetrical LMN deficits in the lower extremities (flaccid weakness, areflexia, calf muscle fasciculations, downgoing toes) with completely intact sensory perception indicate localized viral/inflammatory damage to lower motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior horns of the lumbosacral spinal cord. Option (A) causes UMN spasticity; Option (C) causes UMN signs below lesion; Option (D) causes sensory proprioceptive loss; Option (E) causes UMN hemiplegia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterior horn motor neurons of the lumbosacral spinal cord

stem: A 60-year-old male with chronic neurosyphilis presents with small, irregular pupils bilaterally. Physical examination demonstrates that his pupils do NOT constrict when exposed to bright direct or consensual light. However, when he is asked to focus on a tip of a pen moved close to his nose, both pupils constrict promptly, the eyes converge, and the lenses round up. What is the clinical name for this classic pupillary finding ("light-near dissociation")?

options.A: Marcus Gunn afferent pupil
options.B: Argyll Robertson light-near pupil
options.C: Horner oculosympathetic syndrome
options.D: Adie tonic postganglionic pupil
options.E: Fixed dilated paralytic pupil

explanation: Argyll Robertson pupil is a hallmark manifestation of tertiary neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis). The pupils are characteristically small, irregular, and bilateral; they do NOT constrict when exposed to direct or consensual light (absent pupillary light reflex), but constrict briskly when focusing on a near target during accommodation and convergence. This clinical dissociation ("light-near dissociation") is attributed to bilateral pretectal lesions in the dorsal rostral midbrain that interrupt light reflex fibers while sparing ventral accommodation fibers projecting directly from the visual cortex to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
high_yield_pearl: Argyll Robertson pupils feature light-near dissociation (accommodate but do not react to light), classically caused by neurosyphilis injuring dorsal midbrain pretectal fibers.

stem: A 67-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents with sudden onset of horizontal diplopia. Examination demonstrates that his left eye cannot abduct past the midline when looking to the left. When looking to the right, conjugate eye movement is normal. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Left abducens nerve palsy causing failure of left lateral rectus abduction
options.B: Left oculomotor nerve palsy causing failure of left medial rectus adduction
options.C: Right frontal eye field stroke causing voluntary saccadic horizontal failure
options.D: Left medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causing internuclear ophthalmoplegia
options.E: Parinaud syndrome causing paralysis of conjugate vertical upward gaze

explanation: An inability to abduct the left eye past the midline with normal conjugate movement on rightward gaze defines an isolated left abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy. The abducens nerve innervates solely the lateral rectus muscle, responsible for ocular abduction. Microvascular ischemia (frequently associated with long-standing hypertension and diabetes mellitus) is the most common cause of acute, isolated abducens nerve palsy in older adults, typically resolving spontaneously over 2 to 3 months.
high_yield_pearl: Isolated abduction failure of one eye with horizontal diplopia that worsens looking toward the paretic side is diagnostic of an abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy.

stem: A 10-year-old girl experiences scary, vivid dreams in which she is chased by monsters. She wakes up completely alert during the middle of the night, fully recalls the detailed scary dream, and is comforted by her mother. She remembers the nightmare clearly the next morning. Which parasomnia is represented, and during which sleep stage does it occur?

options.A: Night terrors; N3 slow-wave sleep
options.B: Nightmare disorder; REM sleep
options.C: Somnambulism; N2 sleep
options.D: Nocturnal enuresis; N3 sleep
options.E: Sleepwalking; N1 sleep

explanation: Nightmare disorder is a REM parasomnia occurring in the second half of the night. The child awakens fully alert, recalls detailed scary dream content, is easily comforted, and remembers the event next morning. Option (A) occurs in N3 with amnesia and inconsolability; Option (C) involves sleepwalking in N2/N3; Option (D) is bedwetting; Option (E) is sleepwalking.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Nightmare disorder; REM sleep
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A medical student reviews ocular anatomy and fluid dynamics. Aqueous humor is continuously secreted into the posterior chamber of the eye to maintain intraocular pressure and nourish avascular structures. Which anatomical structure synthesizes and secretes aqueous humor?

options.A: Trabecular meshwork
options.B: Ciliary body
options.C: Canal of Schlemm
options.D: Retinal pigment epithelium
options.E: Cornea

explanation: Aqueous humor is continuously synthesized and secreted by the ciliary body (located in the posterior chamber behind the iris). It flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains through the trabecular meshwork into the Canal of Schlemm. Options (A) and (C) mediate drainage; Option (D) supports photoreceptors; Option (E) is the transparent refractive surface.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ciliary body

stem: A 62-year-old male with long-standing hypertension suffers a stroke. Visual field testing reveals a complete right homonymous hemianopia. A lesion in which of the following locations can produce a complete right homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing?

options.A: Optic chiasm
options.B: Right optic nerve
options.C: Left optic tract
options.D: Right Meyer loop
options.E: Left cuneus gyrus exclusively

explanation: A complete homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing requires complete interruption of visual fibers carrying the contralateral hemifield prior to the visual cortex, such as a complete lesion of the left optic tract, left LGN, or complete left optic radiations. Optic chiasm (A) causes bitemporal hemianopia; Right optic nerve (B) causes right monocular blindness; Right Meyer loop (D) causes left upper quadrantanopia; Left cuneus (E) causes right lower quadrantanopia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left optic tract

stem: A 22-year-old student experiences excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and sleep paralysis. A diagnosis of narcolepsy is made. Genetic testing reveals a strong association with a specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) allele. Which HLA allele is strongly associated with narcolepsy?

options.A: HLA-B27 allele
options.B: HLA-DR4 allele
options.C: HLA-DQB1*0602
options.D: HLA-DR3 allele
options.E: HLA-B51 allele

explanation: Over 90% of patients with Narcolepsy Type 1 (orexin deficiency with cataplexy) carry the specific human leukocyte antigen allele HLA-DQB1*0602, reflecting an autoimmune etiology targeting lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons. Option (A) is associated with ankylosing spondylitis; Option (B) with Graves/SLE; Option (D) with RA; Option (E) with abacavir hypersensitivity.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: HLA-DQB1*0602
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 30-year-old male presents with loss of the cremasteric reflex on the left side following an inguinal hernia repair. The left testicle does not elevate when the inner left thigh is stroked. Which spinal cord segment roots form the reflex arc for this response?

options.A: C5–C6
options.B: C7–C8
options.C: L1–L2
options.D: L3–L4
options.E: S1–S2

explanation: The cremasteric reflex evaluates L1–L2 spinal cord segments. Sensory afferents travel via the ilioinguinal nerve to L1–L2, synapsing onto motor neurons that send efferent axons via the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2) to contract the cremaster muscle and elevate the testicle. Option (A) evaluates C5–C6 (biceps); Option (B) evaluates C7–C8 (triceps); Option (D) evaluates L3–L4 (patellar); Option (E) evaluates S1–S2 (Achilles).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: L1–L2

stem: An anatomical study reviews extraocular muscle functions. Which extraocular muscle elevates the eye when the eye is in an adducted (turned inward) position?

options.A: Superior rectus muscle elevating the eye when in an abducted position
options.B: Inferior oblique muscle elevating the eye when in an adducted position
options.C: Inferior rectus muscle depressing the eye when in an abducted position
options.D: Superior oblique muscle depressing the eye when in an adducted position
options.E: Lateral rectus muscle abducting the eye horizontally in the transverse plane

explanation: To test vertical extraocular muscles clinically, the examiner must align the optical axis with the muscle's primary line of pull. For the rectus muscles, the muscle plane aligns with the optical axis when the eye is ABDUCTED: the superior rectus is tested by asking the patient to look UP when the eye is ABDUCTED. For the oblique muscles, the line of pull aligns with the optical axis when the eye is ADDUCTED: the inferior oblique elevates the eye when it is turned INWARD (ADDUCTED), while the superior oblique depresses the eye when it is turned INWARD (ADDUCTED).
high_yield_pearl: The inferior oblique elevates the eye when in an adducted position, whereas the superior rectus elevates the eye when in an abducted position.

stem: A 30-year-old female undergoes visual testing. Images from the upper visual field strike which specific portion of the retina?

options.A: Superior retina superior to the horizontal raphe
options.B: Inferior retina inferior to the horizontal raphe
options.C: Nasal retina situated medial to the fovea centralis
options.D: Temporal retina situated lateral to the fovea centralis
options.E: Optic disc region containing exiting ganglion axons

explanation: Optical refraction through the cornea and crystalline lens inverts visual images both vertically and laterally. Stimuli from the upper visual field travel in straight lines to strike the lower retina. Stimuli from lower visual field strike upper retina. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) violate optical inversion.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Lower retina

stem: A 23-year-old male presents with difficulty maintaining balance while walking in a straight line. Neurological exam shows that when he stands with his feet together and closes his eyes, he sways significantly and loses his balance (positive Romberg test). Romberg testing evaluates the integrity of which sensory systems working together to maintain erect posture?

options.A: Visual system exclusively
options.B: Proprioceptive and vestibular sensory inputs
options.C: Auditory and corticospinal pathways
options.D: Cerebellar motor execution pathways exclusively
options.E: Autonomic baroreceptor reflexes

explanation: Standing balance relies on proprioception, vestibular inputs, and vision. Closing the eyes eliminates vision during Romberg testing. If proprioception or vestibular input is impaired, removing visual correction causes swaying and loss of balance (positive Romberg sign). Option (A) is eliminated by closing eyes; Option (C) does not maintain balance; Option (D) causes cerebellar ataxia with eyes open; Option (E) regulates blood pressure.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Proprioceptive and vestibular sensory inputs
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with sudden onset of severe dizziness. She describes a sensation that the room is spinning violently around her whenever she tilts her head to the right. The dizziness subsides within 45 seconds if she remains completely still. She denies tinnitus, ear fullness, or hearing difficulty. Physical exam reveals horizontal-rotatory nystagmus during the Dix-Hallpike maneuver. What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.A: Surgical endolymphatic sac decompression and shunting
options.B: Intratympanic gentamicin chemical vestibulotomy therapy
options.C: Canalith repositioning maneuver clearing displaced otoconia
options.D: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy
options.E: Suboccipital craniectomy for microvascular decompression

explanation: Brief (<1 min) spinning vertigo episodes triggered by head position changes, with rotatory positional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike and no hearing loss, define BPPV. First-line treatment is the Epley maneuver to reposition displaced otoconia back into the utricle. Option (A) is for inflammatory neuritis; Option (B) is for bacterial infections; Option (D) is for schwannoma; Option (E) is for Ménière disease.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Canalith repositioning procedure (Epley maneuver)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 61-year-old woman is evaluated in the clinic for difficulty speaking and eating. Examination reveals that when she is asked to open her mouth, her jaw deviates noticeably to the left side. Sensory examination of the face reveals normal perception of touch and pain across all three trigeminal divisions bilaterally. Which of the following underlying lesions is most consistent with this presentation?

options.A: Left corticobulbar tract lesion in the internal capsule
options.B: Left trigeminal motor nucleus or nerve root lesion in the mid-pons
options.C: Right trigeminal motor nucleus lesion in the rostral medulla
options.D: Right corticobulbar tract lesion in the crus cerebri
options.E: Bilateral lesion of the trigeminal sensory nuclei in the caudal pons

explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle opens the jaw and protrudes it toward the opposite side. Normal jaw opening requires balanced bilateral activation. A lower motor neuron lesion injuring the left trigeminal motor nucleus or nerve root (CN V) in the mid-pons weakens the left lateral pterygoid muscle. Upon opening the mouth, the unopposed contraction of the healthy right lateral pterygoid muscle pushes the jaw forward and shifts it toward the weak/lesioned (left) side. Options (A), (C), and (D) are incorrect because unilateral corticobulbar lesions do not cause functional jaw deviation due to bilateral corticobulbar innervation. Option (E) involves sensory nuclei.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left trigeminal motor nucleus or nerve root lesion in the mid-pons

stem: A 67-year-old male presents with gradual vision loss. Fundoscopy shows drusen deposits between the Bruch membrane and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). What visual symptom is characteristic of dry age-related macular degeneration (ARMD)?

options.A: Loss of peripheral vision with preserved central vision
options.B: Painless loss of central vision and visual distortion
options.C: Total monocular blindness in one eye
options.D: Severe eye pain with halos around lights
options.E: Flashes of light followed by a curtain drawn over vision

explanation: Age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) damages the macula/fovea centralis, producing painless, progressive loss of central visual acuity, metamorphosis (visual distortion), and central scotomas, impairing detailed tasks like reading and driving. Peripheral vision (A) is preserved; Monocular blindness (C) indicates optic nerve damage; Eye pain with halos (D) indicates acute glaucoma; Flashes and curtain (E) indicate retinal detachment.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Painless loss of central vision and visual distortion

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with tongue weakness. Physical examination reveals that her tongue is severely atrophied on the left side with active fasciculations present. When she is asked to protrude her tongue, it deviates sharply to the left. Body strength and sensation are completely normal bilaterally. Which of the following anatomical locations holds the primary lesion causing her tongue deviation?

options.A: Right precentral gyrus face representation area
options.B: Left hypoglossal nucleus or exiting nerve root in the rostral medulla
options.C: Right corticobulbar tract in the genu of the internal capsule
options.D: Left nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla
options.E: Right crus cerebri in the midbrain

explanation: Lower motor neurons for the tongue originate in the hypoglossal nucleus in the rostral medulla and project via CN XII to ipsilateral tongue muscles. An LMN lesion of the left hypoglossal nucleus or nerve root produces denervation, resulting in left tongue atrophy, active fasciculations, and deviation of the tongue toward the weak/lesioned side (left) upon protrusion. Option (A) causes contralateral tongue deviation without atrophy or fasciculations; Option (C) causes contralateral UMN tongue deviation without atrophy; Option (D) causes uvula deviation; Option (E) causes contralateral UMN tongue weakness.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left hypoglossal nucleus or exiting nerve root in the rostral medulla

stem: An investigator measures action potential frequencies in primary auditory afferent fibers exiting the cochlea. When sound waves cause the basilar membrane to deflect upward toward the tectorial membrane, stereocilia on hair cells bend toward the single tallest cilium (the kinocilium). What bioelectric event occurs within the hair cell during this directional bending?

options.A: Closure of mechanically-gated potassium channels leading to hyperpolarization
options.B: Opening of mechanically-gated potassium channels leading to influx of K+ and depolarization
options.C: Influx of sodium ions through voltage-gated Na+ channels causing repolarization
options.D: Efflux of calcium ions leading to total cessation of neurotransmitter release
options.E: Complete enzymatic degradation of intracellular rhodopsin

explanation: Bending hair cell stereocilia toward the kinocilium opens mechanically-gated potassium channels at tip links. Because endolymph has an exceptionally high K+ concentration (+80 mV potential), K+ rushes INTO the hair cell down electrical and concentration gradients, producing depolarization and neurotransmitter release. Option (A) occurs when bending away from kinocilium; Option (C) is incorrect as endolymph is high K+/low Na+; Option (D) causes neurotransmitter release; Option (E) is visual photopigment.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Opening of mechanically-gated potassium channels leading to influx of K+ and depolarization
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 68-year-old male suffers an acute ischemic stroke involving the primary visual cortex (occipital lobe). Perimetry testing reveals a left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Why is the central visual field (macula) preserved in cortical ischemic strokes involving the primary visual cortex?

options.A: Macula receives direct uncrossed fibers from the chiasm bypassing cortex
options.B: Macula has extensive cortical representation and dual PCA and MCA perfusion
options.C: Macula projects exclusively to subcortical tectal collicular reflex centers
options.D: Macula is represented bilaterally within the anterior temporal pole cortex
options.E: Macula contains exclusively rod photoreceptors that project to the thalamus

explanation: Macular sparing occurs in occipital lobe visual cortex strokes because the cortical territory representing the macula (at the occipital pole) is exceptionally large and receives collateral dual blood supply from penetrating branches of both the PCA and MCA. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misrepresent anatomical vascularization and pathways.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: The cortical representation of the macula is large and receives dual blood supply from both the Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA) and Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)

stem: An investigator evaluates the mechanics of frequency discrimination along the mammalian basilar membrane within the cochlea. Sound waves transmitted through the perilymph of the scala vestibuli induce traveling waves that reach maximum displacement at specific tonotopic regions. Which of the following structural properties characterizes the base of the basilar membrane near the oval window, and which acoustic frequencies does it preferentially transduce?

options.A: Wide and flexible membrane; low frequencies
options.B: Narrow and stiff membrane; high frequencies
options.C: Wide and stiff membrane; intermediate frequencies
options.D: Narrow and flexible membrane; low frequencies
options.E: Constant width membrane with gelatinous otoconia; ultra-low frequencies

explanation: The basilar membrane is tonotopically organized. Near the base (oval window), the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff, vibrating maximally at high acoustic frequencies (e.g., 20,000 Hz). Toward the apex (helicotrema), it is wide and flexible, vibrating maximally at low acoustic frequencies (e.g., 20 Hz). Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misdescribe the anatomical gradient.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Narrow and stiff membrane; high frequencies
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: An experimental researcher selectively stimulates the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) in an animal model. Which network of brainstem structures and projections constitutes the ARAS to maintain wakefulness and cortical arousal?

options.A: Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic nucleus in rostral midbrain
options.B: Brainstem reticular formation nodes projecting to thalamus and cortex
options.C: Nucleus ambiguus branchial motor neurons projecting via CN IX and X
options.D: Vestibular nuclear maculae projecting via lateral vestibulospinal tracts
options.E: Ventral horn alpha motor neurons projecting via anterior spinal roots

explanation: The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) consists of interconnected brainstem tegmental nodes (locus coeruleus, raphe, pedunculopontine, tuberomammillary) projecting to the thalamus and cortex to maintain wakefulness and cortical arousal. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) represent motor/autonomic/vestibular circuits.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Brainstem tegmental nodes projecting through widespread connections to the thalamus and cortex
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 55-year-old male presenting with visual difficulties is evaluated by a neurologist. Testing reveals that his visual sensation, visual fields, and acuity are entirely normal. However, when shown a common object such as a key or a watch, he cannot name or identify the object by sight alone, although he immediately identifies it when allowed to touch it. What term describes this cognitive perceptual deficit?

options.A: Anopia
options.B: Agnosia
options.C: Hemianopia
options.D: Quadrantanopia
options.E: Strabismus

explanation: Agnosia is a cognitive perceptual deficit where primary sensory reception (visual acuity, fields) is intact, but visual association cortex damage prevents interpretation or recognition of perceived sensory stimuli. Anopia (A), hemianopia (C), and quadrantanopia (D) represent primary visual field deficits. Strabismus (E) is ocular misalignment.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Agnosia

stem: A 40-year-old patient with insomnia takes zolpidem at bedtime. Zolpidem promotes sleep by enhancing the action of which primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system?

options.A: Gamma-aminobutyric acid neurotransmitter
options.B: Glutamate excitatory amino acid transmitter
options.C: Norepinephrine adrenergic locus coeruleus transmitter
options.D: Histamine tuberomammillary wakefulness transmitter
options.E: Substance P primary nociceptive neurotransmitter

explanation: Zolpidem enhances GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission by selectively binding to the alpha-1 subunit of the GABAA receptor, opening chloride channels and hyperpolarizing post-synaptic neurons. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) are not the primary mediator of zolpidem action.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: GABA
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 64-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of brief, sudden vertigo lasting 20 to 30 seconds. The episodes are triggered exclusively by changing his head position relative to gravity, such as turning over in bed or tilting his head back to look at a high shelf. He denies hearing loss, tinnitus, or focal weakness. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver induces transient torsional nystagmus with a 5-second latency. Which pathophysiological mechanism underlies this condition (BPPV)?

options.A: Excess accumulation of endolymph within the endolymphatic sac
options.B: Dislodged calcium carbonate otoconia floating into a semicircular canal
options.C: Post-viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve root
options.D: Schwann cell tumor compressing the internal auditory meatus
options.E: Ischemic stroke involving the lateral medulla

explanation: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) occurs when calcium carbonate otoconia from the utricular macula detach and float into a semicircular canal (most commonly posterior canal). Head position changes cause otoconia to shift in endolymph, deforming the cupula and triggering brief (<1 min) vertigo episodes with latenced, fatigable nystagmus. Option (A) describes Ménière disease; Option (C) describes vestibular neuritis; Option (D) describes schwannoma; Option (E) describes Wallenberg syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Dislodged calcium carbonate otoconia floating into a semicircular canal
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 26-year-old male is evaluated for a visual field deficit. The clinician notes that images from the right visual hemifield project to which side of the primary visual cortex?

options.A: Right primary visual cortex
options.B: Left primary visual cortex
options.C: Bilateral frontal lobes
options.D: Parietal lobes exclusively
options.E: Temporal lobes exclusively

explanation: Because optics invert visual hemifields and nasal fibers decussate at the optic chiasm, information from the complete right visual hemifield (from both eyes) projects exclusively to the left primary visual cortex (V1) in the left occipital lobe. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) violate contralateral visual processing.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left primary visual cortex

stem: A 22-year-old college student presents with severe daytime sleepiness, short-lived episodes of sudden muscle weakness triggered by laughter (cataplexy), and vivid, terrifying dream-like hallucinations right as she falls asleep (hypnagogic hallucinations). A deficiency in which neurochemical transmitter is pathognomonic for this disorder (Narcolepsy Type 1)?

options.A: Gamma-aminobutyric acid inhibitory neurotransmitter
options.B: Serotonergic inhibitory neurotransmitter
options.C: Orexin neuropeptide produced in lateral hypothalamus
options.D: Melatonin neurohormone synthesized in pineal gland
options.E: Glycine inhibitory neurotransmitter in spinal cord

explanation: Narcolepsy Type 1 is caused by selective loss of orexin-producing (hypocretin-producing) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Orexin stabilizes the sleep-wake switch. Orexin deficiency produces the tetrad: excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (triggered by emotions like laughter), hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis. Options (A), (B), (D), and (E) are not the primary depleted neuropeptide.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Orexin (hypocretin)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 64-year-old female presents with a tumor in the left temporal lobe. The mass compresses Meyer's loop. What visual field defect will be detected on formal field testing?

options.A: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.B: Right lower homonymous quadrantanopia
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Left upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.E: Monocular left anopia

explanation: Meyer's loop loops through the temporal lobe, carrying fibers from the lower retina (representing the upper visual field) on the same side as the pathway (left). Damage to left Meyer's loop produces a right upper (superior) homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"). Left parietal loop (B) causes right lower quadrantanopia; Chiasm (C) causes bitemporal loss; Right temporal loop (D) causes left upper quadrantanopia; Left optic nerve (E) causes monocular loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician due to fever, irritability, and right ear pain following an upper respiratory tract infection. Otoscopic examination demonstrates a bulging, erythematous right tympanic membrane with decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Which of the following underlying anatomical factors predisposes young children to recurrent middle ear infections (otitis media)?

options.A: Abnormally wide and vertical external auditory canal
options.B: Short, horizontal, and immature Eustachian tube
options.C: Absence of outer hair cells in the basal cochlea
options.D: Malformation of the semicircular canal cupula
options.E: Hypertrophy of the superior olivary complex

explanation: Infants and young children are predisposed to acute otitis media because their Eustachian tube is shorter, wider, and oriented more horizontally than in adults. This structural immaturity impairs fluid drainage and permits nasopharyngeal pathogens to ascend into the middle ear. Option (A) is incorrect; Option (C) affects inner ear hearing; Option (D) affects vestibular function; Option (E) is a central auditory nucleus.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Short, horizontal, and immature Eustachian tube
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 38-year-old male driver involved in an accident is evaluated for narcolepsy. Polysomnography reveals that he transitions directly from awake state into REM sleep within 5 minutes of falling asleep (shortened REM latency / SOREMP). What is the normal REM latency (time from sleep onset to first REM period) in a healthy adult?

options.A: 5 to 10 minutes
options.B: 20 to 30 minutes
options.C: 80 to 100 minutes
options.D: 180 to 240 minutes
options.E: 360 minutes

explanation: Normal sleep architecture progresses from N1 to N2 to N3, returning to N2 before entering the first REM episode. REM latency (time from sleep onset to first REM period) normally lasts 80 to 100 minutes. Narcolepsy features pathologically shortened REM latency (<15 minutes, SOREMP). Options (A) and (B) represent pathological SOREMPs; Options (D) and (E) represent multiple full cycles.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: 80 to 100 minutes
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 60-year-old male presents with a left-sided lower facial droop. He can close both eyes tightly and wrinkle his forehead bilaterally without difficulty. When asked to smile, the left corner of his mouth does not move. Strength in his left arm is 4/5, and the left biceps reflex is 3+. Which motor pathway is damaged, and on which side of the neuraxis is the lesion located?

options.A: Central core of the ventral horn gray matter
options.B: Lateral funiculus of the spinal cord white matter
options.C: Dorsal funiculus carrying ascending sensory fasciculi
options.D: Ventral funiculus carrying uncrossed axial motor axons
options.E: Substantia gelatinosa receiving primary nociceptive inputs

explanation: Lower facial motor neurons receive contralateral corticobulbar projections, whereas upper facial motor neurons receive bilateral projections. An UMN lesion interrupting the right corticobulbar tract causes left lower facial droop with forehead sparing. Concomitant right corticospinal tract damage causes contralateral (left-sided) body arm weakness and hyperreflexia. Option (B) causes total upper and lower left facial paralysis (Bell palsy); Option (C) causes right face/arm weakness; Option (D) causes total right facial paralysis; Option (E) causes palatal drooping.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right corticobulbar and corticospinal tracts

stem: An anatomical cross-section through the brainstem shows the midbrain colliculi. Which pair of dorsal midbrain structures receives visual projections and coordinates reflex eye and head movements toward visual stimuli?

options.A: Inferior colliculi
options.B: Superior colliculi
options.C: Lateral geniculate nuclei
options.D: Red nuclei
options.E: Nucleus gracilis

explanation: The superior colliculi form the upper tectum of the rostral midbrain, receiving direct visual projections and coordinating reflex orientation of head and eyes toward visual stimuli. Inferior colliculi (A) process auditory signals; LGN (C) is thalamic; Red nuclei (D) control motor tone; Nucleus gracilis (E) processes lower body touch.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Superior colliculi

stem: A 50-year-old male patient undergoes a sleep study. Polysomnography records electroencephalography, muscle activity, breathing parameters, and oxygen saturation. What term describes this comprehensive diagnostic recording of sleep parameters?

options.A: Polysomnogram
options.B: Electrocardiogram
options.C: Electromyogram
options.D: Electro-oculogram
options.E: Magnetoencephalogram

explanation: A polysomnogram is a comprehensive overnight sleep study that simultaneously records electroencephalography (EEG), electro-oculography (EOG), electromyography (EMG), heart rate, airflow, and respiratory effort to evaluate sleep architecture and sleep disorders. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) evaluate single isolated organ systems.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Polysomnogram
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty walking and loss of balance, worse in the dark. Examination reveals loss of vibration and joint position sense in both lower extremities. Romberg sign is positive. Motor strength is 5/5 throughout, but deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities are completely absent. Serological testing is positive for Treponema pallidum. Which structure in the spinal cord is primarily degenerated in this patient?

options.A: Lateral corticospinal tract
options.B: Anterior horn motor neurons
options.C: Dorsal columns and dorsal roots
options.D: Ventral white commissure
options.E: Anterolateral system

explanation: Tabes dorsalis (tertiary syphilis) causes slow degeneration of dorsal roots and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus). Loss of primary sensory neurons in dorsal roots abolishes deep tendon reflexes (areflexia). Loss of dorsal columns impairs fine touch, vibration, and proprioception, producing sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign. Option (A) causes spasticity and hyperreflexia; Option (B) causes LMN motor weakness and fasciculations; Option (D) causes suspended cape-like pain/temperature loss; Option (E) causes loss of pain and temperature perception.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Dorsal columns and dorsal roots

stem: A 45-year-old female presents to an optometry clinic complaining of difficulty reading fine print up close. She notes that she must hold books at arm's length to see the letters clearly. Distant vision is unchanged. Refractive testing indicates that images of nearby objects are being focused behind her retina due to age-related loss of lens elasticity and stiffness. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Myopia
options.B: Presbyopia
options.C: Astigmatism
options.D: Hyperopia
options.E: Congenital glaucoma

explanation: Presbyopia is an age-related loss of lens elasticity and stiffening of the crystalline lens, impairing accommodation for near vision so that images of close objects focus behind the retina. Myopia (A) occurs when the eye is too long (image focused in front of retina). Hyperopia (D) is farsightedness due to a structurally short eye present from youth. Astigmatism (C) is corneal curvature irregularity. Glaucoma (E) is optic neuropathy from elevated IOP.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Presbyopia

stem: A 24-year-old male presents following a head injury. Visual field testing reveals a right lower (inferior) homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor"). Which anatomical structure in the left hemisphere has been damaged by this lesion?

options.A: Left temporal lobe Meyer loop fibers
options.B: Left superior parietal optic radiations
options.C: Right superior parietal optic radiations
options.D: Optic chiasm decussating nasal fibers
options.E: Left lingual gyrus inferior visual cortex

explanation: A right lower (inferior) homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor") is caused by a lesion interrupting the superior optic radiations (dorsal loop) traveling through the left parietal lobe (or left cuneus gyrus). Left temporal loop (A) causes right upper quadrantanopia; Right parietal loop (C) causes left lower quadrantanopia; Optic chiasm (D) causes bitemporal hemianopia; Left lingual gyrus (E) causes right upper quadrantanopia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left superior optic radiations in the parietal lobe (dorsal loop)

stem: An ophthalmology researcher compares photoreceptor characteristics. Which set of features correctly describes rod photoreceptors compared to cone photoreceptors?

options.A: Low light sensitivity; high acuity; color vision; concentrated in fovea
options.B: High light sensitivity; low acuity; black and white vision; located in peripheral retina
options.C: Low light sensitivity; low acuity; color vision; located in optic disc
options.D: High light sensitivity; high acuity; color vision; concentrated in fovea
options.E: Absence of visual pigments; direct generation of action potentials

explanation: Rods exhibit high light sensitivity (specialized for dim/night vision), low visual acuity, black and white perception, and are concentrated in the peripheral retina using rhodopsin. Cones exhibit low light sensitivity (bright light), high acuity, color vision, and are concentrated in the fovea using cone opsins. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) mix rod and cone properties.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: High light sensitivity; low acuity; black and white vision; located in peripheral retina

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with acute, disabling room-spinning vertigo that woke her from sleep this morning. She reports intense nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, and steady horizontal nystagmus. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, or focal neurological deficits. The nystagmus suppresses significantly when she fixates her vision on a stationary thumb. Which of the following features strongly categorizes this patient's presentation as peripheral vertigo rather than central vertigo?

options.A: Non-fatigable nystagmus that changes direction with gaze shift
