options.B: Absence of visual suppression during gaze fixation
options.C: Suppression of intense vertigo and nystagmus by visual fixation
options.D: Presence of dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and limb ataxia
options.E: Co-occurrence of lower cranial nerve palsies

explanation: Peripheral vertigo (inner ear/CN VIII) is characterized by acute intense vertigo, unidirectional nystagmus with latency, and significant suppression of nystagmus/vertigo by visual fixation. Central vertigo (brainstem/cerebellum) exhibits non-suppressible, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus with central neurological signs. Option (A) indicates central vertigo; Option (B) indicates central vertigo; Option (D) indicates cerebellar central stroke; Option (E) indicates brainstem central stroke.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Suppression of intense vertigo and nystagmus by visual fixation
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 30-year-old female executive presents to her physician complaining of painful bumps on her forehead. She explains that over the past few months, she has repeatedly bumped her head on the open upper cabinets in her kitchen because she fails to notice them. Visual field testing demonstrates a right upper (superior) homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"). A lesion in which structure accounts for this specific defect?

options.A: Left temporal lobe involving Meyer loop
options.B: Left parietal lobe involving the dorsal loop
options.C: Right temporal lobe involving Meyer loop
options.D: Optic chiasm decussating nasal retinal fibers
options.E: Right parietal lobe involving the dorsal loop

explanation: A right upper (superior) homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky") is caused by a lesion interrupting Meyer's loop in the left temporal lobe (or left lingual gyrus). Meyer's loop carries fibers from the lower retina (which receives light from the upper visual field). Left parietal loop (B) causes right lower quadrantanopia; Right temporal loop (C) causes left upper quadrantanopia; Optic chiasm (D) causes bitemporal hemianopia; Right parietal loop (E) causes left lower quadrantanopia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left temporal lobe (Meyer loop)

stem: A 64-year-old male presents with difficulty speaking. Examination reveals that his tongue is atrophied on the right side with prominent fasciculations. On extension, his tongue deviates to the right. Strength in his body is 5/5, but deep tendon reflexes are 3+ on the left side of his body, and the left plantar response is upgoing. What type of brainstem syndrome is represented by this combination of ipsilateral lower motor neuron cranial nerve deficit and contralateral upper motor neuron body deficit?

options.A: Medial medullary syndrome from anterior spinal artery occlusion
options.B: Lateral medullary syndrome from posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion
options.C: Weber syndrome from posterior cerebral artery penetrating branch occlusion
options.D: Claude syndrome from dorsal midbrain tegmental infarction
options.E: Benedikt syndrome from ventral and tegmental midbrain infarction

explanation: Alternating hemiplegia occurs when a brainstem lesion damages an exiting cranial nerve or nucleus (ipsilateral LMN deficit) alongside the uncrossed corticospinal pyramid (contralateral UMN body hemiplegia). In Medial Medullary Syndrome, damage to the right hypoglossal nerve/nucleus causes ipsilateral (right) tongue atrophy, fasciculations, and deviation to the right, while damage to the right medullary pyramid causes contralateral (left-sided) body spastic hemiplegia. Option (B) spares the corticospinal pyramid; Option (C) affects dorsal midbrain vertical gaze; Option (D) affects sympathetic fibers; Option (E) affects lumbosacral roots.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Alternating hemiplegia (Medullary medial syndrome)

stem: An anatomical cross-section of the caudal midbrain is examined under a microscope. A prominent pair of rounded, dorsal nuclear masses is identified, forming the lower tectum. These structures receive auditory projections via the lateral lemniscus and project to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. What are these dorsal midbrain structures?

options.A: Superior colliculi
options.B: Inferior colliculi
options.C: Red nuclei
options.D: Substantia nigra
options.E: Nucleus gracilis

explanation: The dorsal caudal midbrain tectum contains the inferior colliculi, which receive ascending auditory fibers from the lateral lemniscus and project via the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) of the thalamus. Superior colliculi mediate visual reflexes. Option (A) is visual; Option (C) gives rise to rubrospinal tract; Option (D) produces dopamine; Option (E) processes lower body touch.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Inferior colliculi
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: An auditory researcher presents a 1000 Hz tone to a test subject's left ear. Action potentials ascend from the left cochlear nucleus. Some axons cross the midline in the caudal pons to reach the contralateral superior olivary complex. What is the name of this transverse decussating axon bundle in the caudal pontine tegmentum?

options.A: Corpus callosum
options.B: Trapezoid body
options.C: Brachium conjunctivum
options.D: Anterior white commissure
options.E: Medial longitudinal fasciculus

explanation: Second-order auditory axons from the ventral cochlear nucleus cross the midline in the caudal pontine tegmentum to reach the contralateral superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus. This transverse decussating axon bundle in the caudal pons is the trapezoid body. Option (A) connects cerebral hemispheres; Option (C) forms superior cerebellar peduncle; Option (D) carries decussating spinothalamic fibers in the spinal cord; Option (E) connects extraocular and vestibular nuclei.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Trapezoid body
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 65-year-old male presents with progressive leg weakness and urinary retention. Examination reveals bilateral lower extremity spasticity, ankle clonus, hyperactive patellar reflexes, and upgoing toes bilaterally. Sensory exam shows a distinct level where pinprick and temperature perception are lost below the T4 dermatome (nipple line). Fine touch and vibration are preserved bilaterally. Which spinal cord pathway lesion accounts for the loss of pinprick sensation below T4?

options.A: Dorsal columns conveying fine touch and vibration sensation
options.B: Anterolateral spinothalamic tracts conveying pain and temperature
options.C: Lateral corticospinal tracts conveying voluntary distal motor commands
options.D: Spinocerebellar tracts conveying unconscious muscle proprioception
options.E: Reticulospinal tracts modulating bilateral postural anti-gravity tone

explanation: Pain and temperature fibers decussate in the ventral white commissure and ascend in the anterolateral system (spinothalamic tract). Bilateral disruption of spinothalamic tracts at T4 blocks ascending pain and temperature signals from all dermatomes below that level (T4 nipple line). Option (A) carries fine touch/proprioception; Option (C) carries voluntary motor commands; Option (D) carries peripheral nerve fibers; Option (E) carries lower body proprioception/vibration.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterolateral system (spinothalamic tracts) bilaterally

stem: A 28-year-old male receives an intravenous course of gentamicin for a severe Gram-negative infection. One week into therapy, he develops oscillopsia, severe imbalance, and bilateral high-frequency hearing loss. Gentamicin causes ototoxicity by destroying which cells?

options.A: Hair cells within the cochlea and vestibular organs
options.B: Oligodendrocytes myelinating the proximal optic nerve
options.C: Thalamic relay neurons in the medial geniculate body
options.D: Peripheral Schwann cells enveloping the facial nerve
options.E: Pyramidal projection neurons in the auditory cortex

explanation: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin) generate reactive oxygen species in inner ear endolymph that selectively destroy mechanosensitive hair cells in the organ of Corti (causing sensorineural hearing loss) and vestibular organs (causing oscillopsia and ataxia). Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) are not the primary target of aminoglycoside ototoxicity.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Inner and outer hair cells in the cochlea and vestibular organs
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 29-year-old male presents with excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy. He is diagnosed with Narcolepsy Type 1. Which brain region houses the orexin-producing neurons that are deficient in this patient?

options.A: Lateral hypothalamus
options.B: Substantia nigra
options.C: Nucleus basalis of Meynert
options.D: Median raphe nucleus
options.E: Caudate nucleus

explanation: Orexin-producing (hypocretin-producing) neurons reside in the lateral hypothalamic area. Autoimmune destruction of these neurons causes Narcolepsy Type 1. Option (B) produces dopamine; Option (C) produces acetylcholine; Option (D) produces serotonin; Option (E) is basal ganglia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Lateral hypothalamus
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 35-year-old male shift worker experiences difficulty sleeping during the day after working night shifts. Physiology experiments demonstrate that during periods of darkness, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) signals through a sympathetic pathway to stimulate the synthesis and secretion of a hormone that promotes sleep. Which structure secretes this sleep-promoting hormone, and what is the hormone?

options.A: Anterior pituitary gland secreting adrenocorticotropic hormone
options.B: Epithalamic pineal gland secreting evening melatonin
options.C: Posterior pituitary gland secreting arginine vasopressin
options.D: Adrenal cortex secreting diurnal glucocorticoid hormones
options.E: Thyroid gland follicular cells secreting levothyroxine

explanation: In darkness, SCN relief of sympathetic inhibition stimulates the pineal gland to synthesize and secrete melatonin. Melatonin promotes sleep onset and synchronizes circadian rhythms. Option (A) secretes growth hormone; Option (C) secretes wake-promoting orexin; Option (D) secretes GABA locally; Option (E) secretes epinephrine.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Pineal gland; melatonin
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A neurophysiologist measures extraocular muscle activity during horizontal saccades. To execute a voluntary conjugate horizontal gaze to the right, the right Frontal Eye Field (FEF) projects across the midline to activate which pontine structure?

options.A: Left Edinger-Westphal nucleus within the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.B: Right frontal eye field projecting across the midline to the left PPRF
options.C: Right trochlear nucleus projecting dorsally around the periaqueductal gray
options.D: Right superior colliculus projecting to the spinal accessory motor nucleus
options.E: Left ciliary ganglion projecting postganglionic fibers via short ciliary nerves

explanation: Voluntary horizontal saccadic eye movements are generated by the frontal eye field (FEF) in the precentral cortex (area 8). To direct horizontal gaze to the left, the RIGHT FEF fires and projects descending decussating axons across the midline to the LEFT paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) in the caudal pons. The left PPRF activates the adjacent left abducens nucleus, which directly drives the left lateral rectus and sends crossing internuclear axons through the right MLF to activate the right medial rectus, executing a conjugate saccade to the left.
high_yield_pearl: Voluntary horizontal saccades to the left require activation of the right frontal eye field, which projects across the midline to the left PPRF.

stem: A 30-year-old male undergoes a complete neurological examination. The physician tests the accommodation reflex by asking the patient to focus on a finger as it moves rapidly from 1 meter away to 10 centimeters from his nose. What three characteristic physiological responses occur simultaneously during the accommodation reflex?

options.A: Pupillary dilation, lens flattening, and bilateral eye abduction
options.B: Pupillary constriction, lens rounding, and bilateral eye convergence
options.C: Horizontal nystagmus, upper eyelid ptosis, and facial anhidrosis
options.D: Upward vertical gaze elevation, mydriasis, and eyelid retraction
options.E: Pupillary miosis, upper facial paralysis, and ipsilateral jaw deviation

explanation: The accommodation-convergence reflex (near response) is triggered when visual fixation shifts from a distant target to a nearby object. It consists of a classic physiological triad: 1) pupillary constriction (parasympathetic stimulation of sphincter pupillae to increase optical depth of field), 2) lens rounding / thickening (parasympathetic stimulation of the ciliary muscle relaxes zonular fibers, allowing the lens to become more convex and increase refractive power), and 3) convergence of the optical axes (bilateral oculomotor nerve stimulation of the medial recti to align both foveas on the near object).
high_yield_pearl: The accommodation triad for near vision consists of pupillary constriction, lens rounding (ciliary muscle contraction), and convergence (medial recti).

stem: A 58-year-old male with a history of cervical spondylosis presents with weakness in extending his left elbow. Reflex testing reveals an absent triceps reflex on the left side, whereas the biceps reflex is 2+ bilaterally. Which spinal cord roots form the efferent limb of the triceps reflex arc?

options.A: C5–C6
options.B: C6–C8
options.C: L1–L2
options.D: L3–L4
options.E: S1–S2

explanation: The triceps reflex arc tests C6–C8 (predominantly C7) spinal roots and the radial nerve. Muscle spindle afferents enter C6–C8 dorsal horn, synapsing onto alpha motor neurons in C6–C8 ventral horn that send motor axons via the radial nerve to contract the triceps muscle. Option (A) evaluates C5–C6; Option (C) evaluates L1–L2; Option (D) evaluates L3–L4; Option (E) evaluates S1–S2.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: C6–C8

stem: A 62-year-old female suffers a small, localized lacunar infarct involving the right lateral lemniscus in the rostral pons. Which of the following best describes the expected auditory impairment resulting from this unilateral brainstem lesion?

options.A: Total bilateral sensorineural deafness for high-frequency acoustic pure tones
options.B: Complete unilateral conductive hearing loss involving the low-frequency range
options.C: Impaired spatial localization of sound with minimal loss of auditory thresholds
options.D: Severe rotational vertigo accompanied by prominent spontaneous downbeat nystagmus
options.E: Selective loss of bone conduction with completely preserved air conduction

explanation: Above the cochlear nuclei, ascending auditory pathways ascend bilaterally through the lateral lemniscus. Because each lateral lemniscus receives input from both ears, a unilateral brainstem lesion above the cochlear nucleus (e.g., right lateral lemniscus) does not cause monaural deafness, but disrupts binaural processing, impairing sound localization in space. Option (A) occurs only with CN VIII or cochlear nucleus lesions; Option (B) describes conductive loss; Option (D) is incorrect as frequency perception is maintained bilaterally; Option (E) requires bilateral cortical lesions.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Impaired precision of sound localization in space, with minimal loss of hearing thresholds
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 50-year-old patient presents with a Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect) in the left eye caused by optic neuritis. When a swinging flashlight is moved from the healthy right eye to the affected left eye, what paradoxical response is observed in both pupils?

options.A: Both pupils constrict further symmetrically when light enters the left eye
options.B: Both pupils dilate paradoxically when the light is swung to the affected left eye
options.C: The left pupil dilates while the right pupil constricts completely
options.D: Both upper eyelids develop complete flaccid ptosis and facial drooping
options.E: The left eye deviates sharply medially due to unopposed medial rectus tone

explanation: A Marcus Gunn pupil, or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), is diagnostic of an incomplete unilateral lesion of the optic nerve (CN II) or severe unilateral retinal disease (frequently caused by optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis). When the "swinging flashlight test" is performed, shining light into the normal right eye elicits robust bilateral pupillary constriction. When the light is rapidly swung across to the affected left eye, the diminished afferent sensory transmission is perceived by the brainstem as a decrease in overall illumination, causing paradoxical dilation of BOTH pupils relative to their previously constricted state.
high_yield_pearl: In a Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD), the swinging flashlight test elicits paradoxical bilateral pupillary dilation when light is moved to the affected eye.

stem: A neurophysiologist investigates the sensory receptors within the vestibular apparatus that detect head rotation (angular acceleration) versus linear acceleration. Which specific vestibular structure houses hair cells embedded in a gelatinous cupula that responds to fluid movement induced by head pitch, roll, and yaw?

options.A: Macula of the utricle
options.B: Macula of the saccule
options.C: Ampulla / Crista of the semicircular canals
options.D: Organ of Corti in the scala media
options.E: Spiral ganglion of the cochlea

explanation: Semicircular canals detect angular acceleration (head rotation). Each canal ampulla contains a crista ampullaris lined with hair cells embedded in a gelatinous cupula that deforms with fluid movement during pitch, roll, and yaw. Utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration. Option (A) detects horizontal linear acceleration; Option (B) detects vertical linear acceleration; Option (D) processes acoustic sound; Option (E) contains auditory cell bodies.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ampulla / Crista of the semicircular canals
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 22-year-old medical student reviews retinal histology. Arrange the three main cellular layers of the neural retina in the order that light passes through them before reaching the photoreceptors:

options.A: Photoreceptors -> Bipolar cells -> Ganglion cells
options.B: Ganglion cells -> Bipolar cells -> Photoreceptors
options.C: Bipolar cells -> Photoreceptors -> Ganglion cells
options.D: Retinal pigment epithelium -> Photoreceptors -> Bipolar cells
options.E: Photoreceptors -> Ganglion cells -> Bipolar cells

explanation: Light travels through the anterior neural layers before reaching the photoreceptors at the back of the retina. Thus, light passes through 3rd order Retinal Ganglion Cells first, then 2nd order Bipolar Cells, and finally hits 1st order Photoreceptors (rods and cones) adjacent to the pigmented layer. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) misorder retinal histology relative to light path.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ganglion cells -> Bipolar cells -> Photoreceptors

stem: A neurophysiologist maps the central auditory pathway following acoustic stimulation of the left ear. Action potentials originate in the spiral ganglion, travel along the cochlear division of CN VIII, and enter the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle. Where do these first-order auditory axons synapse onto second-order neuronal cell bodies?

options.A: Superior olivary nucleus in the caudal pons
options.B: Ipsilateral cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction
options.C: Inferior colliculus in the caudal midbrain
options.D: Medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
options.E: Transverse temporal gyrus of the cerebral cortex

explanation: Bipolar cell bodies in the spiral ganglion (1st order neurons) send peripheral processes to hair cells and central processes via CN VIII to synapse on 2nd order cell bodies in the ipsilateral cochlear nuclei (dorsal and ventral) at the pontomedullary junction. Option (A) contains 3rd order neurons; Option (C) contains 4th order neurons; Option (D) contains 5th order neurons; Option (E) is the primary auditory cortex.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ipsilateral cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: An investigator traces primary sensory signals from the eye to the cerebral cortex. Arrange the following visual pathway structures in the correct order of ascending signal transmission: (1) Optic tract, (2) Retinal ganglion cells, (3) Optic radiations, (4) Lateral geniculate nucleus, (5) Optic chiasm, (6) Primary visual cortex.
explanation: Ascending visual transmission order: Retinal ganglion cells (2) -> Optic nerve -> Optic chiasm (5) -> Optic tract (1) -> Lateral geniculate nucleus (4) -> Optic radiations (3) -> Primary visual cortex V1 (6). Sequence: 2 -> 5 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 6.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: 2 -> 5 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 6

stem: A 25-year-old male experiences an acute focal motor seizure originating from an irritative focus in his left Frontal Eye Field (FEF). During the active seizure burst, toward which direction will his eyes involuntarily turn?

options.A: Toward the left side and toward the irritative seizure focus
options.B: Toward the right side and away from the irritative seizure focus
options.C: Directly upward toward the superior orbital margin
options.D: Directly downward toward the inferior orbital margin
options.E: Strictly fixed in the neutral primary midline position

explanation: While a destructive lesion of the frontal eye field (FEF) causes the eyes to deviate toward the side of the lesion, an irritative lesion (such as an epileptogenic focal seizure originating in the FEF) produces the exact opposite effect. Seizure discharge hyperactivates the left FEF, driving forceful conjugate horizontal gaze across the midline to the contralateral (right) side. Therefore, during the active ictus, the patient's eyes involuntarily turn AWAY from the irritative cortical focus (to the right) and TOWARD the side of contralateral motor seizure activity.
high_yield_pearl: An irritative seizure focus in the frontal eye field drives conjugate eye deviation AWAY from the focus (contralaterally), opposite to a destructive stroke.

stem: A 35-year-old male suffers a severe pelvic fracture in a motorcycle accident. On examination, light stroking of the skin on the upper medial thigh fails to produce elevation of the testicle on the ipsilateral side (absent cremasteric reflex). Which spinal cord segments contain the primary reflex arc components for this response?

options.B: L1–L2
options.C: L3–L4
options.D: L5–S1
options.E: S3–S4

explanation: The cremasteric reflex is a superficial reflex where light stroking of the upper inner thigh stimulates sensory afferents carried by the ilioinguinal nerve to L1–L2 spinal segments. Synaptic transmission within L1–L2 activates motor neurons that send efferents via the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2) to contract the cremaster muscle and elevate the testicle. Option (A) evaluates T10–T11; Option (C) evaluates L3–L4; Option (D) evaluates L5–S1; Option (E) evaluates S3–S4.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: L1–L2

stem: A 65-year-old woman with chronic hypertension presents with a sudden visual field defect. Neuroimaging confirms an ischemic stroke involving the left lingual gyrus below the calcarine sulcus. Which visual field deficit will be present on formal perimetry?

options.A: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.B: Right lower homonymous quadrantanopia
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Left upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.E: Complete monocular blindness of the left eye

explanation: The lingual gyrus forms the lower bank of the calcarine sulcus in the occipital lobe, receiving fibers from Meyer's loop (lower retina, upper visual field). A lesion of the left lingual gyrus causes a right upper (superior) homonymous quadrantanopia. Right lower quadrantanopia (B) involves the cuneus; Bitemporal hemianopia (C) involves chiasm; Left upper quadrantanopia (D) involves right lingual gyrus; Left monocular blindness (E) involves left optic nerve.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia

stem: A 25-year-old male wrestler sustains a spinal injury during a match. Examination reveals loss of voluntary motor function, loss of fine touch, and loss of proprioception in his right leg. In his left leg, he has complete loss of pain and temperature sensation below the L2 level, but motor strength and fine touch are normal. Which motor tract is interrupted on the right side of his spinal cord?

options.A: Right lateral corticospinal tract
options.B: Left lateral corticospinal tract
options.C: Right anterolateral system
options.D: Left dorsal column pathway
options.E: Anterior corticospinal tract bilaterally

explanation: Spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard syndrome) on the right side at L2 interrupts the right lateral corticospinal tract (ipsilateral UMN leg weakness below L2), right dorsal column (ipsilateral proprioceptive/touch loss below L2), and right anterolateral system (contralateral pain/temperature loss below L2). Option (B) controls left leg motor function; Option (C) carries left body pain/temperature; Option (D) carries left leg touch/proprioception; Option (E) carries axial trunk motor drive.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right lateral corticospinal tract

stem: A 55-year-old male with chronic insomnia is evaluated. During sleep onset, the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) becomes active. Which neurochemical transmitter is released by VLPO neurons to inhibit wake-promoting centers in the brainstem?

options.A: Glutamate excitatory neurotransmitter
options.B: Gamma-aminobutyric acid neurotransmitter
options.C: Norepinephrine adrenergic neurotransmitter
options.D: Histamine wake-promoting neurotransmitter
options.E: Substance P nociceptive neurotransmitter

explanation: Neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) release GABA (and galanin) to inhibit wake-promoting nodes in the ascending reticular activating system, initiating NREM sleep. Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) are excitatory/wake-promoting transmitters.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 50-year-old female presents with episodic vertigo. During examination, the clinician performs the Dix-Hallpike test: the patient is lowered rapidly from a sitting position to a supine position with her head turned 45 degrees to the right and extended 30 degrees backward. After a 4-second latency, the patient experiences severe vertigo and horizontal-rotatory nystagmus beating toward the right ear, which fatigues and stops after 20 seconds. What is the clinical significance of the fatiguability and latency observed in this test?

options.A: Diagnostic of an acute central brainstem or cerebellar infarction
options.B: Characteristic of a benign peripheral vestibulopathy such as BPPV
options.C: Pathognomonic for compressive vestibulocochlear nerve schwannoma
options.D: Indicative of toxic chemical labyrinthitis from ototoxic medication
options.E: Characteristic of progressive autoimmune inner ear disease

explanation: In Dix-Hallpike testing, a peripheral origin (BPPV) exhibits a 2- to 5-second latency period and fatiguability (nystagmus and vertigo cease within 30–60 seconds). Central lesions produce immediate, non-fatigable, non-habituating nystagmus. Option (A) describes central lesions; Option (C) is incorrect as BPPV does not cause nerve loss; Option (D) is central; Option (E) is incorrect.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Indicates a benign peripheral vestibulopathy (e.g., BPPV)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 35-year-old male presents with difficulty maintaining sleep. He is prescribed suvorexant. Suvorexant promotes sleep by antagonizing which receptors?

options.A: Orexin receptors
options.B: Melatonin receptors
options.C: Dopamine receptors
options.D: Muscarinic receptors
options.E: Beta-adrenergic receptors

explanation: Suvorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA) that promotes sleep by blocking wake-promoting orexin A and orexin B neuropeptides from binding to OX1R and OX2R receptors. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) are not suvorexant targets.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Orexin receptors
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 16-year-old high school student presents with extreme daytime drowsiness. Polysomnography reveals normal nocturnal sleep duration with intact sleep architecture. Multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) shows a mean sleep latency of 4 minutes with rapid entry into REM sleep. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy
options.B: Psychophysiological primary insomnia
options.C: Severe obstructive sleep apnea syndrome
options.D: Restless legs movement disorder
options.E: Slow-wave sleep night terror parasomnia

explanation: Excessive daytime sleepiness with intact nocturnal sleep, mean sleep latency <8 minutes on MSLT, and rapid entry into REM sleep (SOREMPs) defines narcolepsy. Option (B) is nocturnal sleep initiation loss; Option (C) features apneas on polysomnogram; Option (D) features leg dysesthesias; Option (E) features N3 terrors.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Narcolepsy
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with a tumor compressing the left lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) in the thalamus. What visual field deficit will be produced?

options.A: Right homonymous hemianopia
options.B: Left homonymous hemianopia
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Monocular left anopia
options.E: Right upper quadrantanopia

explanation: The left lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) processes all visual information from the right visual hemifield (ipsilateral temporal retina and contralateral decussating nasal retina). Complete destruction of the left LGN produces a complete right homonymous hemianopia. Left homonymous hemianopia (B) involves right LGN; Bitemporal (C) involves chiasm; Monocular loss (D) involves optic nerve; Right upper quadrantanopia (E) involves left Meyer loop.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right homonymous hemianopia

stem: A 25-year-old medical student tilts her head backward and forward while standing on a moving elevator that accelerates vertically upward. Which vestibular receptor organ is specialized to detect vertical linear acceleration and gravitational pull?

options.A: Ampulla of the horizontal semicircular canal
options.B: Macula of the vertically oriented saccule
options.C: Macula of the horizontally oriented utricle
options.D: Crista ampullaris of the anterior canal
options.E: Basilar membrane of the apical cochlea

explanation: Otolith organs contain maculae. The saccular macula is oriented vertically along the anatomical wall, specializing in detecting vertical linear acceleration (elevator movement) and gravity when upright. Utricular macula is horizontal, detecting horizontal linear acceleration. Option (A) detects rotation; Option (C) detects horizontal acceleration; Option (D) detects rotation; Option (E) processes sound frequency.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Macula of the saccule
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 60-year-old male with obstructive sleep apnea presents with daytime somnolence and fatigue. Polysomnography demonstrates recurrent nocturnal airway collapse. What pathophysiological consequence results from recurrent apneas during sleep?

options.A: Transient hypoxemia and sleep fragmentation leading to daytime fatigue
options.B: Hyperventilation causing persistent respiratory alkalosis
options.C: Direct destruction of alveolar septa by orexin deficiency
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of phrenic nerve lower motor neurons
options.E: Selective loss of growth hormone secretion during N3 sleep

explanation: Obstructive sleep apnea involves recurrent pharyngeal collapse causing transient hypoxemia, hypercapnia, micro-arousals, and sleep fragmentation, which results in excessive daytime fatigue and elevated cardiovascular risk. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) misrepresent OSA pathophysiology.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Transient hypoxemia and sleep fragmentation leading to daytime fatigue
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 30-year-old factory worker presents with a loss of pain and temperature sensation across both shoulders and upper arms in a "cape-like" distribution. Tactile sensation, vibration, and joint position sense remain intact throughout the entire body. Strength in the upper extremities is currently 5/5, but muscle tone is normal. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals a fluid-filled cavity within the central canal of the cervical spinal cord (syringomyelia). Which neural pathway is directly compressed to produce this specific pattern of sensory loss?

options.A: Main sensory axons in the dorsal columns
options.B: Primary afferent axons crossing in the ventral white commissure
options.C: Descending motor fibers in the lateral corticospinal tract
options.D: Lower motor neurons in the lateral ventral horn
options.E: Autonomic preganglionic fibers in the intermediolateral column

explanation: Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) expanding within the central canal of the spinal cord (most commonly cervical). It selectively compresses decussating second-order spinothalamic axons in the ventral white commissure, producing bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in a "cape-like" distribution across corresponding dermatomes (C5–T2). Dorsal columns remain intact, preserving fine touch and proprioception (dissociated sensory loss). Option (A) impairs fine touch/vibration; Option (C) causes lower limb spasticity; Option (D) causes LMN hand weakness; Option (E) causes Horner syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Primary afferent axons crossing in the ventral white commissure

stem: A 31-year-old female presents with left-sided facial weakness and left-sided hearing loss. Physical examination shows an inability to close her left eye or smile on the left side, loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of her tongue on the left, and left sensorineural hearing loss. Where is the anatomical site of the lesion compressing these two cranial nerves together?

options.A: Jugular foramen at the posterior cranial base
options.B: Cerebellopontine angle at the internal acoustic meatus
options.C: Foramen rotundum within the sphenoid greater wing
options.D: Superior orbital fissure at the sphenoid apex
options.E: Carotid canal within the petrous temporal bone

explanation: CN VII and CN VIII exit the pontomedullary junction together and traverse the cerebellopontine angle (CPA) into the internal auditory meatus. Lesions in this space (vestibular schwannoma) compress both nerves, causing sensorineural hearing loss/tinnitus/vertigo (CN VIII) and facial muscle weakness/taste loss (CN VII). Option (A) houses CN IX, X, XI; Option (C) transmits CN V3; Option (D) transmits CN III, IV, V1, VI; Option (E) transmits CN XII.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Cerebellopontine angle (CPA) / internal auditory meatus
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 35-year-old woman is evaluated for a broad-based gait and frequent tripping. Neurological examination reveals increased muscle tone in both legs, with passive movement meeting maximal resistance at the onset of extension before suddenly giving way ("clasp-knife" spasticity). What electrophysiological change occurs in the spinal stretch reflex circuit following a chronic upper motor neuron lesion that causes this spasticity?

options.A: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causing combined upper and lower motor neuron loss
options.B: Myasthenia gravis causing autoantibody destruction of postsynaptic ACh receptors
options.C: Guillain-Barré syndrome causing acute inflammatory peripheral demyelination
options.D: Lambert-Eaton syndrome causing presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel loss
options.E: Polymyositis causing autoimmune inflammatory destruction of skeletal muscle

explanation: Spasticity is characterized by velocity-dependent resistance to passive stretch. Descending UMN tracts (corticospinal and cortico-bulbo-spinal) deliver tonic inhibitory modulation to spinal motor circuits. Interruption of UMN pathways leaves spinal lower motor neurons uninhibited and hyper-reactive, causing unchecked monosynaptic reflex firing upon passive muscle stretch. Option (A) is incorrect as afferents remain intact; Option (C) causes LMN flaccidity; Option (D) describes Lambert-Eaton; Option (E) is incorrect as alpha motoneuron hyper-excitability drives spasticity.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Uninhibited hyper-reactivity of lower motor neurons due to loss of descending UMN inhibition

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with severe daytime fatigue. A multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) is ordered. During the MSLT, the patient is given 5 scheduled nap opportunities spaced 2 hours apart. What parameter does the MSLT specifically quantify to evaluate excessive daytime sleepiness?

options.A: Maximum nadir of systemic arterial oxygen saturation on oximetry
options.B: Mean sleep latency to sleep onset and number of sleep-onset REM periods
options.C: Amplitude and frequency of synchronized delta waves during N3 sleep
options.D: Periodic limb movement index per hour of total recorded sleep time
options.E: Total fractional percentage of cerebral blood flow during phasic REM

explanation: The Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) measures daytime sleep latency (time to fall asleep) and presence of sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) across 5 scheduled daytime naps to diagnose narcolepsy (<8 min latency, ≥2 SOREMPs). Options (A), (C), (D), and (E) are not the primary parameter quantified by MSLT.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Time elapsed from lights out to the onset of sleep (sleep latency) and occurrence of REM periods
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A neuroscientist evaluates sleep-promoting circuitry in a mammalian brain model. Lesions in a specific hypothalamic nucleus result in severe, chronic insomnia. This nucleus normally promotes sleep onset by releasing gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) to inhibit the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS). Which nucleus is this?

options.A: Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus in the anterior hypothalamus
options.B: Tuberomammillary nucleus in the posterior hypothalamus
options.C: Locus coeruleus in the rostral pontine tegmentum
options.D: Dorsal raphe nucleus in the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.E: Pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus in the rostral pons

explanation: The ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) in the anterior hypothalamus is the primary sleep-promoting center. VLPO neurons release GABA and galanin to inhibit wakefulness centers in the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS). Lesions cause severe chronic insomnia. Option (B) promotes wakefulness via orexin; Option (C) secretes oxytocin/vasopressin; Option (D) is the circadian clock; Option (E) controls motor output.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 60-year-old male suffers a stroke affecting the left parietal lobe, damaging the superior optic radiations (dorsal loop). Which visual field deficit is expected?

options.A: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.B: Right lower homonymous quadrantanopia
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Monocular visual loss in left eye
options.E: Left lower homonymous quadrantanopia

explanation: The superior optic radiations (dorsal loop) travel through the parietal lobe to the cuneus gyrus, carrying information from the upper retina (lower visual field). A lesion of the left parietal dorsal loop produces a right lower (inferior) homonymous quadrantanopia. Left temporal Meyer loop (A) causes right upper quadrantanopia; Chiasm (C) causes bitemporal loss; Left optic nerve (D) causes left monocular loss; Right parietal loop (E) causes left lower quadrantanopia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right lower homonymous quadrantanopia

stem: A 43-year-old female presents with hoarseness, difficulty swallowing solids and liquids, and frequent coughing spells when drinking water. Examination of the pharynx demonstrates that at rest, the left palatal arch is drooping. When the patient is asked to say "Ah," the uvula deviates to the right side. The gag reflex is absent when the left posterior pharyngeal wall is stimulated but present when the right side is stimulated. Which of the following structures is damaged?

options.A: Right nucleus ambiguus
options.B: Left nucleus ambiguus
options.C: Left hypoglossal nucleus
options.D: Right corticobulbar tract
options.E: Left trigeminal motor nucleus

explanation: Lower motor neurons for CN IX and X reside in the nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla, innervating muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx. Damage to the left nucleus ambiguus causes LMN weakness of the left soft palate, causing it to droop. Upon phonation ("Ah"), the intact right levator veli palatini pulls the uvula away from the lesioned side (toward the right). Left CN X/IX motor loss also abolishes the efferent limb of the gag reflex on the left. Option (A) causes right-sided palatal weakness and uvular deviation to the left; Option (C) affects tongue movement; Option (D) causes minimal palatal deviation due to bilateral corticobulbar input; Option (E) affects muscles of mastication.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left nucleus ambiguus

stem: A 70-year-old female presents with an acute stroke. Examination reveals that her eyes are locked in a position looking to the left. Which two anatomical lesions could independently produce a resting gaze preference toward the left side?

options.A: Left frontal eye field destructive stroke or right PPRF destructive stroke
options.B: Right frontal eye field destructive stroke or left PPRF destructive stroke
options.C: Left oculomotor nucleus infarction or right trochlear nucleus infarction
options.D: Bilateral medial longitudinal fasciculi demyelinating plaques
options.E: Left optic nerve traumatic transection or right ciliary ganglion avulsion

explanation: Conjugate horizontal eye deviation looking locked toward the left can arise from two distinct anatomical lesion locations: 1) A destructive cortical stroke involving the LEFT frontal eye field (FEF). The left FEF normally drives gaze to the right; its destruction allows the intact right FEF to drive the eyes to the left ("eyes look toward the hemispheric lesion"). 2) A destructive pontine stroke involving the RIGHT paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF). The right PPRF normally drives gaze to the right; its destruction allows the intact left PPRF to drive the eyes to the left ("eyes look away from the pontine lesion").
high_yield_pearl: Conjugate horizontal gaze locked to the left occurs with a destructive left FEF stroke (toward the lesion) or a destructive right PPRF stroke (away from the lesion).

stem: An experimental study measures neuronal firing rates in the superior olivary complex of the caudal pons during acoustic stimulation. The investigators observe that neurons in the medial superior olive fire maximally when there is a minute microsecond delay between the arrival of a sound wave at the left ear versus the right ear. What primary auditory function is mediated by this binaural processing center?

options.A: Analysis of speech syntax and semantics
options.B: Discrimination of complex pitch harmonics
options.C: Sound localization in the horizontal plane
options.D: Voluntary damping of the tympanic membrane
options.E: Transduction of linear vertical acceleration

explanation: The superior olivary complex in the caudal pons receives bilateral auditory input. The medial superior olive compares interaural time differences, and the lateral superior olive compares interaural intensity differences. This binaural processing enables sound localization in the horizontal plane. Option (A) is Wernicke area; Option (B) is primary cortex/cochlea; Option (D) is CN VII/V3 reflex; Option (E) is saccule macula.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Sound localization in the horizontal plane
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 62-year-old male with severe insomnia is prescribed a short course of a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic agent. What is the mechanism of action of non-benzodiazepines like zolpidem and zaleplon?

options.A: Allosteric modulation of the GABA-A receptor at the benzodiazepine site
options.B: Agonist activation of melatonin MT1 and MT2 G-protein coupled receptors
options.C: Competitive antagonist blockade at dual OX1 and OX2 orexin receptors
options.D: Antagonist blockade of postsynaptic H1 histamine receptors in cortex
options.E: Agonist activation of presynaptic D2 and D3 dopamine auto-receptors

explanation: Non-benzodiazepines (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) act as selective agonists at the alpha-1 subunit of GABAA receptors at the benzodiazepine site, increasing GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission to induce sleep. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) describe other drug classes.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Binding to the GABA-A receptor at the benzodiazepine site to facilitate GABA-A receptor opening
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 48-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo, tinnitus, and progressive hearing loss in his right ear. Over time, he notices that his hearing loss has become prominent for low-frequency tones. He is started on a low-sodium diet and a diuretic to reduce endolymphatic fluid pressure. What condition is being treated?

options.A: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
options.B: Ménière disease
options.C: Vestibular schwannoma
options.D: Otitis media
options.E: Superior canal dehiscence

explanation: Episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear fullness define Ménière disease (endolymphatic hydrops). Management includes a low-sodium diet and diuretics to reduce endolymphatic fluid pressure. Option (A) is treated with Epley maneuver; Option (C) is managed surgically; Option (D) is treated with antibiotics; Option (E) requires surgical bone repair.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Ménière disease
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with a brainstem stroke. Examination reveals that when he attempts horizontal gaze to the right, neither eye moves to the right. When he attempts horizontal gaze to the left, his left eye abducts normally with nystagmus, but his right eye cannot adduct. What complex gaze syndrome is present ("one-and-a-half syndrome")?

options.A: Combined lesion of the right PPRF and the right medial longitudinal fasciculus
options.B: Bilateral frontal eye field strokes involving the precentral motor cortex
options.C: Bilateral complete oculomotor nerve palsies from interpeduncular compression
options.D: Combined lesion of the optic chiasm and bilateral optic tract radiations
options.E: Isolated pinealoma compressing the dorsal tectum and superior colliculus

explanation: The patient exhibits "one-and-a-half syndrome." On attempted horizontal gaze to the right, neither eye moves to the right (a complete rightward horizontal conjugate gaze palsy, representing "one"). On attempted horizontal gaze to the left, the left eye abducts normally with nystagmus, but the right eye fails to adduct (a right internuclear ophthalmoplegia, representing the "half"). This unique neuro-ophthalmological syndrome is caused by a single focal unilateral lesion in the caudal dorsal pontine tegmentum involving BOTH the right PPRF (or right abducens nucleus) AND the adjacent crossing right MLF.
high_yield_pearl: One-and-a-half syndrome is caused by a unilateral pontine lesion damaging both the ipsilateral PPRF (conjugate gaze palsy) and ipsilateral MLF (internuclear ophthalmoplegia).

stem: A 65-year-old male presents with sudden hearing loss in his left ear. Audiometry confirms a severe left sensorineural hearing loss. Weber test lateralizes to the right (good) ear. Rinne test is positive bilaterally (AC > BC). An MRI of the brain demonstrates an ischemic stroke involving a small artery that branches off AICA to supply the inner ear structures, entering via the internal auditory meatus. Which artery is occluded?

options.A: Labyrinthine artery
options.B: Middle meningeal artery
options.C: Ophthalmic artery
options.D: Anterior cerebral artery
options.E: Posterior spinal artery

explanation: The labyrinthine artery (internal auditory artery, usually branching from AICA) supplies the membranous inner ear (cochlea and vestibular apparatus), entering via the internal auditory meatus with CN VII and VIII. Occlusion causes sudden monaural sensorineural hearing loss and acute vertigo. Option (B) supplies dura mater; Option (C) supplies orbit/retina; Option (D) supplies medial cortex; Option (E) supplies posterior cord.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Labyrinthine artery
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: An 18-year-old male wrestler presents with weakness in his right upper extremity following a severe traction injury to his neck. Physical examination demonstrates marked weakness of forearm flexion and supination, along with an absent biceps reflex on the right side. Triceps and patellar reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Muscle tone in the right arm is flaccid. Which of the following nerve roots is primary involved in the execution of the biceps stretch reflex arc?

options.A: C3–C4
options.B: C5–C6
options.C: C7–C8
options.D: L1–L2
options.E: L3–L4

explanation: The biceps reflex evaluates C5–C6 spinal cord segments and the musculocutaneous nerve. Tapping the biceps tendon sends Ia afferents via the musculocutaneous nerve to C5–C6 dorsal horn, synapsing onto alpha motor neurons in C5–C6 ventral horn that transmit efferents to contract the biceps brachii. Option (A) innervates diaphragm (phrenic nerve); Option (C) evaluates C6–C8 (triceps); Option (D) evaluates L1–L2; Option (E) evaluates L3–L4.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: C5–C6

stem: A 45-year-old male suffers a temporal bone fracture. On physical examination, tapping the left mastoid process produces sound that is heard clearly, but when the tuning fork is held next to his left ear canal, he hears nothing (BC > AC; negative Rinne). The Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Which structure was damaged by the temporal bone fracture?

options.A: Cochlear division of CN VIII
options.B: Middle ear ossicular chain or tympanic membrane
options.C: Transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl
options.D: Medial geniculate nucleus
options.E: Superior vestibular nucleus

explanation: Negative Rinne on the left (Bone Conduction > Air Conduction) and Weber lateralization to the left ear confirm left conductive hearing loss. Temporal bone fractures causing conductive loss disrupt middle ear mechanics (ossicular chain dislocation or eardrum perforation/hemotympanum). Option (A) causes sensorineural loss; Options (C) and (D) cause central processing deficits; Option (E) causes vestibular loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Middle ear ossicular chain or tympanic membrane
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 54-year-old male undergoes surgical repair of a large abdominal aortic aneurysm. Postoperatively, he develops bilateral lower extremity paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the T10 level. Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception remain completely normal bilaterally in both legs. Which spinal cord syndrome has occurred as a complication of this surgery?

options.A: Posterior cord syndrome
options.B: Anterior cord syndrome
options.C: Brown-Séquard syndrome
options.D: Syringomyelia
options.E: Subacute combined degeneration

explanation: Ischemia of the anterior spinal artery (often following aortic aneurysm repair) causes Anterior Cord Syndrome, damaging the lateral corticospinal tracts (bilateral motor paralysis below lesion) and anterolateral system (bilateral loss of pain and temperature below lesion). The dorsal columns are spared as they are supplied by posterior spinal arteries, preserving fine touch and proprioception. Option (A) affects dorsal columns; Option (C) is a hemisection; Option (D) causes cape-like arm sensory loss; Option (E) affects dorsal and lateral columns without anterior cord pattern.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Anterior cord syndrome

stem: A neurologist evaluates a patient with suspected lower motor neuron pathology. The examiner gently strokes the skin around the anus, observing a visible contraction of the external anal sphincter muscle (anal wink reflex). Which spinal cord segment roots mediate both the afferent and efferent limbs of this spinal reflex?

options.A: L1–L2
options.B: L3–L4
options.C: L5–S1
options.D: S1–S2
options.E: S3–S4

explanation: The anal wink reflex evaluates lower sacral segments S3–S4 and the pudendal nerve. Stroking perianal skin stimulates sensory afferents carried by the pudendal nerve to S3–S4, synapsing onto motor neurons in the S3–S4 ventral horn that send efferents via the pudendal nerve to contract the external anal sphincter. Option (A) evaluates L1–L2; Option (B) evaluates L3–L4; Option (C) evaluates L5–S1; Option (D) evaluates S1–S2.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: S3–S4

stem: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for a sore throat, fever, and left earache. Otoscopic examination demonstrates an intact, dull, amber-colored left tympanic membrane with fluid behind it. No purulent discharge or acute bulging is present. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear, and Rinne test shows bone conduction greater than air conduction on the left. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Cholesteatoma with ossicular chain necrosis
options.B: Otitis media with serous middle ear effusion
options.C: Otosclerosis with stapedial footplate fixation
options.D: Acoustic neuroma within the auditory canal
options.E: Presbycusis with cochlear hair cell atrophy

explanation: Otitis media with effusion (OME) presents with non-purulent fluid behind an intact, dull, amber-colored tympanic membrane without acute bulging or fever. Fluid impedes ossicular vibration, producing conductive hearing loss (Weber to affected ear, negative Rinne). Option (A) presents with ear canal swelling and tragus pain; Option (C) causes vertigo and sensorineural loss; Option (D) is a keratinizing mass; Option (E) is age-related sensorineural loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Otitis media with effusion (serous otitis media)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A neurophysiologist maps the primary visual cortex (V1). The cuneus gyrus is located on the medial surface of the occipital lobe superior to the calcarine sulcus. Which portion of the optic radiations projects to the cuneus gyrus?

options.A: Meyer loop in the temporal lobe carrying upper visual field inputs
options.B: Dorsal loop in the parietal lobe carrying lower visual field inputs
options.C: Nasal retinal decussating fibers carrying temporal visual field inputs
options.D: Temporal retinal uncrossed fibers carrying nasal visual field inputs
options.E: Auditory radiations from the medial geniculate nucleus to cortex

explanation: The cuneus gyrus is the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus, receiving superior optic radiations (dorsal loop) that travel through the parietal lobe carrying signals from the upper retina (lower visual field). Meyer loop (A) projects to the lingual gyrus; Nasal fibers (C) cross at chiasm; Uncrossed fibers (D) carry ipsilateral temporal retina; Auditory radiations (E) project to Heschl's gyrus.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Superior optic radiations / dorsal loop (parietal lobe) carrying lower visual field

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with progressive hearing loss in his right ear over the past two years. Physical examination reveals normal pinnae and uninflamed, clear tympanic membranes bilaterally. A 512 Hz tuning fork is placed on the midline of his forehead (Weber test), and the sound lateralizes distinctly to the left ear. When the tuning fork is placed on the right mastoid process and then moved next to the right external auditory canal (Rinne test), air conduction is determined to be greater than bone conduction (positive test bilaterally). Which of the following anatomical structures is the primary site of pathology in this patient?

options.A: Malleus, incus, and stapes ossicular chain
options.B: External auditory canal epidermoid lining
options.C: Organ of Corti hair cells or cochlear division of CN VIII
options.D: Tympanic membrane pars tensa
options.E: Epithelial lining of the Eustachian tube

explanation: Rinne test is positive bilaterally (Air Conduction > Bone Conduction), ruling out conductive hearing loss. Weber test lateralizes to the left ear (the unaffected ear). In sensorineural hearing loss, Weber lateralizes away from the impaired ear to the good ear. Sensorineural loss results from pathology in the organ of Corti hair cells or cochlear division of CN VIII. Option (A) causes conductive loss (negative Rinne); Option (B) causes conductive loss; Option (D) causes conductive loss; Option (E) causes middle ear effusion and conductive loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Organ of Corti hair cells or cochlear division of CN VIII
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 50-year-old female presents with a 3-month history of progressive stiffness in her left leg. When she walks, her left leg remains extended and she swings it outward in a semicircular arc to prevent her toes from dragging on the ground (circumductive gait). Examination shows 4/5 strength in the left leg, hyperactive patellar reflex (3+), and an upgoing left plantar reflex. Upper extremity and facial motor exams are normal. Where is the lesion located?

options.A: Right medial precentral gyrus / paracentral lobule
options.B: Left lateral precentral gyrus
options.C: Left ventral horn of the lumbar spinal cord
options.D: Right facial motor nucleus in the caudal pons
options.E: Right lateral primary motor cortex

explanation: The lower extremity motor representation resides on the medial surface of the primary motor cortex in the paracentral lobule. Because corticospinal pathways decussate in the medullary pyramids, an UMN lesion in the right medial precentral gyrus / paracentral lobule causes spastic hemiparesis and circumductive gait isolated to the contralateral (left) leg. Option (B) controls right arm/face; Option (C) causes LMN flaccid paralysis in left leg; Option (D) causes facial paralysis; Option (E) represents hand/arm/face.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right medial precentral gyrus / paracentral lobule

stem: A 62-year-old female presents with a complete lesion of the left facial nerve (CN VII) at the stylomastoid foramen. How does this LMN facial nerve lesion impact the pupillary light reflex?

options.A: Corneal reflex is lost on the left side, while pupillary light reflex remains normal
options.B: Pupillary light reflex is lost on the left side, while corneal reflex remains normal
options.C: Both corneal and pupillary light reflexes are lost on the left side completely
options.D: Both pupils become fixed and dilated with complete bilateral cycloplegia
options.E: Consensual pupillary light reflex is selectively lost across the midline

explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) supplies somatic branchial motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression, including the orbicularis oculi, which constitutes the efferent motor limb of the corneal blink reflex (afferent limb is CN V1). A complete peripheral lesion of the left facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen abolishes the efferent blink response in the left eye, so neither eye can blink on the left when either cornea is touched. In contrast, the pupillary light reflex is mediated by the optic nerve (CN II, afferent) and oculomotor nerve (CN III, efferent); it does NOT involve the facial nerve at all and remains completely intact.
high_yield_pearl: Facial nerve (CN VII) lesions impair the efferent limb of the corneal blink reflex (orbicularis oculi) but leave the pupillary light reflex (CN II / CN III) completely normal.

stem: A 67-year-old male presents with difficulty localizing where sounds are coming from while walking in traffic. He can hear that a car horn is blowing, but cannot determine whether the car is approaching from his left or his right. Auditory processing testing demonstrates an inability to process interaural time and intensity differences. Which central brainstem auditory nucleus is primarily responsible for sound localization?

options.A: Spiral ganglion
options.B: Superior olivary complex
options.C: Medial geniculate nucleus
options.D: Transverse temporal gyrus
options.E: Inferior vestibular nucleus

explanation: Sound localization requires processing interaural time differences (medial superior olive) and interaural intensity differences (lateral superior olive). The superior olivary complex in the caudal pons is the first central structure to receive binaural auditory input. Option (A) is monaural; Option (C) is a thalamic relay; Option (D) is auditory cortex; Option (E) is vestibular.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Superior olivary complex
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: An auditory neurophysiologist traces the pathway of acoustic processing from the brainstem to the cerebral cortex. Arrange the following central auditory structures in the correct order of ascending signal transmission: (1) Inferior colliculus, (2) Cochlear nucleus, (3) Medial geniculate nucleus, (4) Superior olivary complex, (5) Transverse temporal gyrus.
explanation: The ascending central auditory pathway sequence is: Spiral ganglion -> Cochlear nucleus (2) -> Superior olivary complex (4) via trapezoid body -> Inferior colliculus (1) via lateral lemniscus -> Medial geniculate nucleus (3) -> Transverse temporal gyrus (5) via sublenticular internal capsule. Sequence: 2 -> 4 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: 2 -> 4 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with myopia (nearsightedness). Refractive testing reveals that light rays entering his eye are focused in front of the retina. What structural abnormality of the eye causes myopia?

options.A: Eye axial length too short
options.B: Eye axial length too long
options.C: Irregular curvature of the cornea
options.D: Stiffening of the crystalline lens
options.E: Absence of the iris

explanation: Myopia (nearsightedness) occurs when the axial length of the eyeball is structurally too long relative to its refractive power, causing parallel light rays from distant objects to focus in front of the retina. Eye too short (A) causes hyperopia. Corneal irregularity (C) causes astigmatism. Lens stiffening (D) causes presbyopia. Aniridia (E) is iris absence.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Eye axial length too long

stem: A 33-year-old male involved in a high-speed collision sustains a severe hyperextension injury to his neck. Physical examination demonstrates marked weakness in both upper extremities (strength 2/5), whereas strength in both lower extremities is relatively preserved (4/5). Loss of pain and temperature sensation is present across the neck and arms, while proprioception is preserved throughout. What spinal cord syndrome is represented?

options.A: Anterior cord syndrome
options.B: Central cord syndrome
options.C: Posterior cord syndrome
options.D: Brown-Séquard syndrome
options.E: Cauda equina syndrome

explanation: Central cord syndrome (common in cervical hyperextension injuries) selectively damages the central region of the cervical spinal cord, affecting medial fibers of lateral corticospinal tracts (arm representation) and decussating spinothalamic fibers in the ventral white commissure. This results in motor weakness disproportionately greater in the upper extremities than lower extremities, with cape-like pain and temperature loss and spared dorsal columns. Option (A) causes total motor/pain loss below level; Option (C) causes proprioceptive loss; Option (D) causes hemisection deficits; Option (E) affects lumbosacral roots.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Central cord syndrome

stem: A 61-year-old male suffers a stroke involving the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA), injuring the left parietal lobe white matter. Which pathway is damaged, and what visual field deficit results?

options.A: Meyer loop damage causing right upper quadrantanopia
options.B: Dorsal loop damage causing right lower quadrantanopia
options.C: Optic chiasm damage causing complete bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Optic tract damage causing left homonymous hemianopia
options.E: Lingual gyrus damage causing left upper quadrantanopia

explanation: An MCA stroke affecting the left parietal lobe white matter damages the superior optic radiations (dorsal loop), which carry lower visual field fibers from the upper retina. This produces a right lower (inferior) homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor"). Meyer loop (A) travels through temporal lobe; Chiasm (C) causes bitemporal loss; Optic tract (D) causes homonymous hemianopia; Lingual gyrus (E) is PCA territory.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Superior optic radiations (dorsal loop); Right lower quadrantanopia

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with difficulty reading fine print. He states that he has good distance vision, but near vision has gradually worsened over the past 10 years. Refractive testing confirms presbyopia. What is the physiological cause of presbyopia?

options.A: Excessive progressive elongation of the axial length of the globe
options.B: Age-related loss of lens elasticity and stiffening of the capsule
options.C: Progressive corneal endothelial decompensation and stromal clouding
options.D: Elevation of intraocular pressure causing optic nerve cupping
options.E: Selective apoptotic degeneration of peripheral rod photoreceptors

explanation: Presbyopia is an age-related physiological accommodation deficit caused by progressive stiffness and loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens, preventing the lens from rounding up to focus on near objects. Eyeball elongation (A) causes myopia; Corneal clouding (C) causes vision loss; IOP elevation (D) causes glaucoma; Ganglion cell loss (E) occurs in optic neuropathy.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Age-related loss of lens elasticity and stiffening of the crystalline lens

stem: A 48-year-old woman is evaluated for progressive muscle weakness and localized twitching in her arms over the past six months. Examination reveals pronounced muscle wasting in the intrinsic muscles of both hands, along with visible, spontaneous muscle twitches under the skin. Deep tendon reflexes in the biceps and brachioradialis are absent bilaterally. Electromyography confirms the presence of fibrillations and fasciculations in the upper extremity muscles. Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms directly accounts for the loss of muscle mass in this patient?

options.A: Interruption of descending inhibitory reticulospinal tracts
options.B: Denervation-induced degradation of muscle fibers from lower motor neuron loss
options.C: Continuous hyperactivation of the monosynaptic stretch reflex arc
options.D: Ischemic necrosis of Betz cells in the precentral gyrus
options.E: Autoimmune destruction of post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

explanation: Muscle wasting, fasciculations (spontaneous involuntary twitches of single motor units), fibrillations, and absent deep tendon reflexes define a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion. Alpha motor neurons in the spinal ventral horns provide neurotrophic support and tonic activation to skeletal muscle. Loss of these motoneurons deprives muscle tissue of neurotrophic support, leading to denervation atrophy. Option (A) causes spasticity; Option (C) reflects uninhibited UMN stretch reflexes; Option (D) produces UMN signs without fasciculations or LMN muscle wasting; Option (E) describes myasthenia gravis, which presents with fatigable weakness without fasciculations or areflexia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Denervation-induced degradation of muscle fibers from lower motor neuron loss

stem: A 28-year-old woman with a 3-year history of multiple sclerosis presents with diplopia when looking to the left. Physical examination reveals normal conjugate eye movements when looking to the right. However, on attempted leftward horizontal gaze, the left eye abducts normally with fine horizontal nystagmus, but the right eye fails to adduct past the midline. When tested for convergence during accommodation, both eyes adduct fully to the midline without difficulty. Where is the anatomical lesion located?

options.A: Right abducens nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum
options.B: Right medial longitudinal fasciculus in the brainstem tegmentum
options.C: Left oculomotor nucleus in the rostral midbrain tegmentum
options.D: Left paramedian pontine reticular formation in the caudal pons
options.E: Right frontal eye field within the precentral motor cortex

explanation: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), the heavily myelinated brainstem tract that coordinates conjugate horizontal gaze by transmitting signals from the abducens nucleus (PPRF) to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus subnucleus). The affected MLF is named for the side that fails to adduct. Here, on leftward horizontal gaze, the right eye fails to adduct past the midline, while the left eye abducts normally with horizontal nystagmus; convergence during accommodation is intact because convergence pathways bypass the MLF and project directly from cortical visual association areas to the oculomotor nuclei. Multiple sclerosis is the leading cause of bilateral or unilateral INO in young adults.
high_yield_pearl: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) localizes to the MLF on the side of the adduction deficit; convergence is preserved because accommodation pathways bypass the MLF.

stem: A 29-year-old male undergoes a complete transection of the right optic tract. What visual field defect will be observed on formal perimetry?

options.A: Right homonymous hemianopia
options.B: Left homonymous hemianopia
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.E: Monocular blindness in the right eye

explanation: The right optic tract carries visual information from the ipsilateral temporal retina (right eye) and contralateral nasal retina (left eye), representing the complete left visual hemifield. Complete transection of the right optic tract produces a complete left homonymous hemianopia. Right homonymous hemianopia (A) involves left optic tract; Bitemporal hemianopia (C) involves chiasm; Right upper quadrantanopia (D) involves left Meyer loop; Monocular loss (E) involves optic nerve.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left homonymous hemianopia

stem: A 70-year-old male presents with double vision. Examination shows that his right eye is deviated medially at rest. When asked to look to the right, the right eye cannot abduct. Facial sensation and facial motor function are normal. Where is the lesion located?

options.A: Right abducens nerve causing isolated failure of right lateral rectus abduction
options.B: Right facial nerve causing ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of facial muscles
options.C: Left paramedian pontine reticular formation causing bilateral gaze palsy
options.D: Right oculomotor nerve causing ptosis and a fixed and dilated pupil
options.E: Left frontal eye field causing conjugate eye deviation toward the left

explanation: An inward (medial) deviation of the right eye at rest (esotropia) with an isolated inability to abduct the right eye past the midline, in the absence of any other cranial nerve or long tract findings, localizes to the right abducens nerve (CN VI). The abducens nerve innervates solely the lateral rectus muscle. When the lateral rectus is paralyzed, unopposed resting tone of the medial rectus adducts the eye toward the nose, resulting in horizontal binocular diplopia.
high_yield_pearl: Medial strabismus (esotropia) at rest with isolated abduction failure localizes to the abducens nerve (CN VI).

stem: A 34-year-old female presents with difficulty sleeping due to painful, persistent involuntary teeth grinding during the night. Her husband reports a loud grinding sound. Dental exam shows severe wear of the molar enamel. During which sleep stage does bruxism primarily occur?

options.A: Awake state
options.B: N1 stage NREM
options.C: N2 stage NREM
options.D: N3 stage NREM
options.E: REM sleep

explanation: Nocturnal teeth grinding (bruxism) occurs predominantly during N2 stage NREM sleep. Options (A), (B), (D), and (E) are not the primary sleep stage for bruxism.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: N2 stage NREM
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 58-year-old female presents with a destructive lesion involving the right Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF / horizontal gaze center) in the caudal pons. Which pattern of gaze paralysis will be observed on physical examination?

options.A: Inability to execute voluntary conjugate horizontal gaze to the right
options.B: Inability to execute voluntary conjugate horizontal gaze to the left
options.C: Selective paralysis of vertical upward conjugate eye movements
options.D: Isolated failure of left eye adduction with right abducting nystagmus
options.E: Bilateral complete pupillary dilation unresponsive to illumination

explanation: The paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) serves as the brainstem horizontal gaze center. Located in the caudal pontine tegmentum adjacent to the abducens nucleus, each PPRF coordinates ipsilateral conjugate horizontal gaze: right PPRF activation fires the right abducens nucleus, which stimulates the right lateral rectus and sends crossing MLF fibers to activate the left medial rectus. A destructive lesion of the right PPRF abolishes voluntary horizontal saccades toward the right side. At rest, unopposed contralateral PPRF drive causes the eyes to deviate AWAY from the pontine lesion (toward the left side).
high_yield_pearl: Destructive lesions of the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) cause paralysis of conjugate horizontal gaze toward the side of the lesion.

stem: A 45-year-old female presents for evaluation of daytime fatigue. A full-night polysomnogram is performed. The continuous EEG tracing reveals periods characterized by prominent sleep spindles (12–14 Hz bursts) and sudden, high-voltage K-complexes. Teeth grinding (bruxism) is most likely to occur during this specific stage. Which sleep stage is depicted?

options.A: Awake state
options.B: N1 stage NREM
options.C: N2 stage NREM
options.D: N3 stage NREM
options.E: REM sleep

explanation: N2 (Stage 2 NREM) accounts for ~45–55% of total nocturnal sleep. EEG displays two pathognomonic waveforms: sleep spindles (12–14 Hz bursts) and K-complexes (high-voltage biphasic waves). Involuntary nocturnal teeth grinding (bruxism) occurs predominantly during N2 sleep. Option (A) displays beta/alpha waves; Option (B) displays theta waves; Option (D) displays delta waves; Option (E) displays desynchronized sawtooth waves.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: N2 stage NREM
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 75-year-old male presents with an acute stroke involving the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) affecting the left cuneus gyrus (above the calcarine sulcus). What visual field defect will be detected?

options.A: Right lower homonymous quadrantanopia
options.B: Right upper homonymous quadrantanopia
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Left lower homonymous quadrantanopia
options.E: Complete left monocular anopia

explanation: The cuneus gyrus is the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus in the primary visual cortex, receiving parietal optic radiations carrying signals from the upper retina (lower visual field). A stroke of the left cuneus gyrus produces a right lower (inferior) homonymous quadrantanopia. Right upper quadrantanopia (B) involves lingual gyrus; Bitemporal (C) involves chiasm; Left lower quadrantanopia (D) involves right cuneus; Monocular loss (E) involves optic nerve.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right lower homonymous quadrantanopia

stem: A 60-year-old female presents with progressive hearing loss and occasional dizziness. A tuning fork exam shows a positive Rinne test bilaterally (AC > BC). Weber test lateralizes to the left ear. Audiometry confirms a right-sided sensorineural hearing loss. An MRI of the brain is ordered to evaluate for a vestibular schwannoma. What is the characteristic appearance of a vestibular schwannoma on contrast-enhanced MRI?

options.A: Non-enhancing fluid-filled cavity in the central spinal cord
options.B: Well-circumscribed, brightly enhancing mass at the cerebellopontine angle
options.C: Ring-enhancing lesion in the basal ganglia with surrounding edema
options.D: Multiple demyelinating white matter plaques periventricularly
options.E: Pituitary stalk compression with a calcified suprasellar mass

explanation: Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrates vestibular schwannomas as well-circumscribed, intensely enhancing masses centered in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA), often extending into and widening the internal auditory meatus. Option (A) is syringomyelia; Option (C) is brain abscess/glioma; Option (D) is multiple sclerosis; Option (E) is craniopharyngioma.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Well-circumscribed, brightly enhancing mass at the cerebellopontine angle
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Auditory & Vestibular Systems

stem: A 60-year-old male with long-standing hypertension presents with acute dysarthria and left-sided body weakness. On oral examination, when the patient is asked to extend his tongue, it protrudes significantly to the right side. Inspection reveals no tongue atrophy or fasciculations. Facial exam reveals a right-sided lower face droop with normal forehead wrinkling bilaterally. Which of the following is the anatomical site of the lesion?

options.A: Left hypoglossal nerve peripheral fibers in the deep submandibular tissue
options.B: Left corticobulbar and corticospinal tracts in the posterior limb of internal capsule
options.C: Right hypoglossal motor nucleus situated in the dorsal rostral medulla
options.D: Right corticobulbar projection tract traversing the ventral caudal pons
options.E: Bilateral facial motor nuclei situated in the ventrolateral pontine tegmentum
