explanation: Corticobulbar projections to the hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII) are predominantly crossed (contralateral). An UMN lesion interrupting the left corticobulbar tract disconnects the right hypoglossal nucleus. Upon extension, the healthy left genioglossus pushes the tongue forward and shifts it contralateral to the UMN lesion (toward the right/weak side). Concomitant right lower facial droop (forehead spared) and right body weakness confirm a left-sided hemispheric/internal capsule stroke affecting UMN corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers. Option (A) causes ipsilateral tongue atrophy and fasciculations; Option (C) causes right tongue LMN atrophy; Option (D) causes left face/tongue weakness; Option (E) causes bilateral total face paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left corticobulbar and corticospinal tracts in the internal capsule/brainstem

stem: A 35-year-old male presents with a pupil abnormality. In bright light, his left pupil remains dilated, whereas his right pupil constricts normally. When the room lights are brightened further, the anisocoria increases (left pupil fails to constrict in light). Which autonomic pathway is impaired, and in which eye?

options.A: Parasympathetic pupillomotor pathway impairment involving the left eye
options.B: Sympathetic pupillodilator pathway impairment involving the right eye
options.C: Sympathetic pupillodilator pathway impairment involving the left eye
options.D: Primary retinal photoreceptor degeneration involving the right eye
options.E: Intermediolateral cell column destruction involving the T1 spinal segment

explanation: In bright illumination, normal pupils constrict briskly to minimize retinal light entry via parasympathetic activation of the sphincter pupillae muscles. If the left pupil remains dilated in bright light while the right pupil constricts normally, and the anisocoria worsens as light intensity increases, the defective pupil is the left one, and the underlying impairment is in the parasympathetic pupillomotor system (e.g., CN III lesion, uncal herniation, or pharmacological mydriasis).
high_yield_pearl: Failure of pupillary constriction in bright light localizes the pathology to the efferent parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

stem: A 19-year-old female with narcolepsy undergoes a Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) following an overnight polysomnogram. Which set of diagnostic findings on the MSLT confirms the diagnosis of narcolepsy?

options.A: Mean sleep latency >15 minutes with complete absence of REM sleep
options.B: Mean sleep latency <8 minutes with multiple sleep-onset REM periods
options.C: Persistent low-amplitude delta wave bursts during waking EEG
options.D: Severe prolongation of slow-wave sleep exceeding 40 percent
options.E: Complete absence of sleep spindles and K-complexes in N2 sleep

explanation: Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) diagnosis of narcolepsy requires mean sleep latency <8 minutes across 5 nap opportunities combined with two or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs), reflecting pathological daytime sleepiness and rapid REM intrusion. Option (A) represents normal alertness; Option (C) is non-diagnostic; Option (D) excludes narcolepsy; Option (E) reflects fibrositis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Mean sleep latency <8 minutes and two or more sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs)
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 30-year-old male undergoes polysomnography. The EEG recording shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency brain waves, and the patient easily awakens when his name is called, reporting that he was only "dosing off." Which stage of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep is represented, and which characteristic EEG wave pattern is observed?

options.A: N1 stage; theta waves
options.B: N2 stage; sleep spindles and K-complexes
options.C: N3 stage; delta waves
options.D: REM sleep; sawtooth waves
options.E: Awake state; beta waves

explanation: N1 (Stage 1 NREM sleep) is the lightest sleep stage marking transition from wakefulness. EEG shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency theta waves (4–7 Hz). Patients easily awaken with light stimuli, often reporting they were only "dosing off." Option (B) defines N2 sleep; Option (C) defines N3 sleep; Option (D) defines REM sleep; Option (E) defines alert wakefulness.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: N1 stage; theta waves
source: In-House Step 1 Bank 2: Sleep & Sleep Disorders

stem: A 52-year-old female presents with sudden onset of right-sided body weakness and left eye movement abnormality. Examination reveals that her left eye is fixed in a "down and out" position with a dilated left pupil that does not respond to light. Motor exam shows 2/5 spastic weakness in the right arm and right leg, with hyperreflexia and an upgoing right plantar response. Which region of the brainstem contains the single lesion responsible for this presentation?

options.A: Left ventral rostral midbrain involving exiting CN III fibers and crus cerebri
options.B: Right caudal pons involving CN VI nucleus and lateral spinothalamic tract
options.C: Left rostral medulla involving hypoglossal nucleus and medial lemniscus
options.D: Right mid-pons involving trigeminal motor nucleus
options.E: Left caudal midbrain involving trochlear nucleus

explanation: A single lesion in the left ventral rostral midbrain damages exiting oculomotor (CN III) fascicles (causing ipsilateral LMN CN III palsy: "down and out" eye, ptosis, fixed dilated pupil) and the adjacent crus cerebri (causing contralateral UMN spastic hemiplegia of the arm/leg and lower face). Option (B) causes CN VI/VII palsies in the pons; Option (C) causes medial medullary syndrome (CN XII and pyramid); Option (D) causes CN V motor palsy; Option (E) causes CN IV palsy in caudal midbrain.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Left ventral rostral midbrain involving exiting CN III fibers and crus cerebri

stem: A 24-year-old medical student is practicing neurological examination techniques on a classmate. When testing deep tendon reflexes, tapping the patellar tendon with a reflex hammer stretches the quadriceps muscle, eliciting a sudden extension of the leg at the knee. Which spinal cord segment levels are directly evaluated by this specific reflex arc?

options.A: C5–C6
options.B: C6–C8
options.C: L1–L2
options.D: L3–L4
options.E: S1–S2

explanation: The patellar reflex (knee-jerk) evaluates L3–L4 spinal segments and the femoral nerve. Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, sending Group Ia afferents via L3–L4 dorsal roots to synapse directly onto alpha motor neurons in the L3–L4 ventral horn, contracting the quadriceps. Option (A) evaluates C5–C6 (biceps); Option (B) evaluates C6–C8 (triceps); Option (C) evaluates L1–L2 (cremasteric); Option (E) evaluates S1–S2 (Achilles).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: L3–L4

stem: A 50-year-old male undergoing a routine physical examination is found to have an absent Achilles tendon reflex on the right side. Tapping the right Achilles tendon fails to produce plantarflexion of the foot. The left Achilles reflex is 2+. Strength in ankle plantarflexion is slightly diminished on the right. Which spinal root level is primarily responsible for the execution of the Achilles reflex?

options.A: L1–L2
options.B: L3–L4
options.C: L5
options.D: S1–S2
options.E: S3–S4

explanation: The Achilles tendon reflex (ankle-jerk) tests S1–S2 spinal segments and the tibial nerve. Stretching the Achilles tendon activates muscle spindle afferents entering at S1–S2, synapsing onto lower motor neurons that transmit efferents via the tibial nerve (S1–S2) to contract gastrocnemius/soleus muscles and plantarflex the foot. Option (A) evaluates L1–L2; Option (B) evaluates L3–L4; Option (C) evaluates L5; Option (E) evaluates S3–S4 (anal wink).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: S1–S2

stem: A 38-year-old male presents with visual complaints. Examination demonstrates a loss of the temporal visual field in the left eye and loss of the temporal visual field in the right eye (bitemporal hemianopia). A compression of decussating nasal fibers at which location causes this deficit?

options.A: Optic chiasm
options.B: Left optic tract
options.C: Right optic tract
options.D: Left Meyer loop
options.E: Right dorsal loop

explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia ("tunnel vision") is caused by compression or damage to the optic chiasm. The optic chiasm contains crossing axons originating from the nasal hemiretinae of both eyes, which carry light signals from the temporal visual fields bilaterally. Options (B), (C), (D), and (E) produce homonymous or quadrantic field loss.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Optic chiasm

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with a hoarse voice and difficulty coughing. Examination shows that his soft palate droops on the right side, and when he says "Ah," his uvula pulls toward the left. Examination of the tongue shows no atrophy or deviation. Shoulder shrug is normal bilaterally. Which cranial nerve nucleus is damaged?

options.A: Left hypoglossal nucleus
options.B: Right nucleus ambiguus
options.C: Left nucleus ambiguus
options.D: Right trigeminal motor nucleus
options.E: Right facial motor nucleus

explanation: Lower motor neurons in the nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X) innervate the levator veli palatini. A right nucleus ambiguus lesion causes right soft palate drooping. On phonation ("Ah"), the intact left levator veli palatini contracts unopposed, pulling the uvula toward the healthy (left) side, away from the lesion. Option (A) causes tongue deviation to the left; Option (C) causes uvula deviation to the right; Option (D) causes jaw deviation; Option (E) causes facial paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right nucleus ambiguus

stem: A 58-year-old female presents with difficulty closing her right eye and a droop on the right side of her mouth. Physical exam demonstrates that she cannot wrinkle her right forehead, raise her right eyebrow, close her right eye, or smile on the right side. She also reports that sound seems uncomfortably loud in her right ear. Body strength and sensation are normal bilaterally. What is the location of the lesion?

options.A: Left primary motor cortex precentral gyrus facial homunculus
options.B: Right facial nerve peripheral fibers within the facial canal
options.C: Left corticobulbar tract fibers within the posterior internal capsule
options.D: Right trigeminal sensory nerve fibers within the mandibular division
options.E: Left facial motor nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum

explanation: A peripheral LMN lesion of the right facial nerve (Bell palsy) causes total right-sided facial paralysis affecting both upper (forehead, eye closure) and lower (smile, mouth) facial muscles. Hyperacusis occurs due to involvement of the nerve to the stapedius in the facial canal. Option (A) causes right lower facial droop with forehead sparing; Option (C) causes contralateral lower face droop and body hemiplegia; Option (D) causes contralateral lower face droop; Option (E) causes palatal paralysis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Right facial nerve (CN VII) in the facial canal / stylomastoid foramen

stem: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated following an acute blast injury near an explosion. Otoscopic examination demonstrates perforation of the right tympanic membrane and minor disruption of the ossicular chain in the middle ear cavity. Which of the following best describes the physiological consequence of losing the normal mechanical impedance-matching function provided by the middle ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes)?

options.A: Total abolition of nerve action potential generation in the spiral ganglion
options.B: Retrograde degeneration of the primary auditory cortex in Heschl's gyrus
options.C: Significant loss of acoustic wave amplification prior to reaching the fluid-filled cochlea
options.D: Selective loss of low-frequency sound transduction with complete preservation of high frequencies
options.E: Inability of stereocilia to hyperpolarize in response to mechanical deflection

explanation: Sound waves in air must be transmitted into perilymph within the inner ear. The middle ear ossicles and tympanic membrane function as an impedance-matching system, amplifying sound pressure ~20- to 30-fold (~30 dB). Disruption of ossicular continuity or eardrum perforation causes significant conductive hearing loss due to loss of acoustic amplification. Option (A) is incorrect because action potentials can still be generated if sound is amplified or conducted via bone; Option (B) does not occur; Option (D) causes generalized conductive loss; Option (E) is incorrect as hair cell mechanotransduction remains functional.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Point: Significant loss of acoustic wave amplification prior to reaching the fluid-filled cochlea
